Resort closed after Hurricane Irma (2017); reported reopened December 2024.

markers.name: Mustique, St. Vincent (The Mustique Company)
markers.ctx: About 1,400 acres. Colin Tennant developed it and gave Princess Margaret a 10-acre plot as a wedding present (1960) - a plot, never the island. In 1976 Tennant sold a 60% controlling interest in The Mustique Company to Venezuelan industrialists Hans Neumann and Alberto Vollmer. The island is owned by The Mustique Company, itself owned by the island's homeowners. No British royal has owned Mustique.

markers.name: Makepeace Island, Australia (Branson)
markers.ctx: Heart-shaped island in the Noosa River, Queensland, co-owned by Richard Branson and Virgin Australia co-founder Brett Godfrey; Branson's Australian home, let to up to 22 guests. His third private island, in another hemisphere.

markers.name: Great Saint James, USVI (Epstein)
markers.ctx: 165 acres. Bought by Jeffrey Epstein in January 2016 for about US$22.5 million (two purchases, $17.5M and $5M) through Great St. Jim LLC. The USVI sued his estate in 2020. In May 2023 Stephen Deckoff's SD Investments announced the purchase of Great and Little St. James for $60 million - see Little St. James. The estate holds neither island.

markers.name: Île Sainte-Marguerite, France (Man in the Iron Mask)
markers.ctx: Fort Royal prison - Man in the Iron Mask held here 1687-1698. Historical precedent: islands as both sanctuary and prison. Same geography protects the powerful and imprisons the inconvenient.

markers.name: Robben Island, South Africa (Mandela)
markers.ctx: Mandela imprisoned 18 years (1964-1982). Island-as-control pattern: powerful retreat to islands, inconvenient are confined on them. Same geography, inverse purpose.

markers.name: Poveglia, Venice, Italy
markers.ctx: Quarantine station for incoming ships and cargo from the late 18th century; from 1922 a long-term care facility, described as a psychiatric hospital, closed 1968, then state property. In 2025 the northern part was granted to the association Poveglia per tutti for a public park.

markers.name: Nauru - Mining + Detention Island
markers.ctx: 8.1 sq mi. Smallest republic. Phosphate mining stripped 80% of surface. Australia's offshore detention center - asylum seekers held on a stripped-mining island. Resource extraction and human containment share coordinates.

markers.name: Norman's Cay, Exumas, Bahamas
markers.ctx: Carlos Lehder used the island as the Medellín Cartel's transshipment base for cocaine flown into the US, 1978 to about 1982, extending the airstrip to about 1,000 m and guarding it with armed men and dogs.

markers.name: Four Seasons Mahé, Seychelles (Prince–Dmitriev meeting, 11 Jan 2017)
markers.ctx: Erik Prince met Kirill Dmitriev (RDIF) on 11 January 2017 at the Four Seasons on Mahé, after an earlier meeting the same day at George Nader's villa; Nader advised the UAE crown prince. Prince called it a chance encounter; the Mueller report records it as arranged in advance. Meeting: documented. Purpose: contested.

markers.name: Buck Island, BVI (The Aerial BVI)
markers.ctx: Private island off Tortola, site of the BVI's first airstrip; developed by Carl and Sharon Nilsen 1998-2008, now run as The Aerial BVI wellness retreat. The island reporting links to Larry Page is Eustatia, not this one (see that marker).

markers.name: Kaua'i Estate, Hawaii (Zuckerberg)
markers.ctx: Mark Zuckerberg bought 700 acres on Kaua'i in 2014 and has built it into a 1,450-1,500-acre estate, spending at least $145 million. In January 2017 he filed quiet-title suits against hundreds of Native Hawaiian part-owners of small parcels inside it, then dropped them after criticism.

markers.name: The World Islands, Dubai
markers.ctx: About 300 artificial islands off Dubai shaped as a world map, built by Nakheel from 2003; work halted in the 2008 financial crisis and most islands remain undeveloped. The islands are sold as private real estate but remain UAE territory.

markers.name: Gruinard Island, Scotland
markers.ctx: UK anthrax bioweapons test by Porton Down scientists, 1942-43 (Operation Vegetarian). Quarantined for 48 years; decontamination with formaldehyde began in 1986 and the island was declared safe on 24 April 1990. Islands as zones where biological weapons can be tested beyond public view.

markers.name: Devil's Island, French Guiana
markers.ctx: French penal colony (Bagne de Cayenne), 1852-1953. Alfred Dreyfus, wrongly convicted of spying, was held on Devil's Island 1895-99. More than 80,000 prisoners were sent to the system; the vast majority never returned to France, many dying of disease and harsh conditions.

markers.name: Alcatraz Island, San Francisco
markers.ctx: Federal penitentiary 1934-63. Before that: military fortification and military prison. Native American occupation 1969-71. The island-as-prison pattern repeated across centuries and jurisdictions.

markers.name: Snake Island (Zmiinyi), Ukraine
markers.ctx: 'Russian warship, go f**k yourself.' Feb 24, 2022 - Ukrainian border guards defied Russian Navy cruiser Moskva. The cruiser later sank. Strategic Black Sea island fought over since antiquity.

markers.name: Île d'Arros & St Joseph Atoll, Seychelles (Save Our Seas Foundation)
markers.ctx: Private island since 1975 (Prince Shahram Pahlavi Nia of Iran); bought by L'Oréal heiress Liliane Bettencourt in 1998 for US$18M; sold in Aug 2012 with St Joseph Atoll for US$60M, to be managed by the Save Our Seas Foundation; nature reserve since 2014. SOSF was founded in Geneva in 2003 by Saudi businessman Abdulmohsen Abdulmalik Al-Sheikh - Al ash-Sheikh, the clerical family, not Al Saud. 1.71 km2 with an unpaved airstrip; St Joseph lies 2.3 km east across a 1 km channel and has no strip.

markers.name: Desroches Island, Seychelles (IDC / Four Seasons)
markers.ctx: Amirantes island about 50 km ESE of d'Arros, managed by the state-owned Islands Development Company (IDC). Paved airstrip of about 1,372 m, the longest in the group. Resort sold to Four Seasons in 2016. IDC houses the Island Conservation Society's centre here. The runway is state logistics, not a private strip.

markers.name: Poivre Atoll, Seychelles (IDC)
markers.ctx: Amirantes atoll about 37 km south of d'Arros, managed by the state-owned Islands Development Company. Unpaved airstrip of about 1,100 m on Poivre Nord, served occasionally by IDC aircraft. Former coconut plantation. Coordinates approximate (atoll centroid).

markers.name: Rémire (Eagle) Island, Seychelles (IDC)
markers.ctx: Amirantes island about 33 km north of d'Arros. Paved airstrip of about 460 m (ICAO FSSR), the shortest in the group. Reserved as a presidential retreat until 2010; since then run by the state-owned IDC, which opened a small guest house in 2012.

markers.name: Marie Louise Island, Seychelles (IDC)
markers.ctx: Southern Amirantes, about 86 km SSW of d'Arros. Unpaved airstrip of about 550 m (ICAO FSMA), no regular air service. Managed by the state-owned IDC; about 11 residents, most of them IDC staff.

markers.name: Islands Development Company (IDC), Victoria, Mahé
markers.ctx: Seychelles government-owned parastatal, established 29 April 1980, that manages the outer islands and Silhouette: Alphonse, Assomption, Astove, Coëtivy, Cosmoledo, Desnoeufs, Desroches, Farquhar, Ile Plate, Marie-Louise, Poivre, Providence, Rémire and Silhouette. Runs its own aviation department (Pointe Larue) and co-owns the supply vessel Enterprise II. Four of the five Amirantes airstrips are IDC-run state infrastructure: remote runways that look like private power from orbit are here a public logistics network. Head office: Ile du Port, Mahé (coordinates approximate).

markers.name: Eustatia Island, BVI (linked to Larry Page - attributed, unconfirmed)
markers.ctx: About 30 acres in North Sound near Virgin Gorda, close to Branson's Necker and Moskito. Held through BVI companies whose beneficial owners are not public; local reporting attributes it to Google co-founder Larry Page, who has never confirmed it. ATTRIBUTED, not documented.

markers.name: NYPD International Liaison post - Israel National Police Sharon District HQ, Kfar Saba
markers.ctx: The NYPD - a MUNICIPAL police force - has run permanent overseas liaison posts for two decades, 14 overseas and 3 domestic in the NYPD's own 2021 account, with detectives embedded inside foreign national police services. The Israel post opened around September 2012 NOT at the US Embassy but inside the Israel National Police Sharon District headquarters at Kfar Saba. Officers' salaries are public money; travel, housing and office costs are paid by the private New York City Police Foundation. No statute, local law, council resolution or published MOU creating the programme has been found and the NYPD has never cited one. The City Comptroller has never audited the Intelligence Division; the NYPD Inspector General, whose mandate expressly covers partnerships with other law-enforcement agencies, has published nothing on it in twelve years. COORDINATES APPROXIMATE (Kfar Saba).

markers.name: Laucala Island, Fiji (Red Bull / Mateschitz)
markers.ctx: About 12 km2 (roughly 2,970 acres). Bought in 2003 by Red Bull co-founder Dietrich Mateschitz (d. 2022) from the Forbes family heirs for GBP 7 million; now the Laucala resort, from about US$7,000 a night. Its earlier inhabitants had been moved to neighbouring Qamea.

markers.name: Guantánamo Bay, Cuba
markers.ctx: US naval base since 1903 under a lease Cuba signed under the Platt Amendment; since 1959 the Cuban government has called it imposed by force and illegal. Detention camp since January 2002: about 780 men held over its history, most never charged, designated 'enemy combatants' rather than POWs.

markers.name: Christmas Island, Australia
markers.ctx: Australian external territory, 2,600 km northwest of Perth. A temporary immigration detention centre opened in 2001; the North West Point centre has since been closed, reopened and used intermittently (empty as of 31 Dec 2023). Same offshore-processing policy as Nauru and Manus.

markers.name: Manus Island, Papua New Guinea
markers.ctx: Site of Australia's second offshore immigration detention centre (2001-2017), at Lombrum Naval Base on Los Negros Island, Manus Province: opened under the Pacific Solution, disused in the mid-2000s, reopened 2012, closed 2017. PNG hosted the people Australia would not land.

markers.name: Hashima Island (Gunkanjima), Japan
markers.ctx: Undersea coal mine bought by Mitsubishi in 1890; population peaked at 5,259 on 6.3 ha in 1959, among the densest ever recorded; abandoned 1974. Conscripted Korean civilians and Chinese prisoners of war did forced labour here from the 1930s to 1945. Listed by UNESCO in July 2015 on Japan's pledge to tell that history; the World Heritage Committee has since found the pledge unfulfilled, and Seoul calls Tokyo's 2020 information centre revisionist.

markers.name: Niihau, Hawaii (Robinson Family)
markers.ctx: 'The Forbidden Island.' 69.5 sq mi. Bought from King Kamehameha V in 1864 for $10,000 by Elizabeth Sinclair, whose descendants, the Robinsons, still own it. Population 84 (2020), Hawaiian-speaking. No paved roads, no running water, no power lines. Entry by invitation.

markers.name: Palmyra Atoll, Pacific (Nature Conservancy)
markers.ctx: The only incorporated US territory. Most of the land was bought in 2000 by The Nature Conservancy for US$30M from the Fullard-Leo family; now a wildlife refuge. Used in 1962 as an observation site for high-altitude nuclear tests over Johnston Atoll. Site of the 1974 Sea Wind case: the murder, and possible double murder, of a San Diego couple.

markers.name: Porthcurno, Cornwall, UK - Cable Landing Station
markers.ctx: Submarine cable station since 1870, when the first cable of the UK-India telegraph link landed here; eventually eleven cables radiated from Porthcurno (the All Red Line). Modern fibre systems still land on the Cornish coast, part of the UK's transatlantic chokepoint; GCHQ's Tempora cable access is documented at Bude, not here.

markers.name: Bude, Cornwall, UK - GCHQ Cable Tap
markers.ctx: GCHQ Bude - Tempora program intercept station. Snowden documents confirmed GCHQ taps submarine cables with 200+ probes, buffering 3 days of internet traffic and 30 days of metadata. Shared with NSA. The Five Eyes cables tap.

markers.name: Marseille, France - Cable Landing Hub
markers.ctx: Major Mediterranean cable landing hub connecting Europe to Africa, the Middle East and Asia. French press (L'Obs, 2015) reported DGSE intercept access at cable landings - attributed.

markers.name: Fujairah, UAE - Cable Landing Station
markers.ctx: Strategic Gulf cable landing point on the UAE's east coast, outside the Strait of Hormuz; FLAG and other Europe-Asia systems land here.

markers.name: Mumbai, India - TATA Landing Station
markers.ctx: Major South Asian submarine cable hub; Tata Communications operates landing stations here for systems including TGN-Eurasia and SEACOM.

markers.name: Singapore - Cable Landing Hub
markers.ctx: Southeast Asia's primary cable hub, with landing stations at Changi and Tuas among others. Singapore's position makes it a transit point for Asia-Pacific data - the digital Strait of Malacca.

markers.name: Tuas, Singapore - Equinix Cable Station
markers.ctx: Major cable landing for trans-Pacific and intra-Asian cables. Equinix data center colocation. Where submarine cables meet cloud infrastructure.

markers.name: Manasquan, New Jersey - TAT-14 Landing
markers.ctx: Transatlantic cable landing on the New Jersey coast; TAT-14 (BT, AT&T, Deutsche Telekom and others) landed at Tuckerton/Manasquan until it was retired on 15 Dec 2020.

markers.name: Tuckerton, New Jersey - Cable Landing
markers.ctx: Historic and active submarine cable landing on the New Jersey transatlantic corridor; TAT-14 landed here until its retirement on 15 Dec 2020.

markers.name: Long Island, New York - Cable Landing
markers.ctx: Multiple submarine cables terminate on Long Island's shores. Connects to Manhattan data centers. Dense concentration of transatlantic cable landings along the northeastern U.S. coast.

markers.name: Miami, Florida - AMPATH Cable Landing
markers.ctx: Americas cable hub. ARCOS, Bahamas Internet Cable System, and multiple Latin American cables terminate here. Connects North America to Caribbean, Central and South America. NAP of the Americas data center.

markers.name: Fortaleza, Brazil - Cable Landing
markers.ctx: South American cable hub. SACS (South Atlantic Cable System) connects directly to Angola. EllaLink connects to Europe. Brazil's northeastern coast is the landing point for South Atlantic cables.

markers.name: Luzon, Philippines - Cable Landing
markers.ctx: Major Asia-Pacific cable landing. Multiple cables including Asia-America Gateway (AAG) and Southeast Asia-Japan Cable (SJC). Strategic Pacific data hub.

markers.name: Lantau Island, Hong Kong - Cable Landing
markers.ctx: Hong Kong cable landing; Hong Kong is a principal international cable hub for southern China and Asia-Pacific.

markers.name: Busan, South Korea - Cable Landing
markers.ctx: East Asian cable hub; the Korea-Japan Cable Network and other regional systems land at Busan, connecting the peninsula to trans-Pacific backbones.

markers.name: Sydney, Australia - Cable Landing Hub
markers.ctx: Australia's primary cable landing area; Southern Cross lands at Alexandria and Brookvale, alongside other trans-Pacific systems. Australia is a Five Eyes member.

markers.name: Djibouti - Cable Chokepoint
markers.ctx: Critical submarine cable chokepoint - 10+ cables transit the Bab-el-Mandeb between Africa and Arabia and land or pass at Djibouti. Djibouti also hosts the US base Camp Lemonnier; the two are separate facilities.

markers.name: Egypt - Suez Canal Cable Corridor
markers.ctx: 15+ submarine cables cross Egyptian territory between the Mediterranean and Red Sea coasts. Cuts near Alexandria in January 2008 (SEA-ME-WE 4, FLAG) and in 2013 disrupted internet for millions in the Middle East and South Asia. Single geographic chokepoint for Europe-Asia data.

markers.name: Strait of Malacca - Cable Transit
markers.ctx: Critical strait transited by multiple Asia-Pacific submarine cables. Over 94,000 vessels a year (2008) carry about a quarter of the world's traded goods through the same chokepoint.

markers.name: Vladivostok, Russia - Polar Express cable terminus
markers.ctx: Pacific terminus of 'Polar Express', a proposed 12,650 km Arctic cable from Murmansk (Teriberka) to Vladivostok along the Northern Sea Route, decreed in October 2020 - a Russian route independent of Five Eyes chokepoints. An earlier ROTACS project did not proceed.

markers.name: Cape Canaveral / Kennedy Space Center, FL
markers.ctx: Primary US launch range. SpaceX launches Starlink from here (over 6,000 launched by May 2024); NRO reconnaissance satellites also launch from the Cape and Vandenberg.

markers.name: Vandenberg Space Force Base, CA
markers.ctx: West coast satellite launch facility. NRO, Space Force, and SpaceX launches. Starlink polar orbit launches. Military and commercial satellite infrastructure co-located.

markers.name: Buckley Space Force Base / ADF-C, Aurora, CO
markers.ctx: Aerospace Data Facility-Colorado (ADF-C) - NRO ground station at Buckley SFB, associated with Space Delta 20. Processes NRO satellite data. Reported (The Verge, 2019; attributed) to feed 'Sentient', a classified NRO system that uses automated tipping and cueing to retask satellites. NSA Colorado is on the same installation. Space Delta 4 (SBIRS missile warning).

markers.name: Schriever Space Force Base, Colorado Springs, CO
markers.ctx: GPS Master Control Station - operates the Global Positioning System constellation (24+ satellites), now under the US Space Force (formerly Air Force Space Command). The facility that controls global positioning for military and civilian use.

markers.name: Weilheim Ground Station, Bavaria, Germany
markers.ctx: DLR (German Aerospace Center) satellite tracking and control ground station supporting European and international missions. Galileo is controlled from Oberpfaffenhofen and Fucino, not here.

markers.name: Fucino Space Centre, Abruzzo, Italy
markers.ctx: Telespazio ground station. Controls Galileo (EU GPS alternative), COSMO-SkyMed (Italian military radar satellites), and commercial communications satellites. Europe's largest commercial satellite ground station.

markers.name: Svalbard Satellite Station (SvalSat), Arctic Norway
markers.ctx: Satellite ground station on Platåberget, Svalbard. With TrollSat in Antarctica, one of only two stations that can see low polar-orbiting satellites on every revolution. Customers include NASA, NOAA, ESA and EUMETSAT. About 2.4 km from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault.

markers.name: GCHQ Bude, Cornwall, UK - Satellite Intercept
markers.ctx: GCHQ satellite communications intercept station. Linked to Echelon. Taps Intelsat and other commercial satellite traffic. Dual-function: cable tap and satellite intercept at same facility.

markers.name: Starlink Gateway, Merrillan, WI
markers.ctx: SpaceX Starlink ground gateway station. Routes internet traffic between Starlink satellites and the terrestrial internet backbone. Musk's satellite network requires terrestrial ground stations - each one is a potential intercept point.

markers.name: Starlink Gateway, Conrad, MT
markers.ctx: SpaceX Starlink ground gateway, northern US. Starlink is the largest satellite constellation (6,000+ launched by May 2024), operated by SpaceX, which Musk controls.

markers.name: Eutelsat OneWeb Ground Station, Fairbanks, AK
markers.ctx: OneWeb low-Earth-orbit gateway. OneWeb (founded 2012, bankrupt 2020, recapitalised by Bharti Global and the UK government) merged into Eutelsat in 2023. Competitor to Starlink; Arctic ground station for polar-orbit coverage.

markers.name: Beijing Aerospace Command and Control Center, China
markers.ctx: Command centre for China's crewed (Shenzhou, Tiangong) and lunar (Chang'e) missions, in Haidian District. China's satellite tracking and control network, including BeiDou, is run from the Xi'an Satellite Control Center.

markers.name: Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan
markers.ctx: Soviet-era cosmodrome on Kazakh soil, leased to Russia until 2050. Soyuz crew launches to the ISS. Russia's military launches mostly use Plesetsk, and it is building Vostochny on its own territory.

markers.name: NRO Headquarters, Chantilly, VA
markers.ctx: National Reconnaissance Office - builds and operates US reconnaissance satellites. Its proliferated architecture added roughly 180+ SpaceX-built satellites by April 2025 (NROL-145). The Advanced Systems & Technology directorate runs 'Sentient', a classified system reported (The Verge, 2019; attributed) to use automated tipping and cueing to retask satellites; a retired CIA analyst described its aim as ingesting 'everything', from imagery to financial records.

markers.name: Aerospace Data Facility-East (ADF-E) / Area 58, Fort Belvoir, VA
markers.ctx: ADF-E, NRO ground station on Fort Belvoir, also known as Area 58 (formerly DCEETA). Reported (Bamford, Richelson) to manage KH-11 imagery and Lacrosse radar satellites. NGA's headquarters is on Fort Belvoir's North Area. About 19 miles from NRO headquarters.

markers.name: Aerospace Data Facility-Southwest (ADF-SW), White Sands, NM
markers.ctx: ADF-SW - NRO ground station inside White Sands Missile Range, one of three NRO ground stations in the continental US (with ADF-C and ADF-E), responsible for command and control of reconnaissance satellites. The range also includes the Trinity site (1945) and saw the first US launches of captured V-2s.

markers.name: BlackSky Technology, Herndon, VA
markers.ctx: BlackSky - commercial geospatial intelligence company with a high-revisit Earth-observation constellation; an NRO commercial imagery provider. Its Spectra AI platform is marketed as fusing satellite imagery with other data sources (company claims include data from 100M+ mobile devices - attributed). Herndon HQ is about 6 miles from NRO headquarters.

markers.name: Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), Westminster, CO
markers.ctx: Maxar split in October 2025: Maxar Intelligence became Vantor (Westminster, CO) and Maxar Space Systems became Lanteris (Palo Alto). Vantor operates the WorldView constellation and is a principal NRO commercial imagery supplier; the company says it provides '90% of the foundational GEOINT' used by the US government (company claim). About 20 miles from Buckley SFB/ADF-C.

markers.name: Planet Labs, San Francisco, CA
markers.ctx: Planet Labs - operates a large constellation of small Earth-observation satellites (Doves) with the stated goal of imaging Earth's landmass daily. Commercial imagery supplier to the US government. Unlike tasked spy satellites, it images continuously whether anyone asked or not.

markers.name: SpaceX Starshield / MILNET, Hawthorne, CA
markers.ctx: SpaceX headquarters. SpaceX's Starshield line builds satellites for the NRO, Space Development Agency and Space Force: at least 183 Starshield satellites launched by April 2025 (NROL-145). The same company operates the commercial Starlink constellation - same operator, factories and launch vehicles.

markers.name: Kolwezi, DRC - Cobalt Mining
markers.ctx: Heart of the DRC cobalt belt (Lualaba). Glencore operates Kamoto Copper Company (KCC: Glencore 70%, Gécamines 25%, DRC state 5%, per KCC) and Mutanda (Glencore 95%), about 40 km east. The DRC mined about 73% of the world's cobalt in 2025 (USGS). Amnesty (2016) found children as young as seven in artisanal mining. The US Labor Department lists DRC cobalt for child labour (since 2009) and for forced labour of adults (2024), and lists Chinese lithium-ion batteries made with it (2024).

markers.name: Lubumbashi, DRC - Copper/Cobalt Hub
markers.ctx: Capital of Haut-Katanga and commercial hub of the copper-cobalt belt; seat of state miner Gécamines. Chinese firms, among them CMOC (Tenke Fungurume, in neighbouring Lualaba), are leading operators. The US Labor Department (2024) lists DRC cobalt for child labour and for forced labour of adults, 'prevalent ... in the Copperbelt region, particularly in Haut-Katanga and Lualaba.'

markers.name: Kipushi, DRC - Zinc/Copper Mine
markers.ctx: Underground zinc-copper mine (formerly Prince Léopold Mine), producing from the 1920s to 1993 under Belgian colonial and then Gécamines operation. Now Ivanhoe Mines 68%, Gécamines 32%.

markers.name: Salar de Atacama, Chile - Lithium Triangle
markers.ctx: Chile's largest salt flat; its core brine has the highest lithium concentration of any brine source (0.15% by weight). SQM and Albemarle, among the world's largest lithium producers, pump brine here. Water use is contested by the Likan Antay (Atacameño) communities around the salar.

markers.name: Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia - Lithium Triangle
markers.ctx: Largest salt flat on Earth (about 10,582 km2), over brine exceptionally rich in lithium; Bolivia keeps lithium under state control. In early November 2019 Evo Morales cancelled a lithium joint venture with Germany's ACI Systems; days later he resigned after a disputed election, an OAS audit reporting irregularities and calls from the military and police, and called it a coup. A shared timeline is not a chain: no document links the deal to his fall.

markers.name: Salta Province, Argentina - Lithium Triangle
markers.ctx: Argentine corner of the 'lithium triangle': salt flats across Argentina, Bolivia and Chile estimated in 2017 to hold about 54% of the world's lithium reserves. They are separate basins strung along a crescent from Salar de Surire (Chile) to Maricunga, not one formation, divided among three governments.

markers.name: Bayan Obo, Inner Mongolia, China - Rare Earths
markers.ctx: World's largest known rare-earth deposit. China mined about 69% of the world's rare earths in 2025 (USGS: 270,000 of 390,000 t). Rare earths go into fighter jets, guided missiles, satellites, smartphones and MRI machines - the material basis for Section X's surveillance technology and for military hardware.

markers.name: Mount Weld, Western Australia - Rare Earths
markers.ctx: Lynas Rare Earths' mine near Laverton. Its concentrate feeds Lynas's plant in Malaysia, the largest rare-earth production facility outside China. Australia's main bid to break China's hold on rare earths for defence and technology.

markers.name: Permian Basin, Texas/New Mexico - Oil & Gas
markers.ctx: Highest-producing oil field in the US (about 4.2 million barrels a day in 2019), across west Texas and southeast New Mexico. Major operators include ExxonMobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips. The shale boom here reshaped US energy policy - and powers the infrastructure documented in this report.

markers.name: Ghawar Field, Saudi Arabia - World's Largest Oil
markers.ctx: By far the largest conventional oil field in the world (about 280 x 30 km), roughly a third of Saudi Arabia's cumulative oil output. Operated by Saudi Aramco, listed on 11 Dec 2019 at about $1.9 trillion and above $2 trillion the next day. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, an Aramco shareholder, put a reported $2 billion into Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners.

markers.name: Groningen Gas Field, Netherlands
markers.ctx: Largest natural-gas field in Europe, producing from 1963. Extraction caused subsidence and, from 1991, induced earthquakes (largest: M3.6 at Huizinge, 2012) that damaged houses across the province; the National Ombudsman called it a 'national crisis' (2021). The field was closed in 2024.

markers.name: Niger Delta, Nigeria - Oil Extraction
markers.ctx: Shell, ExxonMobil and Chevron have pumped oil here since the 1950s amid repeated spills. Ken Saro-Wiwa, writer and leader of the Ogoni campaign against Shell's pollution, was hanged with eight others on 10 November 1995 after a special military tribunal convicted them of murders they denied; the trial was condemned internationally. The writer killed for documenting the extraction.

markers.name: Grasberg Mine, Papua, Indonesia
markers.ctx: Copper-gold mine run by PT Freeport Indonesia (Indonesian state 51.23%, Freeport-McMoRan 48.77% since 2018), on Amungme and Kamoro land. Between 1998 and 2004 Freeport paid Indonesian military and police nearly $20 million (NYT, 2005). Norway's pension fund excluded Freeport and Rio Tinto over its environmental damage. Henry Kissinger sat on Freeport's board (attributed).

markers.name: Carajás Mine, Pará, Brazil - Iron Ore
markers.ctx: Vale's Carajás complex, the largest iron ore mine in the world. Same company: Vale's Brumadinho tailings dam in Minas Gerais collapsed on 25 Jan 2019, killing 272 people; Vale managers and TÜV SÜD engineers who had certified the dam were arrested, and prosecutors allege the risk was known (allegation, not a finding).

markers.name: Oyu Tolgoi, Mongolia - Copper/Gold
markers.ctx: Copper-gold mine in the Gobi: Rio Tinto (via Turquoise Hill) 66%, Government of Mongolia 34%. Development cost rose from US$4.6bn (2010) to about $10bn (2013). Herders say it drains the region's water - it uses over a billion gallons a month. Rio Tinto also destroyed the Juukan Gorge rock shelters in Western Australia, with 46,000 years of human occupation, in May 2020.

markers.name: Cerrejón, Colombia - Coal Mine
markers.ctx: Largest coal mine in Latin America (over 690 km2), now owned by Glencore (formerly shared with BHP and Anglo American). In June 2020 lawyers for local Wayuu communities asked the UN special rapporteur to halt work over environmental harm; stream diversions for expansion are contested.

markers.name: Escondida Mine, Chile - Copper
markers.ctx: World's largest copper mine (about 1.28 million tonnes of copper in 2024, roughly 5% of world mine output). BHP 57.5%, Rio Tinto 30%, Japanese partners 12.5%. Copper for wiring, circuit boards, data centres and submarine cables.

markers.name: South China Sea - Offshore Drilling
markers.ctx: Disputed maritime territory with hydrocarbon reserves of contested size. China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei have overlapping claims. China has built artificial islands with military facilities. Source: Wikipedia, Territorial disputes in the South China Sea.

markers.name: Arctic - Drilling Frontier
markers.ctx: Arctic oil and gas development by Russia (Gazprom, Rosneft) and Norway (Equinor) in the Barents region expands as sea ice retreats.

markers.name: Kola Superdeep Borehole, Russia
markers.ctx: Deepest human-made hole: 12,262 m true vertical depth, reached 1989. Drilling from 1970; stopped 1992 at 180°C against ~100°C expected; closed 1995. Penetrated about a third of the Baltic Shield crust; microscopic plankton fossils found 6 km down.

markers.name: Dulce, New Mexico - Archuleta Mesa
markers.ctx: Alleged underground base beneath Archuleta Mesa on the Jicarilla Apache Nation reservation - a claim with no documentary support at any tier. About 80 miles north of Los Alamos National Laboratory.

markers.name: Camp Hero / Montauk AFS, Long Island
markers.ctx: Montauk Air Force Station (Camp Hero), 1942-1981. Joined SAGE in 1958; its AN/FPS-35 radar (126-ft reflector) became operational in 1960 and was abandoned in place when the station closed in January 1981. The 'Montauk Project' mind-control story is folklore with no documentary support.

markers.name: Plum Island Animal Disease Center
markers.ctx: USDA Plum Island Animal Disease Center (1954 - September 2025): foot-and-mouth and other foreign animal disease research. The Army Chemical Corps had reactivated Fort Terry in 1952; Cold War anti-livestock bioweapons research there ended in 1969. Its work moved to NBAF, Manhattan, Kansas.

markers.name: Brookhaven National Laboratory, Long Island
markers.ctx: DOE national laboratory. Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC, operating from 2000), one of the world's two operating heavy-ion colliders; site of the planned Electron-Ion Collider. Particle and nuclear physics, nanotechnology.

markers.name: Hollywood, Los Angeles
markers.ctx: Entertainment industry as cultural manufacturing. Carl Bernstein (Rolling Stone, 1977) reported that more than 400 US journalists had carried out assignments for the CIA; the CIA's 'Project Mockingbird' was a separate 1963 wiretap of two columnists. Some 1960s musicians had military fathers - Jim Morrison's father commanded US naval forces during the Gulf of Tonkin incident; Frank Zappa's father worked at the Edgewood Arsenal chemical-warfare facility. No mechanism linking those families to the counterculture is documented.

markers.name: Burbank - Lockheed Skunk Works / Studios
markers.ctx: Lockheed operated in Burbank 1928-1994; the Skunk Works (from 1943) designed the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 here. ALSO: Warner Bros, Walt Disney Studios, NBC/Universal. The city that built stealth aircraft builds entertainment content - same zip code, different product lines. THE EXIT, DATED: Skunk Works headquarters moved to Palmdale in 1992; the Burbank shutdown completed in 1994. Burbank kept the visible image industry and lost the invisible one. WHAT STAYED: the site sits inside the San Fernando Valley Superfund site, listed 1986 (Burbank Operable Unit) - TCE, PCE, hexavalent chromium and 1,4-dioxane in groundwater, with roughly 3.3 billion gallons treated and returned to municipal supply annually. THE OTHER HALF OF THE SENTENCE: Burbank built the airframe; Rochester, NY made and processed the film it carried (see Kodak Hawkeye Works). Sources: EPA San Fernando Valley Superfund record; Lockheed Burbank plant histories.

markers.name: Glendale, California
markers.ctx: DreamWorks Animation HQ (1000 Flower Street). Forest Lawn Memorial Park - burial ground of many entertainment-industry figures. Nestle USA was headquartered here until its 2017-18 move to Arlington, Virginia.

markers.name: Laurel Canyon, Los Angeles
markers.ctx: Lookout Mountain Air Force Station - classified US Air Force film studio (1947-1969) that produced films of nuclear tests and military operations. It sat above the canyon that became a centre of the 1960s music scene; no documented link between the studio and the musicians.

markers.name: Fayetteville, North Carolina - Bledsoe Encounters
markers.ctx: Chris Bledsoe reports UAP/NHI encounters near Fayetteville from 2007 - testimony tier (evidence of an experience, not of a cause). Fayetteville adjoins Fort Bragg (named Fort Liberty 2023-25), home of the 82nd Airborne, JSOC and Delta Force.

markers.name: Esalen Institute, Big Sur, California
markers.ctx: Human potential movement centre (founded 1962). John C. Lilly, inventor of the isolation tank, taught here; in 1974 he described an 'Earth Coincidence Control Office' (ECCO) - a hierarchy he believed arranges coincidences.

markers.name: Fullerton, CA - Philip K. Dick / VALIS
markers.ctx: Philip K. Dick (1928-1982). Fiction adapted as Blade Runner, Minority Report, A Scanner Darkly, Total Recall, The Man in the High Castle, The Adjustment Bureau. His home was burglarised in November 1971 (unsolved). In October 1972 he wrote to the FBI about Thomas Disch. In February-March 1974 ('2-3-74'), after sodium pentothal given for a wisdom-tooth extraction, he experienced visions he called VALIS and wrote the Exegesis, whose recurring thesis is that 'the Empire never ended'. Donated his papers to Cal State Fullerton; died in Santa Ana, 1982.

markers.name: HAARP, Gakona, Alaska
markers.ctx: High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program. 3.6 MW, 180 antenna array. Originally DARPA/Air Force/Navy. Transferred to University of Alaska Fairbanks (2015). Ionospheric heater: communications disruption, over-the-horizon radar, ELF submarine communication. Transfer to university changed FOIA jurisdiction, not capability.

markers.name: Clear Space Force Station, Alaska
markers.ctx: AN/FPS-132 UEWR missile warning radar. NORAD ballistic missile detection. Ground-based midcourse defense architecture. Northern early warning line.

markers.name: Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska
markers.ctx: NORAD Alaska Region. Pacific Air Forces (11th Air Force). U.S. Army Alaska. Primary Arctic airpower projection. Joint base combining Air Force and Army at Alaska's population center.

markers.name: Fort Greely, Alaska - Missile Defense
markers.ctx: Ground-based Midcourse Defense (GMD) operational interceptors. Anti-ballistic missile shield's northern component. The missiles that defend against missiles, stationed in permafrost.

markers.name: Eareckson AFS, Shemya Island, Alaska
markers.ctx: Aleutian Islands intelligence station. Cobra Dane phased-array radar (from 1977), built for treaty-verification intelligence on Soviet missile tests; also used by Cobra Ball missile-monitoring aircraft. The listening post at the western end of the Aleutian chain.

markers.name: McMurdo Station, Antarctica (US)
markers.ctx: Ross Island. Largest community in Antarctica - ~1,000 in summer, up to 1,200. Run by the NSF's U.S. Antarctic Program with military logistics (Operation Deep Freeze); harbour and airfields. PM-3A nuclear reactor 1962-1972, removed after leaks. The Antarctic Treaty permits military personnel and equipment for scientific or peaceful purposes.

markers.name: Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station (US)
markers.ctx: Geographic South Pole. NSF research station; IceCube Neutrino Observatory uses the 2-mile ice sheet to detect neutrinos. Supplied by New York Air National Guard LC-130 flights from McMurdo.

markers.name: Vostok Station, Antarctica (Russia)
markers.ctx: Lowest reliably measured temperature on Earth: −89.2°C (21 July 1983). Russian drilling reached subglacial Lake Vostok, sealed under ~4 km of ice for an estimated 15-25 million years.

markers.name: Concordia Station, Antarctica (France/Italy)
markers.ctx: Dome C, East Antarctic Plateau. ESA Mars conditions analog - testing Mars habitation protocols in Antarctica. The space agency rehearses planetary colonization at the bottom of this planet.

markers.name: Rothera Station, Antarctica (UK)
markers.ctx: Adelaide Island. British Antarctic Survey's main station, with a 900 m crushed-rock runway, hangar and wharf - the logistics hub for UK Antarctic flights.

markers.name: Palmer Station, Antarctica (US)
markers.ctx: Anvers Island, Antarctic Peninsula. Marine and terrestrial biology. The only U.S. Antarctic station north of the Antarctic Circle.

markers.name: Pine Island Glacier, Antarctica
markers.ctx: Fastest-melting glacier in Antarctica, about 13% of the continent's ice loss. Pine Island and neighbouring ice streams would raise sea level about 1.5 m if lost, and their loss would destabilise the West Antarctic Ice Sheet. Monitored by satellite.

markers.name: Ramstein Air Base, Germany
markers.ctx: HQ USAFE-AFAFRICA. Reported since 2014 (NDR, WDR, Sueddeutsche; Snowden documents) as a satellite relay for U.S. drone operations in Yemen, Somalia and Pakistan; Yemeni families sued Germany over it in 2019. The Kaiserslautern Military Community houses about 54,000 U.S. service members.

markers.name: Aviano Air Base, Italy
markers.ctx: 31st Fighter Wing. NATO forward deployment for Mediterranean and Middle East operations. Used in Kosovo, Libya, Afghanistan campaigns. Southern European power projection.

markers.name: Naval Support Activity Naples, Italy
markers.ctx: U.S. Naval Forces Europe / Naval Forces Africa / Sixth Fleet headquarters. Commands naval operations across Europe and Africa from Italian soil.

markers.name: NAS Sigonella, Sicily, Italy
markers.ctx: 'Hub of the Med.' Primary logistics and ISR hub for Mediterranean, North Africa, and Middle East. Drone operations base. The surveillance eye in the center of the Mediterranean.

markers.name: RAF Lakenheath, Suffolk, UK
markers.ctx: 48th Fighter Wing - F-15E and, since 2021, F-35A. 2024 contracts for nuclear-weapons storage facilities; July 2025 flight evidence suggested B61-12 bombs were delivered (unconfirmed by the U.S. or UK).

markers.name: Naval Station Rota, Spain
markers.ctx: Forward base for Aegis BMD destroyers - four, expanding to six under a 2022 agreement signed May 2023. Supports Sixth Fleet operations at the Atlantic-Mediterranean gateway.

markers.name: Souda Bay, Crete, Greece
markers.ctx: NATO and Hellenic Navy base; deep, naturally protected harbour whose K-14 quay is the only Mediterranean pier able to berth supercarriers. U.S. munitions and logistics hub for the eastern Mediterranean.

markers.name: Camp Bondsteel, Kosovo
markers.ctx: Built 1999 by U.S. Army engineers with Kellogg Brown and Root, then a Halliburton subsidiary; Dick Cheney was Halliburton CEO 1995-2000 before becoming Vice President in 2001. 955 acres; KBR also ran camp operations.

markers.name: Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base), Greenland
markers.ctx: Northernmost U.S. base; renamed Pituffik Space Base 6 April 2023. Ballistic-missile early warning and space surveillance. Project Iceworm (1959-67) planned mobile nuclear missile sites under the ice, tested at Camp Century; Denmark never consented and the plan came to light only in 1995.

markers.name: Aegis Ashore, Deveselu, Romania
markers.ctx: U.S. Aegis Ashore missile-defence site, operational May 2016. Its Mk 41 launchers are of a type that can fire Tomahawks, but the U.S. says these are configured for SM-3 interceptors only; Russia cites the site as an offensive threat.

markers.name: Aegis Ashore, Redzikowo, Poland
markers.ctx: Second European Aegis Ashore site, opened summer 2024, about 155 km from the Kaliningrad exclave border. Mk 41 launchers configured for SM-3 interceptors; Russia claims they could fire cruise missiles.

markers.name: Kelley Barracks, Stuttgart - U.S. AFRICOM HQ
markers.ctx: Kelley Barracks (Stuttgart-Mohringen): headquarters of U.S. Africa Command since its activation 1 Oct 2008, responsible for 53 African nations (all but Egypt) from European soil. U.S. European Command sits nearby at Patch Barracks.

markers.name: Landstuhl Regional Medical Center, Germany
markers.ctx: Largest American hospital outside the United States; the main treatment stop for U.S. wounded evacuated from Middle East and African theatres.

markers.name: Grafenwöhr Training Area, Germany
markers.ctx: Largest U.S. military training area in Europe. 232 sq km. Used continuously since 1910 - through both World Wars, Cold War, and present. American soldiers train on the same Bavarian ground the Imperial German Army used.

markers.name: Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar
markers.ctx: Combined Air Operations Center (CAOC) - commands all U.S. air operations across Middle East. 10,000+ U.S. personnel. Qatar hosts both Al Udeid AND Al Jazeera - the base that commands the bombing and the network that broadcasts it in the same 4,468 sq mi country.

markers.name: Camp Arifjan, Kuwait
markers.ctx: U.S. Army Central (ARCENT) forward headquarters. Third Army. Largest ground force concentration in the Middle East. Pre-positioned equipment for rapid regional deployment.

markers.name: NSA Bahrain - U.S. Fifth Fleet HQ
markers.ctx: Commander, Naval Forces Central Command / U.S. Fifth Fleet. Controls naval operations from the Suez Canal to the Strait of Hormuz. Based in a Sunni-ruled kingdom with a Shia majority population.

markers.name: Incirlik Air Base, Turkey
markers.ctx: NATO nuclear-weapons storage - up to 50 B61 bombs (estimate). Host-nation access has been a recurring point of leverage, notably after the 2016 coup attempt.

markers.name: Al Dhafra Air Base, UAE
markers.ctx: UAE Air Force fighter wing, French Air and Space Force fighter squadron (EC 1/7 Provence) and the U.S. 380th Air Expeditionary Wing, which flies RQ-4 Global Hawk and U-2 reconnaissance aircraft.

markers.name: Air Base 201, Agadez, Niger
markers.ctx: U.S. drone base (MQ-9), cost over $100 million. After the July 2023 coup Niger ended military cooperation (March 2024); the last U.S. troops left on 5 Aug 2024 and the base was handed to Niger the next day.

markers.name: Camp Humphreys, South Korea
markers.ctx: Largest U.S. overseas military base: $11 billion, 3,454 acres, USFK and UN Command headquarters (consolidation completed 2018). About 70 miles south of the DMZ.

markers.name: Osan Air Base, South Korea
markers.ctx: 51st Fighter Wing and Seventh Air Force HQ, near Pyeongtaek, 40 miles south of Seoul and about 60 miles from the DMZ.

markers.name: Fleet Activities Yokosuka, Japan
markers.ctx: Home port of the U.S. Seventh Fleet. Forward-deployed carrier strike group. The only forward-deployed U.S. carrier is based in Japan. Commands the Pacific from another nation's harbor.

markers.name: Kadena Air Base, Okinawa, Japan
markers.ctx: Largest and most active USAF base in East Asia; 18th Wing. Okinawa, about 0.6% of Japan's land, hosts about 70% of the land used exclusively by U.S. forces in Japan.

markers.name: MCAS Futenma, Okinawa, Japan
markers.ctx: Marine Corps Air Station in the middle of Ginowan city. Called the most dangerous base in the world (attributed to Donald Rumsfeld, 2003). Relocation agreed in 1996; still operating in 2026.

markers.name: Yokota Air Base, Tokyo, Japan
markers.ctx: USFJ headquarters and Fifth Air Force. Located in western Tokyo - the capital of a sovereign nation hosts foreign military command. Yokota controls the airspace over greater Tokyo. Japanese commercial aircraft route around U.S. military airspace over their own capital.

markers.name: Andersen AFB + Naval Base Guam
markers.ctx: Pacific power-projection hub; the only Western Pacific base able to permanently service heavy bombers (B-1B, B-2, B-52). Guam's delegate to Congress cannot vote on final passage.

markers.name: Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, Cuba
markers.ctx: 45 sq mi leased since 1903; the U.S. pays the equivalent of $4,085 a year, which Cuba has refused since 1959. Detention camp since 2002: at least 780 men held; 15 remained in January 2025. Boumediene v. Bush (2008) gave detainees habeas rights.

markers.name: Soto Cano Air Base, Honduras
markers.ctx: Joint Task Force-Bravo. U.S. military presence in Central America since Cold War. Same Honduras where ISA ran Operation Queens Hunter. Proximity to School of Americas graduates who governed the region.

markers.name: CFS Leitrim, Ottawa, Canada
markers.ctx: Canadian Forces Station Leitrim, south of Ottawa: Canada's oldest operational signals-intelligence collection station (1941), intercepting for CSE and part of the Five Eyes ECHELON system.

markers.name: Chinese Naval Support Base, Djibouti
markers.ctx: China's first overseas military base, in use from 1 Aug 2017; about 11 km from the U.S. Camp Lemonnier.

markers.name: Fiery Cross Reef, South China Sea (China)
markers.ctx: Artificial island on submerged reef. 3,000m runway, hangars, radar, missile systems. The Hague ruled China's claims have 'no legal basis' (2016). China rejected the ruling.

markers.name: Naval Facility Tartus, Syria (Russia)
markers.ctx: Soviet/Russian naval facility from 1971; from 2011 Russia's only naval base outside the former USSR. After the Assad government fell in Dec 2024 Russian ships withdrew (by Feb 2025); the base's future is unsettled.

markers.name: Khmeimim Air Base, Syria (Russia)
markers.ctx: Russian air base from September 2015 (Su-24, Su-34, Su-35). After the Assad government fell in Dec 2024 Russia stayed in reduced form; on 9 Aug 2026 Syria announced the base would become a joint training centre under Syrian civil control of the airport.

markers.name: Denver International Airport (DIA)
markers.ctx: Opened 28 Feb 1995, 16 months late, at a cost of $4.8B - nearly $2B over budget. 33,531 acres. Dedication capstone dated March 19, 1994 ('New World Airport Commission'). Blue Mustang ('Blucifer'), 32 ft, killed its sculptor Luis Jiménez when a section fell on him. Automated underground baggage system abandoned. Leo Tanguma murals.

markers.name: Dulles International Airport (IAD), Virginia
markers.ctx: About 17 miles (27 km) from CIA headquarters at Langley. Named for John Foster Dulles, Secretary of State and brother of CIA Director Allen Dulles (Iran 1953, Guatemala 1954 coups; plot against Lumumba in Congo). Rendition aircraft reported to have used Dulles (attributed).

markers.name: Shannon Airport, Ireland - Rendition Transit
markers.ctx: Amnesty International (2006): four CIA-operated aircraft used in renditions stopped at Shannon at least 77 times since 2001 - second in Europe after Frankfurt. The Rendition Project and Reprieve later identified 11 planes (2002-04) possibly on rendition circuits and 16 more (2002-06) linking secret prisons. Ireland did not search them.

markers.name: Palma de Mallorca Airport, Spain - Rendition Transit
markers.ctx: Documented CIA rendition flight hub. Jeppesen Dataplan (Boeing subsidiary, Denver-based) provided flight planning for rendition aircraft. European Parliament investigation confirmed rendition flights through Spanish territory.

markers.name: Johnston Atoll, Pacific - Chemical/Military
markers.ctx: Remote Pacific atoll ~1,330 km WSW of Honolulu. U.S. nuclear tests (1958, 1962); biological-weapons testing; storage and destruction of chemical weapons until 2000. Now a National Wildlife Refuge, with plutonium clean-up on record.

markers.name: Groom Lake / Area 51 Airstrip, Nevada
markers.ctx: CIA/USAF classified flight test facility. U-2, A-12 (OXCART) and F-117 tested here. JANET flights carry workers from Las Vegas. CIA publicly acknowledged the base on 25 June 2013 through a FOIA release. On land the Western Shoshone hold was never ceded under the 1863 Treaty of Ruby Valley (their position).

markers.name: Tora Bora, Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan
markers.ctx: Spin Ghar (White Mountains) cave complex: natural caverns later expanded into a CIA-financed mujahideen base. In 2001 Western media described an 'impregnable cave fortress' with hydroelectric power and hospitals; after the battle no trace of such a fortress was found. Bin Laden escaped to Pakistan in December 2001.

markers.name: Zhawar Kili, Khost Province, Afghanistan
markers.ctx: Mujahideen base complex near the Pakistan border, built in the Soviet-Afghan war (CIA/ISI support, attributed). Tunnels and caves struck by U.S. cruise missiles in August 1998 (Operation Infinite Reach) and bombed again in January 2002, when SEALs found 50+ tunnels.

markers.name: Khost-Gardez Pass (K-G Pass), Afghanistan
markers.ctx: Mountain road between Khost and Gardez, contested in turn by Soviet, mujahideen, Taliban and U.S. forces. FOB Chapman (CIA) near Khost: suicide bombing on 30 Dec 2009 killed seven Americans, CIA officers and contractors.

markers.name: Khyber Pass, Pakistan-Afghanistan Border
markers.ctx: Mountain pass between Peshawar and Afghanistan, summit 1,070 m. Route for successive invasions and supply lines - Mughal, British, Soviet-era interdiction, NATO supply route. The geography does not change, only the uniforms.

markers.name: Shamsi Airfield (CIA Drone Base), Balochistan, Pakistan
markers.ctx: Airstrip leased to the U.S. 20 Oct 2001 - 11 Dec 2011 for joint CIA/USAF Predator operations against militants in Pakistan's tribal areas. Pakistan ordered the U.S. out on 26 Nov 2011 after the Salala strike killed 24 Pakistani soldiers.

markers.name: Củ Chi Tunnels, Vietnam
markers.ctx: Viet Cong tunnel network (~250 km) with hospitals, command posts and living quarters. U.S. and Australian 'tunnel rat' specialists fought inside; tunnels were attacked with gas, water, explosives and bombing.

markers.name: Vịnh Mốc Tunnels, Quảng Trị, Vietnam
markers.ctx: Village of about sixty families moved underground to survive U.S. bombing, 1966 - early 1972. Three levels, down to 30 m. As many as 17 children were born inside; no villager died in the tunnels.

markers.name: CERN Large Hadron Collider, Geneva
markers.ctx: 27 km particle accelerator in a tunnel up to 175 m beneath the France-Switzerland border. First collisions 2010; Higgs boson discovery announced 2012. Total cost estimated at $13.25B (press estimate).

markers.name: Gotthard Base Tunnel, Switzerland
markers.ctx: World's longest railway tunnel: 57.09 km, up to 2,300m below the Alps. Opened 2016, cost CHF 12.2B. Opening ceremony widely discussed for its theatrical production. Connects northern and southern Europe's rail logistics through the mountain the Swiss built their National Redoubt inside.

markers.name: Channel Tunnel (Chunnel), UK-France
markers.ctx: 50.45 km, up to 75 m below the seabed; two rail tunnels and a service tunnel; the longest undersea section of any tunnel. Opened 1994.

markers.name: CFB North Bay - NORAD Underground, Ontario
markers.ctx: Canadian NORAD Underground Complex, 60 storeys (~600 ft) underground. Built 1959-63; operations from 1 Oct 1963 until October 2006, when air-defence operations moved to a new surface building. Regional HQ moved to Winnipeg in 1997.

markers.name: CFS Alert, Nunavut, Canada
markers.ctx: Northernmost permanently inhabited place on Earth. 817 km from North Pole. Signals intelligence station - Five Eyes Arctic SIGINT. Closer to Moscow than to Ottawa. The listening post at the top of the world.

markers.name: CFB Suffield / DRDC Suffield, Alberta
markers.ctx: Largest army training area in Canada (~2,690 km²); home of the British Army Training Unit Suffield. Expropriated in 1941 for British chemical-warfare experiments. DRDC Suffield is Canada's lead laboratory for chemical and biological defence research.

markers.name: CFS Debert Emergency Government HQ, Nova Scotia
markers.ctx: Regional Emergency Government Headquarters ('Diefenbunker') of CFS Debert, built in the 1960s; CFS Debert closed in the mid-1990s and was decommissioned in 1998. (HMCS Trinity, the naval ocean-surveillance unit, is at CFB Halifax.)

markers.name: CFB Esquimalt, British Columbia
markers.ctx: Royal Canadian Navy Pacific fleet headquarters. Maritime Forces Pacific. Nanoose Bay torpedo testing range. Canadian Pacific naval projection - the other Five Eyes navy on the Pacific Rim.

markers.name: Churchill, Manitoba - Northern Port
markers.ctx: Hudson Bay deep-water port (four Panamax-capable berths) linked south only by the Hudson Bay Railway; open roughly late July to early November. The federal government sold it to US firm OmniTRAX in 1997; OmniTRAX shut it in 2016 and sold port and railway in 2018 to Arctic Gateway Group, a First Nations and community consortium. Grain and Arctic resupply are its trade; ships reach it through Hudson Strait, not the Northwest Passage.

markers.name: Canadian Forces Station St. John's, Newfoundland
markers.ctx: Canadian Forces Station St. John's - armed-forces garrison in St. John's (since 1949). Newfoundland has historically been a landing point for transatlantic cables.

markers.name: Rideau Canal / Parliamentary Precinct Tunnels, Ottawa
markers.ctx: Rideau Canal (UNESCO, 2007): built 1826-32 under Lt-Col John By as a military supply route avoiding the St Lawrence in case of U.S. invasion. 202 km. In winter part of it is a skating rink.

markers.name: Severomorsk - Northern Fleet HQ, Russia
markers.ctx: Headquarters of the Russian Northern Fleet: nuclear submarine force and surface fleet. Ice-free Kola Gulf (Gulf Stream). Submarine bases at Polyarny, Gadzhiyevo and Vidyayevo nearby; Murmansk is the regional port city.

markers.name: Kaliningrad, Russia - Baltic Exclave
markers.ctx: Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania. Iskander nuclear-capable missiles; Baltic Fleet HQ. Konigsberg until 1945 (renamed 1946). The Suwalki Gap - the ~65 km Polish-Lithuanian border between Kaliningrad and Belarus - is NATO's most exposed corridor.

markers.name: Sevastopol, Crimea - Black Sea Fleet
markers.ctx: Black Sea Fleet base since 1783 and its HQ, with Novorossiysk. Cold War submarine base carved into the mountain at Balaklava. Besieged in the Crimean War (1854-55); annexed by Russia in 2014.

markers.name: Novosibirsk - Akademgorodok, Russia
markers.ctx: 'Science City' - founded 1957 under the USSR Academy of Sciences in the Siberian forest near Novosibirsk. 35 research institutes and Novosibirsk State University; at its peak home to 65,000 scientists and their families. Never a closed city.

markers.name: Chelyabinsk-40 / Ozersk, Russia (Mayak)
markers.ctx: Mayak plutonium complex. Kyshtym disaster (1957), the only INES Level 6 accident and third-worst after Chernobyl and Fukushima: 270,000+ people affected, 10,000-12,000 evacuated. Waste dumped in the Techa River and Lake Karachay, once lethal within an hour at its shore; the lake has since been infilled. Closed city.

markers.name: Krasnoyarsk-26 / Zheleznogorsk, Russia
markers.ctx: Mining and Chemical Combine: plutonium reactors built in caverns in a granite mountain (AD 1958, ADE-1 1961, ADE-2 1965; last shut 2010); now stores spent fuel. The closed city also hosts ISS Reshetnev, Russia's largest satellite maker.

markers.name: Perm-36, Ural Region, Russia
markers.ctx: Soviet forced-labour colony ITK-6 near Kuchino, built 1946; from 1972 a strict- and special-regime camp for 'especially dangerous state criminals', mostly dissidents. Closed December 1987. Preserved by Memorial as the only surviving Gulag camp and opened in 1995 as the Museum of the History of Political Repression; regional authorities withdrew support and the NGO museum closed in April 2014. Its state-run successor was reported to recast the camp's history (attributed).

markers.name: Kapustin Yar, Astrakhan Oblast, Russia
markers.ctx: Soviet rocket test range established 13 May 1946 using technology and specialists taken from defeated Germany; early Soviet ballistic-missile launches. Russia's original missile range.

markers.name: Pavlovsk Bay (near Vladivostok) - Pacific Fleet submarine base
markers.ctx: Pacific Fleet submarine base near Vladivostok. The Pacific SSBN force - Borei-class boats with Bulava missiles (6 MIRVs each) - is based at Rybachiy, Vilyuchinsk, on Kamchatka.

markers.name: Sarov / Arzamas-16, Russia (VNIIEF)
markers.ctx: VNIIEF (formerly KB-11), Russia's nuclear-weapons design centre - the Soviet 'Los Alamos'. RDS-1 atomic bombs were produced here. Closed town of ~92,000 (2010 census); entry by permit.

markers.name: Novaya Zemlya, Arctic Russia - Nuclear Test Site
markers.ctx: Arctic nuclear test range: 224 detonations (1955-1990), ~265 Mt total. Tsar Bomba (30 Oct 1961), 50 Mt - largest man-made explosion; blast wave circled the Earth three times; cloud ~67 km high; windowpanes broken up to 900 km away.

markers.name: Lubyanka Building, Moscow - FSB/KGB HQ
markers.ctx: FSB headquarters. Taken over by the Cheka in 1918; later OGPU, NKVD, KGB. Internal prison operational from 1920. Headquarters of the NKVD during Stalin's purges. Russia's civilian security services trace their lineage to this building.

markers.name: Plesetsk Cosmodrome, Arkhangelsk Oblast, Russia
markers.ctx: More orbital launches than any other site (over 1,500 by 1997). Built from 1957 as an R-7 ICBM base; space launches since 17 March 1966 (military satellites, GLONASS, Angara). The USSR did not admit it existed until 1983. Northernmost spaceport until Andoya (Norway) in 2025-26.

markers.name: Norilsk, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia
markers.ctx: Arctic mining city built by Gulag labour: Norillag held 1,200 prisoners in 1935 and 72,500 at its 1951 peak; Memorial estimates about 400,000 passed through. Nornickel is a leading producer of palladium and nickel. A closed city, re-closed to foreigners in 2001. No road link to the rest of Russia; freight rail runs only to the Yenisei port of Dudinka. Repeatedly listed among the world's most polluted places (attributed).

markers.name: Magadan, Russia - Gateway to the Gulag
markers.ctx: Port and base of Dalstroy (1931), which ran some 80 Gulag camps in Kolyma mining gold and other metals; its prisoner count reached about 200,000 (1952). The R504 Kolyma Highway (2,031 km), built by prisoners, is called the 'Road of Bones'; that the dead were buried in the roadbed is a popular account not confirmed by remains. 10,251 deaths were recorded in the Kolyma camps in 1938 alone; totals are contested. Mask of Sorrow by Ernst Neizvestny, unveiled 12 June 1996.

markers.name: Vorkuta, Komi Republic, Russia
markers.ctx: Arctic coal city built on Vorkutlag (1932-1962), one of the largest Gulag camps: about 73,000 prisoners at its 1951 peak. The July-August 1953 uprising at the Rechlag special camp, after Beria's arrest, was one of the major Gulag revolts; it was violently suppressed. Coal is still mined. Population fell from 115,646 (1989 census) to about 55,700 (2025 estimate).

markers.name: Semipalatinsk Test Site (The Polygon), Kazakhstan
markers.ctx: Soviet nuclear test site: 456 tests 1949-1989 (340 underground, 116 atmospheric), including the first Soviet bomb. ~18,000 km². Kazakh experts estimate 1.5 million people were exposed to fallout. Closed 29 August 1991.

markers.name: Kronstadt Naval Fortress, St. Petersburg, Russia
markers.ctx: Baltic Fleet base since 1704 (Peter the Great). Island fortress guarding St. Petersburg. 1921 Kronstadt Rebellion - sailors who made the Revolution revolted against it; crushed by Trotsky. Forts across the Gulf of Finland created kill zones for any naval approach. The fortress that guards the city that guards the Baltic.

markers.name: Severodvinsk / Sevmash, Arkhangelsk Oblast, Russia
markers.ctx: Sevmash - Russia's largest shipyard and today its only nuclear-submarine builder: Borei SSBNs, Yasen SSGNs and Belgorod (Poseidon carrier). Closed city.

markers.name: Nizhny Tagil - Uralvagonzavod, Russia
markers.ctx: Uralvagonzavod - largest main battle tank manufacturer in the world (T-72, T-90, T-14). Opened 11 Oct 1936 as a freight-car works; the Kharkiv tank factory was evacuated here in 1941. About 30,000 employees.

markers.name: Nogales, Arizona-Sonora - Tunnel Corridor
markers.ctx: Major narco-tunnel corridor. 130+ tunnels discovered since 1990. Storm drain system exploited for smuggling. Sinaloa and CJNG cartels. The tunnels they find and the tunnels they don't - border infrastructure as smuggling infrastructure.

markers.name: San Luis, Arizona - Tunnel Zone
markers.ctx: Cross-border tunnel zone on the Arizona-Sonora line. The 4,309-ft record tunnel (announced Jan 2020) ran from Tijuana to Otay Mesa, California, not here.

markers.name: Gaza Tunnel Network, Rafah Crossing
markers.ctx: Smuggling tunnels under the Egypt-Gaza border at Rafah, dug since the early 1980s, numbered about 1,200 before Egypt's military destroyed most of them in 2013-14. Hamas's combat tunnel network inside Gaza grew from that expertise; Israel's 2023-24 ground operation targeted it.

markers.name: Hezbollah Tunnel Network, Southern Lebanon
markers.ctx: Israel's Operation Northern Shield (Dec 2018 - Jan 2019) found and destroyed six Hezbollah cross-border attack tunnels from southern Lebanon.

markers.name: DMZ Tunnels, Korean Peninsula
markers.ctx: Four North Korean infiltration tunnels found since 15 Nov 1974. Third Tunnel: 1,635 m long, ~73 m deep; visitor information says it could move 30,000 men per hour. North Korea first denied it, then called it a coal mine; the rock is granite.

markers.name: Narco-Submarines - Pacific Coast, Colombia
markers.ctx: Semi-submersible and fully submersible vessels built in jungle workshops. Several tonnes of cocaine per trip is typical; the largest known load was 7.7 tonnes (2015). The cartels reverse-engineered submarine technology in the jungle.

markers.name: Balaklava Submarine Base, Crimea
markers.ctx: Object 825 GTS: Soviet submarine base inside Tavros mountain with exits on both sides and a canal to the open sea; caisson gates could seal it; built to protect crews from nuclear fallout. Closed 1993; now a naval museum.

markers.name: Jianggezhuang Submarine Base, Qingdao, China
markers.ctx: PLA Navy North Sea Fleet nuclear submarine base. Underground pens visible in satellite imagery. China's nuclear submarine deterrent - the underwater component of the second-strike capability.

markers.name: Yulin Naval Base, Hainan, China
markers.ctx: PLA Navy South Sea Fleet base at Sanya. Its eastern extension, Longpo (Yulin-East) on Yalong Bay, hosts the nuclear submarines (reported: Type 094 Jin-class SSBNs) and aircraft carriers.

markers.name: London City Airport
markers.ctx: Opened 26 Oct 1987 on the former Royal Docks. Short 1,508 m runway with a steep approach. About 3.5 miles from Canary Wharf; built to serve the Docklands and City business market.

markers.name: Cassidy International Airport, Kiritimati (Christmas Island)
markers.ctx: Kiritimati (Christmas Island). British Operation Grapple (1957-58): nine tests at Malden Island and Kiritimati. U.S. Operation Dominic (1962): airdrop tests off Christmas Island. Servicemen and islanders exposed to radiation. Population 7,369 (2020); the whole island is a wildlife sanctuary.

markers.name: Diego Garcia - U.S./UK military base, Chagos
markers.ctx: U.S./UK base with a 12,000-ft runway for B-52 and B-2 operations. The Chagossian population was forcibly removed 1968-73. ICJ advisory opinion (2019): decolonisation not lawfully completed. A UK-Mauritius treaty signed 22 May 2025 transfers sovereignty while keeping the base for 99 years.

markers.name: RAF Ascension Island, South Atlantic
markers.ctx: Wideawake Airfield - 10,000-ft runway on volcanic island. Critical relay for Falklands War logistics. NASA tracking station. GCHQ/NSA signals intelligence. Shared between military, intelligence, and space agencies on a volcanic rock in the mid-Atlantic.

markers.name: Masirah Island Air Base, Oman
markers.ctx: Remote island airbase, Arabian Sea. Former RAF, now Royal Air Force of Oman with U.S. access agreements. Staging point for Iraq/Afghanistan operations. Desert One (1980 Iran hostage rescue attempt) staged from here. Remote basing for regional force projection.

markers.name: Lajes Field, Terceira, Azores
markers.ctx: Mid-Atlantic staging base. Used for Iraq War rendition flights. Cold War: nuclear weapons storage (confirmed by declassified documents). Portuguese sovereignty, American operations. The mid-ocean refueling stop for everything that shouldn't land on the mainland.

markers.name: Toncontin Airport, Tegucigalpa, Honduras
markers.ctx: One of world's most dangerous airports - mountain approach, short runway. International flights moved to Palmerola in Nov 2021. Honduras: among the highest murder rates in the world after the 2009 coup (U.S. response contested; Washington called it illegal but never formally designated it a coup). Drug trafficking corridor. The dangerous airport in the dangerous country at the center of the narco-state pipeline.

markers.name: Mena Intermountain Airport, Arkansas
markers.ctx: Barry Seal's aircraft maintenance base; a 2020-released FBI/State Police/IRS document records smuggling activity here 1980-84. CIA ties are alleged, not documented.

markers.name: Esrange Space Center, Kiruna, Sweden
markers.ctx: Rocket range and satellite ground station ~40 km east of Kiruna, above the Arctic Circle; owned and operated by SSC Space. Hosts ESA and commercial programmes.

markers.name: Woomera Range Complex, Australia
markers.ctx: Woomera Prohibited Area (~122,000 km²): the largest land-based defence and aerospace range in the world. Britain's nuclear tests at Maralinga (1956-63) took place inside it; Anangu people were displaced and exposed. Former joint U.S.-Australian station at Nurrungar.

markers.name: Kwajalein Atoll / Reagan Test Site, Marshall Islands
markers.ctx: U.S. Army missile testing facility. Space Fence radar installation. 67 nuclear tests on Bikini and Enewetak atolls (1946-58) - Marshallese people permanently displaced. Compact of Free Association gives U.S. military access in exchange for aid. Nuclear testing victims still seeking compensation.

markers.name: London City Island, Leamouth Peninsula
markers.ctx: Residential-led development on the Leamouth Peninsula where the River Lea meets the Thames; also home to the English National Ballet. Named City Island for marketing - it is a peninsula.

markers.name: Kiritimati (Christmas Island), Republic of Kiribati
markers.ctx: One of the world's largest atolls by land area (~312 km2). Cook landed on Christmas Eve 1777. Britain's Operation Grapple (1957-58) used it as base; six of its nine nuclear tests were above or near the island (from Grapple X, 8 Nov 1957). The US detonated 24 devices nearby in 1962 (Operation Dominic). Islanders were usually not evacuated.

markers.name: Isle of Dogs, London
markers.ctx: Canary Wharf sits on the Isle of Dogs, built around the West India Docks (opened 27 Aug 1802) - promoted by West India merchants led by Robert Milligan, a slave trader and Jamaica plantation manager, to land West Indies plantation cargo. The East India Docks (1806) lay adjacent at Blackwall. After the docks closed (1980) the Canary Wharf office district was built around the wet docks; HSBC, Barclays, Morgan Stanley, Citigroup and JPMorgan have occupied towers there.

markers.name: Nauru
markers.ctx: Smallest republic on Earth. Phosphate mining stripped 80% of the island (1906-2002). Richest per-capita country in 1970s, now bankrupt. Australian offshore immigration detention center. Mined to dust, then used as a prison island. The lifecycle of extraction: use it, empty it, fill it with people no one wants.

markers.name: Bouvet Island, South Atlantic
markers.ctx: Norwegian dependency, described as the world's most remote island - ~1,700 km from Queen Maud Land, Antarctica. On 22 Sept 1979 a US Vela satellite registered a double flash over the sea between Bouvet and the Prince Edward Islands (the Vela incident); it has been read as an Israeli-South African nuclear test, a meteoroid or an instrument glitch - contested, never confirmed.

markers.name: Pitcairn Island, South Pacific
markers.ctx: Settled in 1790 by Bounty mutineers and Tahitians; a UK overseas territory. Population about 35 (2023). In 2004 seven island men - a third of its male population - were tried on 55 charges of sexual offences against children and young adults; six were convicted. Six more men living abroad were tried in Auckland in 2005.

markers.name: St. Helena, South Atlantic
markers.ctx: Napoleon exiled here (1815-1821). Only accessible by ship until airport opened 2017. British East India Company administered until 1834. Strategic mid-Atlantic position. The island designed to imprison an emperor - so remote it didn't need walls.

markers.name: Socotra Island, Yemen
markers.ctx: 'Galapagos of the Indian Ocean' - about a third of its plant life is found nowhere else; UNESCO World Heritage Site (2008). Strategic position at the Gulf of Aden. On 30 April 2018 the UAE landed troops and took control of the island's airport, over the Yemeni government's protest; a UAE military presence has followed. Source: Wikipedia, Socotra.

markers.name: Heard Island, Australian External Territory
markers.ctx: Subantarctic volcanic island, uninhabited; Big Ben (summit Mawson Peak, 2,745 m) holds Australia's only active volcanoes. ANARE ran a station here 1947-55. One of the most remote places on Earth; a World Heritage nature reserve.

markers.name: North Sentinel Island, Andaman Sea
markers.ctx: Home of the Sentinelese, one of the last uncontacted peoples; their number is unknown (the 2001 census estimate was 39; other estimates run higher). India bars approach within five nautical miles. In 2018 American missionary John Allen Chau was killed after landing illegally. The modern world keeps trying.

markers.name: Zug, Switzerland - Crypto Valley
markers.ctx: Self-proclaimed 'Crypto Valley.' Ethereum Foundation HQ. Bitcoin Suisse. Cardano Foundation. Polkadot. A low-tax Swiss canton. The offshore finance model applied to cryptocurrency - same geography, updated product.

markers.name: El Zonte, El Salvador - Bitcoin Beach
markers.ctx: Origin of El Salvador's Bitcoin adoption. Anonymous donor seeded BTC in fishing village (2019). President Bukele made BTC legal tender (2021). Chivo wallet - government-run Bitcoin wallet. Legal-tender status rescinded Feb 2025 under the IMF deal. Village experiment scaled to national policy, then rolled back.

markers.name: Volcano Bond Site, Conchagua, El Salvador
markers.ctx: Proposed 'Bitcoin City' at base of Conchagua volcano. Geothermal-powered Bitcoin mining. Proposed $1B 'Volcano Bond' (tokenized sovereign debt), postponed in March 2022. The volcano as power source for a digital currency city that hasn't been built.

markers.name: Genesis Block Café, Hong Kong
markers.ctx: Named after Bitcoin's first block (Jan 3, 2009). Hong Kong: global crypto trading hub before 2023 regulatory shifts. Proximity to mainland China - where 65%+ of Bitcoin mining once concentrated before the ban.

markers.name: Cambridge, UK - ARM Holdings / Silicon Fen
markers.ctx: Silicon Fen technology cluster around Cambridge. Arm Holdings (majority-owned by SoftBank) designs the processor architecture licensed into virtually all modern smartphones.

markers.name: Kourou, French Guiana - Guiana Space Centre
markers.ctx: Guiana Space Centre at Kourou, Europe's spaceport since 1968: ~5°N, near the equator, which raises payload to geostationary orbit; open sea to the east. Ariane 6 launches since July 2024.

markers.name: Tsukuba Science City, Japan
markers.ctx: Purpose-built science city ordered by the national government in September 1963, ~60 km from Tokyo. JAXA Tsukuba Space Center; KEK particle accelerator laboratory; dozens of national research institutes. Government-planned knowledge concentration.

markers.name: Shenzhen, China - Hardware Capital
markers.ctx: Special Economic Zone created 1980; 17.56 million people (2020). Home to Huawei, Tencent, DJI, ZTE and BYD. A global centre of electronics manufacturing.

markers.name: BlackRock HQ, New York City
markers.ctx: BlackRock: US$15.3 trillion AUM (2026), largest asset manager in the world. Aladdin risk platform handled about $21.6T in assets (as of 2020). Larry Fink began at First Boston (1976) as one of the first mortgage-backed-securities traders. The Federal Reserve hired BlackRock in 2008-09 (Bear Stearns/AIG assets) and in March 2020 to run two corporate-bond purchase facilities - an asset manager executing central-bank purchases in markets where it also manages funds.

markers.name: Vanguard HQ, Malvern, Pennsylvania
markers.ctx: US$13.3 trillion AUM (2025). Largest provider of mutual funds; second-largest ETF provider after BlackRock's iShares. Vanguard is owned by the funds it manages, and so by their investors - it has no outside shareholders. With BlackRock and State Street it is one of the 'Big Three' index managers.

markers.name: State Street HQ, Boston
markers.ctx: US$4.7 trillion AUM (2024). Third of the 'Big Three' index managers with BlackRock and Vanguard; custodian bank for institutional money. Fichtner, Heemskerk & Garcia-Bernardo (2017, 2015 data): combined, the Big Three were the largest shareholder in 438 of the S&P 500 (88%) and used coordinated voting strategies, generally voting with management except at director elections.

markers.name: Monsanto HQ (now Bayer), Creve Coeur, Missouri
markers.ctx: Monsanto made PCBs, DDT, Agent Orange and Roundup (glyphosate). Bayer completed its US$66bn takeover on 7 June 2018 and retired the name. Bayer was one of the companies merged into IG Farben (1925), which used concentration-camp slave labour and co-owned Degesch, maker of Zyklon B (attributed). Seed patents bar replanting (Bowman v. Monsanto, 2013). The food supply as intellectual property.

markers.name: Palantir HQ (Denver until 2026; moved to Miami)
markers.ctx: Co-founded 2003 by Peter Thiel, Alex Karp and others. In-Q-Tel, the CIA's venture arm, invested about $2 million early on. Gotham platform: military/intelligence. Foundry: corporate. ICE partnership since 2014. Moved HQ from Palo Alto to Denver in 2020 and announced a move to Miami in February 2026. Named after a seeing-stone from Tolkien.

markers.name: Booz Allen Hamilton, McLean, Virginia
markers.ctx: Headquartered in McLean, Virginia. Edward Snowden was a Booz Allen employee assigned to NSA projects when he disclosed NSA documents (June 2013); the firm fired him. Nearly all revenue comes from US government contracts. A consultancy whose cleared staff do intelligence work - the privatisation of intelligence labour.

markers.name: Halliburton, Houston, Texas
markers.ctx: Dick Cheney: Halliburton chairman and CEO 1995-2000 (HQ then in Dallas), then Vice President 2001-2009, receiving deferred compensation while in office. KBR, then a Halliburton subsidiary, was awarded at least $39.5bn in Iraq-war-related federal contracts over 2003-2013 (FT analysis, 2013), many without competitive bidding, including the $7bn Restore Iraqi Oil contract for which only Halliburton was allowed to bid. Critics alleged the awards reflected Cheney's office; that link is contested, not established. KBR was spun off in 2007.

markers.name: General Dynamics HQ, Reston, Virginia
markers.ctx: General Dynamics, Reston, Virginia - the only US maker of MK-80 series bomb bodies, reported as the primary bomb type in Israel's Gaza campaign and used across the region. Revenue $52.6B (2025). Also owns Gulfstream (business jets). Source: Wikipedia, General Dynamics; General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems.

markers.name: Foxconn - Zhengzhou iPhone plant / Longhua, Shenzhen
markers.ctx: Foxconn's Zhengzhou Technology Park assembles the bulk of Apple's iPhones (about 200,000 workers in Nov 2022; COVID lockdown unrest there that autumn). The 2010 suicide cluster was at its Longhua campus in Shenzhen, 'Foxconn City', where the company installed safety nets; a Zhengzhou worker's suicide was reported in 2016.

markers.name: Nestlé HQ, Vevey, Switzerland
markers.ctx: World's largest food company. Its infant-formula marketing in poor countries, where formula was often mixed with unsafe water, led to a boycott launched in the US on 4 July 1977. Water-bottling disputes in Michigan, California and Pakistan. Chairman Peter Brabeck-Letmathe said in 2005 (We Feed the World) that declaring water a public right was 'an extreme solution' and that water should have a market value; he later said drinking water is a human right.

markers.name: British Museum, London
markers.ctx: About 8 million objects. Holds the Parthenon (Elgin) Marbles, the Rosetta Stone and Benin Bronzes taken in the 1897 British punitive expedition; Greece and Nigeria have long sought return. The museum as colonial warehouse (the site's characterisation).

markers.name: Vatican Secret Archives (Apostolic Archive), Vatican City
markers.ctx: 85 linear kilometers of shelving. Documents spanning 12+ centuries. 'Secret' renamed 'Private' (2019). Access restricted to qualified scholars by application. Contains records of Inquisition, Galileo trial, excommunications, papal bulls authorizing colonization (Doctrine of Discovery). What the church chooses to preserve and who it allows to see it.

markers.name: Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza
markers.ctx: Billion-dollar museum near the Giza pyramids, inaugurated 1 Nov 2025, holding over 100,000 objects including the Tutankhamun collection moved from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, Cairo (~120,000 objects). Access to Egypt's sites and the official narrative run through the antiquities ministry; Zahi Hawass dominated it for decades until 2011.

markers.name: Pergamon Museum, Berlin
markers.ctx: Ishtar Gate of Babylon, Pergamon Altar, Market Gate of Miletus - whole ancient structures excavated abroad and rebuilt in Berlin. Closed since Oct 2023 for renovation, expected mostly closed until 2037-2043.

markers.name: Iraq Museum, Baghdad
