markers.ctx: National Museum of Iraq - looted 10-12 April 2003 during the US-led invasion; about 15,000 items were taken (early reports of 170,000 were wrong), including about 5,000 cylinder seals; thousands remain missing. The National Library and Archives burned the same week. Source: Wikipedia, National Museum of Iraq.

markers.name: Göbekli Tepe Excavation Site Museum, Urfa
markers.ctx: Museum adjacent to world's oldest known temple (pre-12,000 years). Klaus Schmidt excavated 1994-2014 (died 2014). Only 5% excavated. Turkish government controls access and narrative. An archaeological site that rewrites human history - 95% of it deliberately left in the ground.

markers.name: Field Museum, Chicago
markers.ctx: Founded from 1893 World's Columbian Exposition collections. Marshall Field (department stores) funded. 40+ million specimens. Sue the T-Rex ($8.4M, 1997). Indigenous collections: human remains and sacred objects held for decades before NAGPRA compliance. The natural history museum funded by the retail baron.

markers.name: Uffizi Gallery, Florence
markers.ctx: Gallery established 1581 in the Medici offices built by Vasari. The Medici - bankers to the papacy, later dukes, and the source of several popes - used art patronage as a display of power. The gallery as ledger.

markers.name: Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg
markers.ctx: 3 million items. Founded by Catherine the Great (1764). Winter Palace - seat of Romanov power. Survived revolution, Nazi siege (872 days, 1M dead in Leningrad). The museum that survived the empire that built it, the revolution that overthrew it, and the siege that tried to starve it.

markers.name: Palmyra, Syria
markers.ctx: Palmyra - Queen Zenobia's capital; Roman-era colonnaded city. The Temple of Bel (dedicated AD 32) was blown up by ISIS in August 2015 and the monumental arch in October 2015. Syria's antiquities chief said ISIS was searching for gold. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of Bel.

markers.name: Nimrud, Iraq
markers.ctx: Nimrud (Kalhu) - Assyrian imperial capital from 879 BCE under Ashurnasirpal II; Northwest Palace, lamassu statues. In March 2015 the Iraqi government reported that ISIS had bulldozed the excavated remains; ISIS released videos of the destruction. Iraqi forces retook the site in November 2016. Source: Wikipedia, Nimrud.

markers.name: Aleppo, Syria - Ancient City
markers.ctx: Ancient City of Aleppo - UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986), among the oldest continuously inhabited cities. The Great Mosque's minaret was destroyed in April 2013; an estimated 30% of the Ancient City was destroyed (and more damaged) in the Battle of Aleppo. Source: Wikipedia, Ancient City of Aleppo; Great Mosque of Aleppo.

markers.name: Timbuktu, Mali
markers.ctx: Timbuktu - historic centre of Islamic scholarship. Ansar Dine/AQIM destroyed most of its UNESCO-listed mausoleums in 2012 and set fire to the Ahmed Baba Institute on retreat in January 2013; librarians evacuated hundreds of thousands of manuscripts (total number unknown). French Operation Serval retook the city in January 2013. Source: Wikipedia, Timbuktu; Timbuktu Manuscripts.

markers.name: Mes Aynak, Afghanistan
markers.ctx: Mes Aynak, Logar Province - a 40 ha Buddhist monastic settlement (peak 5th-7th century CE) with over 400 Buddha statues and stupas, above an older Bronze Age copper-working site, sitting on Afghanistan's largest known copper deposit. 30-year lease to China Metallurgical Group (MCC), November 2007, US$3 billion. Mining is proceeding at the expense of the site. Source: Wikipedia, Mes Aynak.

markers.name: Sanaa Old City, Yemen
markers.ctx: Old City of Sanaa - UNESCO World Heritage Site, inhabited for more than 2,500 years; multi-storey rammed-earth tower houses. Saudi-led coalition airstrikes from 2015 damaged the Old City. The coalition was armed largely by the US and UK (Section XV); the munitions used in these specific strikes are not established. Source: Wikipedia, Old City of Sanaa.

markers.name: Mosul / Nineveh, Iraq
markers.ctx: Mosul / ancient Nineveh - Assyrian capital, site of the Library of Ashurbanipal (the oldest surviving royal library). ISIS blew up the Nebi Yunus shrine (Tomb of Jonah) in July 2014 and on 26 February 2015 released video of militants smashing statues in the Mosul Museum. Source: Wikipedia, Mosul Museum; Mosque of the Prophet Yunus.

markers.name: Wadi Mathendous - Saharan rock art, Libya
markers.ctx: Wadi Mathendous, Fezzan - prehistoric rock engravings (cattle, giraffes, elephants) from the 'Green Sahara' period. Libya's conflict since 2011 has left such sites largely unprotected. Source: Wikipedia, Wadi Mathendous.

markers.name: Khyber Pass, Afghanistan/Pakistan
markers.ctx: Khyber Pass - mountain pass linking Afghanistan and the Peshawar valley. Mahmud of Ghazni, Muhammad of Ghor, Timur, Babur and Nader Shah used it and nearby passes to invade the Indian subcontinent; it was contested in the Anglo-Afghan wars. Source: Wikipedia, Khyber Pass.

markers.name: Strait of Hormuz
markers.ctx: Strait of Hormuz - about 21 miles wide at its narrowest, between Iran and Oman (Musandam). About a fifth of world oil consumption (2018: 21 million barrels a day) and about 20% of world LNG pass through; the only sea route out of the Persian Gulf, though Saudi and UAE pipelines bypass part of the flow. Source: Wikipedia, Strait of Hormuz; EIA.

markers.name: Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Yemen/Djibouti
markers.ctx: Bab el-Mandeb ('Gate of Tears') - about 20 miles wide; links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, so Suez traffic to and from the Indian Ocean passes through it. Houthi attacks on shipping from 19 November 2023 diverted global shipping; US/UK strikes followed. Source: Wikipedia, Red Sea crisis.

markers.name: Göbekli Tepe Region, Southeastern Turkey
markers.ctx: Gobekli Tepe, Sanliurfa Province - monumental Pre-Pottery Neolithic enclosures (c. 9500 BCE), among the oldest known monumental structures. Southeastern Turkey has been the setting of the Turkish state-PKK conflict; the site itself is open to visitors. Source: Wikipedia, Gobekli Tepe.

markers.name: Angkor Wat Region, Cambodia
markers.ctx: Angkor Wat - the largest religious monument in the world (Khmer Empire, 802-1431). In the same century: US bombing of Cambodia (Operation Menu, March 1969 - May 1970, 108,823 tons; total US tonnage 1965-73 is disputed) and the Khmer Rouge regime (1975-79), under which an estimated 1.5-2 million people died. Source: Wikipedia, Angkor Wat; Operation Menu.

markers.name: Valley of the Kings, Luxor, Egypt
markers.ctx: Royal necropolis with 65 known tombs and chambers, used c. 1539-1075 BC. Most were looted in antiquity; Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) was found intact in 1922. Radar surveys from 2015 for hidden chambers behind KV62 produced conflicting results.

markers.name: Derinkuyu Underground City, Cappadocia, Turkey
markers.ctx: Excavated to ~85 m, with rolling stone doors; large enough for as many as 20,000 people with livestock and stores. Linked to Kaymakli by 8-9 km of tunnels. Carved from volcanic tuff; fully formed in the Byzantine era.

markers.name: Ellora Caves, Maharashtra, India
markers.ctx: 34 caves cut into basalt (AD 600-1000) - Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples side by side. The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) was excavated vertically from the top of the rock downward; an estimated ~200,000 tonnes of rock were removed (estimate).

markers.name: Guatemala - 1954 CIA Coup (Operation PBSUCCESS)
markers.ctx: Operation PBSUCCESS: the CIA overthrew elected President Jacobo Arbenz (June 1954) after a land reform that expropriated United Fruit Company land; United Fruit lobbied for his removal. The civil war that followed (1960-96) killed about 200,000, and the UN-backed truth commission found acts of genocide against the Maya. Source: Wikipedia, 1954 Guatemalan coup; Guatemalan genocide.

markers.name: Iran - 1953 CIA/MI6 Coup (Operation Ajax)
markers.ctx: Operation Ajax/Boot: CIA and MI6 overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh (19 August 1953) after he nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (later BP), restoring the Shah's power. SAVAK, founded 1957 with CIA assistance, policed the monarchy until the 1979 revolution. Source: Wikipedia, 1953 Iranian coup; SAVAK.

markers.name: Congo - Lumumba Assassination, Lubumbashi
markers.ctx: Patrice Lumumba, first democratically elected Prime Minister of Congo, was killed on 17 January 1961 near Elisabethville (Lubumbashi), shot by a Katangan firing squad with Belgian officers present. A Belgian parliamentary commission (2001) found Belgium bore moral responsibility; Belgium apologised in 2002. The Church Committee (1975) documented a CIA plot to poison him that was never carried out and was not the means of death. Mobutu, US-backed, ruled for 32 years. Uranium from Congo's Shinkolobwe mine was used in the Manhattan Project.

markers.name: Chile - 1973 CIA Coup, Santiago
markers.ctx: Coup of 11 September 1973 against Salvador Allende, after years of CIA covert funding of his opposition (including the 1970 Track II effort); US inquiries did not find direct CIA participation in the coup itself. Pinochet's regime: about 3,200 killed or disappeared, 38,254 recognised political prisoners, most tortured (Rettig and Valech commissions). 'Chicago Boys' free-market policies imposed under military rule. Source: Wikipedia, 1973 Chilean coup; Valech Report.

markers.name: Libya - NATO Intervention, Tripoli
markers.ctx: NATO intervention (March-October 2011); Gaddafi killed 20 October 2011 - Hillary Clinton: 'We came, we saw, he died.' Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves and had the continent's highest HDI before the war. A plan for a gold-backed African currency is cited as a motive in one attributed source (a Blumenthal email to Clinton); not established. Slave auctions of migrants were filmed in 2017 (CNN). Source: Wikipedia, 2011 military intervention in Libya.

markers.name: Laos - Secret War, Plain of Jars
markers.ctx: Most heavily bombed country per capita in history: about 270 million cluster bomblets dropped 1964-73, an estimated 80 million unexploded; UXO still kills and maims every year. The Plain of Jars - megalithic stone jars about 2,000 years old, associated with burial practice - became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019 and lies inside the bombed zone. Source: Wikipedia, Plain of Jars.

markers.name: Vietnam - Cu Chi Tunnels, Ho Chi Minh City
markers.ctx: Cu Chi tunnels - about 250 km of tunnels with hospitals, kitchens and command posts, used by the Viet Cong; they survived carpet bombing and defoliation with Agent Orange (made by Monsanto, Dow and others). An estimated 3 million Vietnamese and 58,000 Americans died in the war. The chemical makers paid $180 million to US veterans in a 1984 settlement; Vietnamese victims' suits were dismissed. Source: Wikipedia, Cu Chi tunnels; Agent Orange.

markers.name: Sochi Olympic Park, Russia - 2014 Winter Olympics
markers.ctx: $51B - most expensive Olympics in history. Built on coast of historical Circassia. Circassian Genocide (1864): Russian Empire killed/expelled 1-1.5M Circassians. Russia hosted its celebration games on the land of a genocide it has never acknowledged. Sochi was the port from which Circassians were expelled. The victory lap on a mass grave.

markers.name: Berlin Olympic Stadium - 1936 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: Nazi propaganda showcase. Jesse Owens won four gold medals; the story that Hitler refused his hand is a myth - Hitler had stopped publicly congratulating any winners, and Owens said 'Hitler didn't snub me - it was our president who snubbed me.' Leni Riefenstahl's Olympia pioneered sports-film technique. The Olympics as legitimisation of a fascist state. Stadium still in use.

markers.name: Munich Olympic Village - 1972 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: Munich Massacre: 11 Israeli athletes killed by Black September. German police botched rescue at Fürstenfeldbruck airfield. Mossad launched Operation Wrath of God - targeted assassinations across Europe. The Olympics that became a war zone. Games continued after 34-hour pause. 'The Games must go on.' - Avery Brundage.

markers.name: Beijing National Stadium (Bird's Nest) - 2008 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: US$428M stadium. Mass displacement of hutong neighbourhoods; internet controls tightened; Tibet protests crushed in March 2008. Ai Weiwei, the stadium's artistic consultant, later distanced himself from it as part of a 'pretend smile'. The surveillance state dressed up as a sporting event.

markers.name: Athens Olympic Complex - 2004 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: Cost the Greek state ~EUR 9bn. Most venues later abandoned (Hellinikon rusting). Popular accounts blame the Games for the 2010-18 debt crisis, but there is little evidence for a significant contribution - the debt (later ~180% of GDP) and Troika austerity had wider causes.

markers.name: Rio Olympic Park, Barra da Tijuca - 2016 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: Reported total cost ~US$13bn (sports-related costs ~US$4.6bn per the Oxford study). Favela clearances; sewage in Guanabara Bay; the state of Rio declared a financial emergency weeks before opening. In April 2017 Brazil's Supreme Court opened an investigation of former mayor Eduardo Paes on Odebrecht plea testimony alleging ~US$4.8m solicited in 2012 for Olympic contracts; he denies it and no outcome is recorded here.

markers.name: London Olympic Park, Stratford - 2012 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: £8.77bn against a £9.3bn public funding package. Security relied on extensive CCTV; the G4S security contract failed and troops were called in. East London regeneration displaced working-class communities; legacy housing skewed to luxury flats.

markers.name: Salt Lake City - 2002 Winter Olympics
markers.ctx: Bribery scandal (broke Nov 1998): IOC members received cash, scholarships for children, medical care and land deals from the bid committee. Ten IOC members were expelled and ten sanctioned - the IOC's first sanctions for corruption. Bid leaders Tom Welch and Dave Johnson were charged with bribery and fraud and acquitted of all charges in Dec 2003.

markers.name: Tokyo Olympic Stadium - 2020/2021 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: Postponed by COVID - the only postponement in Olympic history - and held in 2021 in empty stadiums; reported cost ~US$15bn. Zaha Hadid's stadium design was scrapped over cost. Organising-committee executive board member Haruyuki Takahashi was arrested for bribery in 2022; Dentsu was the Games' exclusive marketing agency.

markers.name: PyeongChang Olympic Complex - 2018 Winter Olympics
markers.ctx: Reported cost ~US$13bn. Held months after peak nuclear tension with the DPRK. Kim Yo-jong attended the opening; the two Koreas marched under the Korean Unification Flag and fielded a unified women's hockey team. The Olympics as diplomatic theatre.

markers.name: Sarajevo Olympic Venues - 1984 Winter Olympics
markers.ctx: Beautiful venues built 1984. By 1992: bobsled track used as artillery position. Zetra Olympic Hall: burned, used as morgue. Athletes' Village: sniper positions. The Olympic venues that became a battlefield within 8 years. Siege of Sarajevo: 1,425 days, 11,541 killed. The fastest transformation from celebration to slaughter.

markers.name: Montreal Olympic Stadium - 1976 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: $1.5B cost - 'The Big Owe.' Took 30 years to pay off (2006). Mayor Jean Drapeau: 'The Olympics can no more have a deficit than a man can have a baby.' Retractable roof never worked properly. The stadium whose debt outlasted a generation.

markers.name: Mexico City Olympic Sites - 1968 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: Tlatelolco massacre, 2 Oct 1968 - ten days before the opening ceremony. Mexican army and the Olympia Battalion, a secret government security unit, fired on student protesters in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas: 44 deaths documented by name, with estimates of 300-400. The Games went ahead. Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised fists on the podium and were suspended and expelled from the Games.

markers.name: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum - 1984 Summer Olympics
markers.ctx: Soviet-led boycott (14 Eastern Bloc nations). Peter Ueberroth's 'private enterprise Olympics' - first to turn a profit ($250M). Created the corporate sponsorship model all future Olympics would follow. The Olympics that proved the Games were a business, not a movement.

markers.name: Lausanne, Switzerland - IOC Headquarters
markers.ctx: Olympic House, Vidy, Lausanne - headquarters of the International Olympic Committee (founded 1894), an association under Swiss law. President Kirsty Coventry since 23 June 2025, succeeding Thomas Bach (2013-2025). The body that sells broadcast and sponsorship rights to the Games for billions per Olympic cycle.

markers.name: CIA Headquarters, Langley, Virginia - Art Collection
markers.ctx: The CIA's Cold War cultural programme, run from 1950 by Tom Braden's International Organisations Division, promoted American Abstract Expressionism (Pollock, Rothko, Motherwell, de Kooning) abroad through the Congress for Cultural Freedom and conduits such as the Farfield Foundation, without the artists' knowledge (attributed: Frances Stonor Saunders, The Independent, 22 Oct 1995; 'The Cultural Cold War', 1999). Braden in 1995: 'In order to encourage openness we had to be secret.'

markers.name: Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), New York - CIA Cultural Front
markers.ctx: Nelson Rockefeller, MoMA president from 1939 and a leading backer of Abstract Expressionism ('free enterprise painting'). Per Frances Stonor Saunders (The Independent, 1995; 'The Cultural Cold War'), MoMA was contracted to the CIA-funded Congress for Cultural Freedom to organise and curate its major art shows, and CIA conduits paid for touring exhibitions such as 'The New American Painting' (1958-59). The museum as an instrument of Cold War soft power (attributed).

markers.name: Christie's, King Street, London - Major Auction House
markers.ctx: Founded 1766. Owned by François Pinault through Groupe Artémis since 1998. Sold Leonardo's 'Salvator Mundi' for $450.3M (2017) to Prince Badr bin Abdullah, reported to be bidding for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (attributed). High-end art moves through auctions, private sales and freeport storage with limited public visibility of owners.

markers.name: Sotheby's, New Bond Street, London - Major Auction House
markers.ctx: Founded 1744. Acquired by Patrick Drahi in 2019 (~$3.7bn). Dmitry Rybolovlev accused Swiss dealer Yves Bouvier of overcharging him by nearly $1bn on art bought partly via Sotheby's; the cases against Bouvier were dismissed and the two settled in Dec 2023, and a New York jury cleared Sotheby's on all counts in Jan 2024. The affair exposed how private-sale markups work.

markers.name: Salvator Mundi Sale, Christie's NYC - $450.3M
markers.ctx: Leonardo da Vinci 'Salvator Mundi' - $450.3M (15 Nov 2017), record for any painting at auction. Bought by Prince Badr bin Abdullah, reported to be a stand-in for Mohammed bin Salman (attributed). Bought in 2005 for $1,175 as 'after Leonardo'. Attribution disputed by scholars. Not publicly exhibited since the sale; reported to be in storage in Saudi Arabia - location attributed, not documented. A planned Louvre Abu Dhabi showing was cancelled without explanation.

markers.name: Geneva Freeport, Switzerland - Art Storage Tax Haven
markers.ctx: The largest freeport for art: an estimated US$100bn of art (press estimate) and ~1.2 million works (2013) in duty-suspended warehouses. Bought at auction, stored, resold years later without being seen. Art as bearer bonds.

markers.name: Luxembourg Freeport (Luxembourg High Security Hub) - Art Storage
markers.ctx: Opened Sept 2014 beside Findel airport, founded by Yves Bouvier; designed by Atelier d'Architecture 3BM3. Same model as Geneva - goods stored with duties suspended. MEPs have criticised it as an enabler of tax evasion. Now the Luxembourg High Security Hub.

markers.name: Le Freeport (Singapore Freeport), Changi
markers.ctx: Opened 2010 at Changi by Yves Bouvier's group (built for ~S$100M). Art, gold, wine and cars stored duty-suspended; Deutsche Bank kept gold there until 2019. Sold in 2022 to crypto billionaire Jihan Wu's Bitdeer for S$40M.

markers.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York - Board Patterns
markers.ctx: Trustees and donors include/included David Koch ($65M plaza), Henry Kravis and Leonard Lauder (Cubist collection gift). The Sackler Wing (Temple of Dendur) bore the name of the family whose Purdue Pharma made OxyContin, a driver of the US opioid epidemic; the name was removed in 2021 after protests.

markers.name: Louvre Abu Dhabi - Art as Diplomacy
markers.ctx: Under a 30-year intergovernmental deal (2007) Abu Dhabi pays EUR 400M for the Louvre name (to 2037), EUR 190M for art loans, EUR 165M for management advice and more. Designed by Jean Nouvel. Human Rights Watch documented passport confiscation and forced-labour conditions among construction workers. Salvator Mundi's planned showing here was cancelled.

markers.name: Guggenheim Museum, New York - Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation
markers.ctx: Solomon Guggenheim: mining fortune. Peggy Guggenheim's Venice palazzo is still a museum. Guggenheim Bilbao (Frank Gehry) turned a declining industrial city into a destination - the 'Bilbao Effect'. A Guggenheim Helsinki was rejected by Helsinki City Council in 2016 after polls showed most residents opposed.

markers.name: Tate Modern, London - Turbine Hall
markers.ctx: Unilever Series funded Turbine Hall commissions (2000-2012). BP sponsorship of Tate: protested relentlessly by Liberate Tate. BP dropped 2016 after 26 years. Tate board included oil executives while exhibiting climate-themed art. The oil company sponsoring the museum that showed art about environmental destruction.

markers.name: Museum of Islamic Art, Doha, Qatar
markers.ctx: Designed by I.M. Pei. Qatar Museums (Sheikha Al-Mayassa bint Hamad Al Thani): estimated $1B/year art spending. Qatar bought Cézanne's 'The Card Players' for $250M+ (2011) - highest price ever at the time. The nation-state art collection as soft power infrastructure. Gas wealth converted to cultural capital.

markers.name: The Broad, Los Angeles
markers.ctx: Eli Broad (SunAmerica, KB Home; d. 2021) and Edythe Broad financed the ~$140M building on Grand Avenue to house their own collection (Basquiat, Koons, Warhol, Hirst). Broad also gave $30M to rescue MOCA (2008) across the street and funded LACMA's BCAM. Art philanthropy as immortality project.

markers.name: Fondation Louis Vuitton, Paris
markers.ctx: Bernard Arnault (LVMH). Frank Gehry building in the Bois de Boulogne, opened 2014; projected at EUR 100M, it cost nearly eight times that, and LVMH received EUR 518M in tax breaks (Court of Audit, 2018). Houses the group's collection. Arnault also owned the auction house Phillips 1999-2000s. The vertical integration of taste.

markers.name: Broken Obelisk - Barnett Newman, Rothko Chapel, Houston
markers.ctx: Barnett Newman's 'Broken Obelisk' (designed 1963-67), Cor-Ten steel: an inverted, broken obelisk balanced on a pyramid apex. The Houston cast was installed beside the Rothko Chapel in 1970 in a reflecting pool and, at Dominique de Menil's condition, dedicated to Martin Luther King Jr. The obelisk of power, snapped and turned upside down - the anti-monument.

markers.name: Vigeland Sculpture Park (Frognerparken), Oslo
markers.ctx: Gustav Vigeland: 212 bronze and granite sculptures. The Monolith: 14.12m granite column of 121 intertwined human figures - carved from single block over 14 years. Wheel of Life, Fountain of cosmic cycles. Entire human lifecycle depicted: birth, struggle, death, transcendence. The largest sculpture park by a single artist in the world. Vigeland's obsession: the human body as architecture of existence.

markers.name: The Alamo (Astor Place Cube), New York City
markers.ctx: Tony Rosenthal's 'Alamo' (1967). 8-foot cor-ten steel cube balanced on vertex - rotates when pushed. The spinning cube at the intersection. Cube geometry: Kaaba (Mecca), Black Cube of Saturn symbolism, Borg (Star Trek), 2001: A Space Odyssey monolith. The cube that invites you to spin it. Public art as participatory occult geometry.

markers.name: The Sphere (Koenig), Originally WTC Plaza, Now Liberty Park
markers.ctx: Fritz Koenig's 'The Sphere' (1971). Originally centered in WTC Austin J. Tobin Plaza - between the Twin Towers. Survived 9/11 damaged but intact. Moved to Battery Park, then Liberty Park (2017). The sculpture that stood between two towers and survived their fall. Originally symbolized 'world peace through world trade.' Now a memorial. The sphere between the towers.

markers.name: Cloud Gate (The Bean), Chicago
markers.ctx: Anish Kapoor, 2006. 110-ton polished stainless steel; reflects and distorts the Chicago skyline - the viewer sees themselves warped. Kapoor holds exclusive artistic rights to Vantablack (one of the darkest materials known), licensed by Surrey NanoSystems - an artist with a monopoly on a black. The mirror that bends what it shows.

markers.name: KAWS Companion Sculptures - Various Locations
markers.ctx: Brian Donnelly (KAWS). XX-eyed figures: Mickey Mouse + skull = consumer death. 'Companion' - 45m floating sculpture appeared Hong Kong, Taipei, worldwide. Sotheby's: KAWS 'The KAWS Album' (Simpsons parody) sold $14.8M (2019). Street art → auction house → floating corporate sculpture in Victoria Harbour. The trajectory from graffiti to global capital. Hyperstition: the cartoon that became the commodity that became the monument.

markers.name: Vessel (Hudson Yards), New York City
markers.ctx: Thomas Heatherwick, opened 15 Mar 2019; cost estimated at up to $200M; 154 flights of stairs, 2,500 steps. Four people died by suicide there between Feb 2020 and Jul 2021; it closed, and reopened 28 Oct 2024 behind higher barriers. Developer Related Companies (Stephen Ross, host of a 2019 Trump fundraiser; Related invests in Equinox and SoulCycle). Hudson Yards: a press-estimated $25bn development on a railyard. The monument to going nowhere.

markers.name: Maman (Giant Spider) - Louise Bourgeois, Various Locations
markers.ctx: Louise Bourgeois, 1999. 30-foot bronze spider. Editions at Guggenheim Bilbao, Tate Modern, National Gallery of Canada, Mori Tower Tokyo, Qatar. Named for the artist's mother ('She was my best friend'). The spider as protector - weaving, repairing, creating. Or: the spider as surveillance, the web as network. Bourgeois: 'Art is a guarantee of sanity.' The mother/monster that guards the museum entrance.

markers.name: Charging Bull, Bowling Green, New York
markers.ctx: Arturo Di Modica, 1989: a 7,100-lb (3.2 t) bronze bull installed guerrilla-style on Wall Street on 15 Dec 1989 after the 1987 crash, then moved to Bowling Green. State Street Global Advisors' 'Fearless Girl' faced it from March 2017 until moved to face the NYSE in Dec 2018. The sculpture the financial industry adopted as its totem.

markers.name: Kapoor's Sky Mirror, Rockefeller Center, New York
markers.ctx: Anish Kapoor's Sky Mirror, a 35-foot (11 m) concave stainless-steel dish, stood at Rockefeller Center from 20 Sept to 27 Oct 2006 - convex side to Fifth Avenue, concave to the courtyard, reflecting sky into ground. The original (2001) is outside the Nottingham Playhouse. A temporary inversion in front of the complex built by John D. Rockefeller Jr.

markers.name: Kaaba, Masjid al-Haram, Mecca
markers.ctx: The Kaaba: 13.1 m high, 11.03 x 12.86 m. Black silk kiswah replaced annually. Islamic tradition holds it was built by Ibrahim (Abraham) and Ismail. The Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad), set in the eastern corner, is pre-Islamic; a meteoritic origin has been proposed, not established. The direction of prayer for Muslims worldwide; millions circumambulate it during Hajj.

markers.name: Nevelson Chapel / Chapel of the Good Shepherd - Louise Nevelson, NYC
markers.ctx: Louise Nevelson: white-painted wood assemblages creating monolithic wall sculptures - essentially cubes and boxes nested within boxes. Chapel of the Good Shepherd at St. Peter's Church, NYC: entire environment as sculpture. The church inside the sculpture inside the box. Nevelson's work: the cube repeated, stacked, nested, until the wall becomes architecture.

markers.name: Black Cube HQ, Tel Aviv
markers.ctx: Black Cube (BC Strategy Ltd): private intelligence firm founded in 2010 by former Israeli intelligence officers; offices in Tel Aviv, London and Madrid. Documented: hired on behalf of Harvey Weinstein to surveil accusers and journalists. Reported to have targeted Soros-linked NGOs in Hungary during Viktor Orban's 2018 re-election campaign, using a London cover company and meetings in Vienna (client not established).

markers.name: 2001: A Space Odyssey - MGM-British Studios, Borehamwood
markers.ctx: Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) was among the last films shot at MGM-British Studios. Its black monolith (1:4:9 proportions in Clarke's novel) appears at each evolutionary leap. Kubrick died of a heart attack in March 1999, six days after screening his final cut of Eyes Wide Shut.

markers.name: Karnak Temple Obelisks, Luxor, Egypt
markers.ctx: Obelisks of Thutmose I and Hatshepsut still stand at Karnak. Egypt's obelisks were carried off by later empires from several temples: the Paris obelisk from nearby Luxor Temple, the London and New York 'Cleopatra's Needles' from Heliopolis via Alexandria. The source of power symbols for every subsequent empire.

markers.name: Lateran Obelisk, Piazza San Giovanni, Rome
markers.ctx: The largest standing ancient Egyptian obelisk (32.18 m shaft; 45.7 m with base). Made at Karnak under Thutmose III and Thutmose IV (c.1400 BC). Moved to Alexandria under Constantine I; Constantius II shipped it to Rome in 357 and set it on the Circus Maximus. It fell, was buried, and was excavated and re-erected at the Lateran in 1588 by Domenico Fontana for Pope Sixtus V, topped with a cross.

markers.name: Flaminio Obelisk, Piazza del Popolo, Rome
markers.ctx: From the Temple of Ra at Heliopolis: commissioned by Seti I and completed under Ramesses II (13th century BC). Augustus brought it to Rome c.10 BC after the conquest of Egypt and set it on the Circus Maximus; re-erected in the Piazza del Popolo in 1589. The conqueror's trophy: the enemy's sacred monument in your circus.

markers.name: Montecitorio Obelisk, Rome - Sundial
markers.ctx: From Heliopolis. Erected by Psamtik II (590 BC). Augustus used it as gnomon of the Horologium Augusti - a solar meridian line (sundial) in the Campus Martius. The obelisk that tells time. Power measured by the shadow it casts.

markers.name: Obelisk of Theodosius, Istanbul (Hippodrome)
markers.ctx: Upper part of an obelisk of Thutmose III (1479-1425 BC) from Karnak; originally ~30 m, now 18.54 m (25.6 m with base) - the lower part was damaged in antiquity. Constantius II had it taken to Alexandria (357); Theodosius I set it up on the Hippodrome spina in 390. Its marble base shows Theodosius with captives. Egyptian, Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman: it stayed where Theodosius put it.

markers.name: Axum Obelisk (Stele), Axum, Ethiopia
markers.ctx: 24m tall, 1,700 years old. Aksumite Kingdom funerary marker. Looted by Mussolini's troops (1937) - shipped to Rome. Ethiopia demanded return for 60 years. Finally returned 2005 - re-erected 2008. The obelisk stolen by a fascist dictator and returned only after decades of diplomacy. Italy kept it in Rome near the Circus Maximus. Colonialism as interior decorating.

markers.name: Obelisk of Buenos Aires, Plaza de la República
markers.ctx: Built 1936. 67.5m tall. Commemorates 400th anniversary of first founding of Buenos Aires. Not ancient Egyptian - purpose-built. But the form is the message: Argentina declaring itself heir to the power lineage. Every modern city that builds an obelisk is making a claim about what kind of power it wields.

markers.name: Obelisco de São Paulo, Brazil
markers.ctx: Obelisk of Ibirapuera: 72 m travertine-clad obelisk by Galileo Emendabili, begun 1947, opened 9 July 1955, completed 1970 - the largest monument in São Paulo, honouring the dead of the 1932 Constitutionalist Revolution. The obelisk as assertion.

markers.name: Luxor Hotel Obelisk, Las Vegas
markers.ctx: Las Vegas Luxor: a 30-story glass pyramid with a replica obelisk, a sphinx, and the brightest beam of light on Earth shooting from its apex. Ancient Egyptian sacred architecture replicated as a casino. Pharaonic tomb → gambling hall. The sacred reduced to spectacle. The beam is visible from space. The pyramid that prints money.

markers.name: Bunker Hill Monument, Charlestown, Boston
markers.ctx: 67 m (221 ft) granite obelisk by Solomon Willard, erected 1825-1843, commemorating the Battle of Bunker Hill (17 June 1775). Lafayette laid the cornerstone in 1825 with the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts taking part. One of the earliest American obelisks, pre-dating the Washington Monument: military victory inscribed in Egyptian form.

markers.name: Walled Obelisk (Constantine's Obelisk), Istanbul Hippodrome
markers.ctx: The 32 m masonry 'Walled Obelisk', most likely built under Theodosius to mirror the Egyptian Obelisk of Theodosius at the other end of the Hippodrome spina, as Rome's Circus Maximus had two. In the 10th century Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus restored it and sheathed it in gilt bronze plates, later stripped. The masonry copy beside the Egyptian original.

markers.name: Foro Italico Obelisk (Mussolini's Obelisk), Rome
markers.ctx: Carrara-marble monolith inscribed 'MVSSOLINI DVX', 17.5 m high excluding its base (about 36 m overall), inaugurated 4 Nov 1932 at the Fascist sports complex (Foro Mussolini, now Foro Italico); the block was floated to Rome on the Tiber. It still stands. Mussolini put his own name on an obelisk, in the city of taken obelisks.

markers.name: Place Vendôme Column, Paris
markers.ctx: Not an obelisk but a column (1806-1810) modelled on Trajan's Column for Austerlitz. Its 425 bronze relief plates were said to be cast from captured enemy cannon - the propaganda figure is far above the ~180 guns actually taken at Austerlitz. Torn down by the Paris Commune on 16 May 1871 and rebuilt; Gustave Courbet was billed for reconstruction and died in exile in Switzerland. The column made of enemy weapons, destroyed by revolutionaries, rebuilt by the state.

markers.name: Piazza Navona Obelisk (Fountain of Four Rivers), Rome
markers.ctx: Bernini's Fountain of Four Rivers (1651). Roman-made obelisk (not Egyptian import) - cut in Aswan granite imitating pharaonic style. Bernini: four river gods representing the four known continents. The Nile god's head covered - because the Nile's source was unknown. The obelisk sitting on a void: the power symbol whose origin even its makers didn't fully understand.

markers.name: El Obelisco, Avenida 9 de Julio, Buenos Aires
markers.ctx: 71.5 m concrete obelisk built in 1936 for the 400th anniversary of the city's first founding, at the junction of Corrientes and the 9 de Julio, often called the widest avenue in the world. It stood through the 1976-83 junta, whose disappeared are estimated by human-rights groups at 30,000 (contested), and through repeated economic collapses.

markers.name: Rani ki Vav stepwell, Patan, Gujarat, India
markers.ctx: 11th-century stepwell attributed to Queen Udayamati, descending seven levels to the water with more than 500 principal sculptures. Silted over, rediscovered in the 1940s; UNESCO World Heritage site.

markers.name: Aswan Unfinished Obelisk, Egypt
markers.ctx: Would have been the largest obelisk ever: ~42 m and nearly 1,090 tonnes. Abandoned when cracks appeared during quarrying (15th century BC). Still lies in the quarry, carved directly from bedrock - the failure that explained the method.

markers.name: Hanslope Park - Migrated Archives / Operation Legacy, UK
markers.ctx: FCDO site (also home to HM Government Communications Centre) where the 'migrated archives' were held: about 20,000 files from 41 former colonies, removed at independence. The FCO admitted holding them only in 2011, during the Mau Mau veterans' case (Mutua and others v FCO); they were moved to The National Archives (FCO 141). Operation Legacy was the Colonial Office programme to destroy or remove files that could embarrass Britain. Hanslope also held about 1.2 million other unreleased FCO records. Source: Wikipedia, Migrated Archives; Hanslope Park; Operation Legacy.

markers.name: Porton Down - MoD Chemical/Biological Testing, Wiltshire, UK
markers.ctx: UK Ministry of Defence chemical and biological research site. Up to 20,000 servicemen took part in trials (1949-1989; Operation Antler examined 1939-1989), many without proper informed consent, including nerve agents and, in MI6 tests, LSD. Leading Aircraftman Ronald Maddison died after sarin exposure on 6 May 1953; a 2004 inquest found unlawful killing. In 2008 the MoD paid 360 veterans 3 million pounds without admitting liability. Source: Wikipedia, Porton Down; Ronald Maddison.

markers.name: Mururoa Atoll - French Nuclear Testing, French Polynesia
markers.ctx: France conducted 193 nuclear tests in French Polynesia (1966-1996) at Moruroa and Fangataufa - atmospheric until 1974, then underground; Moruroa alone accounts for 175-181. Soldiers, workers and Polynesian civilians were exposed; the state long denied health effects. The Morin law (2010) created a compensation scheme; INSERM published a collective expert report on health consequences in February 2021. The veterans' association Moruroa e Tatou documented contamination. Source: Wikipedia, Moruroa.

markers.name: Reggane - French Nuclear Tests in Algeria (Sahara)
markers.ctx: First French nuclear test 'Gerboise Bleue' (February 13, 1960) - 4x Hiroshima yield. 17 tests in the Algerian Sahara (1960-66) including 4 atmospheric. Local populations (including French soldiers) exposed without warning. Saharan communities still report elevated cancer rates. Files partially declassified 2013 - 53 years after first detonation. France conducted nuclear tests in its colony, then left.

markers.name: Allan Memorial Institute, McGill University, Montreal
markers.ctx: Dr. Donald Ewen Cameron's MKUltra subproject (1957-1964). CIA-funded experiments on Canadian psychiatric patients: 'psychic driving' (continuous playback of recorded messages for weeks), massive electroshock (30-40x normal), drug-induced coma for months, sensory deprivation. Patients' personalities erased. Canadian government settled in 1992, denied residual liability until 2017. Same program as U.S. MKUltra - Five Eyes jurisdiction.

markers.name: Maralinga Nuclear Test Site, South Australia
markers.ctx: British nuclear tests on Maralinga Tjarutja (Pitjantjatjara) land: Operation Buffalo from 27 September 1956 and further major and minor trials to 1963. Aboriginal people were not adequately protected; the 'black mist' accounts come from the earlier Emu Field tests (1953). The McClelland Royal Commission (1984-85) found significant residual contamination, including plutonium; contaminated soil and debris were buried in trenches. Source: Wikipedia, Maralinga.

markers.name: Katyn Forest, Russia (site of NKVD massacre)
markers.ctx: The NKVD executed about 22,000 Polish officers, police and intelligentsia (21,857 per Soviet documents) in April-May 1940. Germany announced the graves in 1943; the USSR blamed the Nazis and tried to charge Katyn at Nuremberg, where the case failed. The USSR acknowledged NKVD guilt only in 1990. Russia's own investigation was closed in 2004 with most of its 183 volumes classified; 137 were handed to Poland in 2010. Source: Wikipedia, Katyn massacre.

markers.name: ESMA (Navy Mechanics School) - Argentine Dirty War, Buenos Aires
markers.ctx: ESMA (Navy Mechanics School), Buenos Aires - the main clandestine detention and torture centre of Argentina's 1976-1983 dictatorship; an estimated 5,000 prisoners passed through, most disappeared, many killed in 'death flights' over the Rio de la Plata and Atlantic. Now the ESMA Museum and Site of Memory. CONADEP's 'Nunca Mas' (1984) documented 8,961 disappearances; human-rights organisations estimate 30,000.

markers.name: Colonia Dignidad, Chile
markers.ctx: German enclave in Chile (founded 1961) run by Paul Schafer, a former Wehrmacht medic. It served as a DINA detention and torture site under Pinochet, a site of systematic child sexual abuse, an arms cache, and reportedly a laboratory for Project Andrea sarin. Schafer fled child-abuse charges in 1996, was arrested in Argentina in 2005 and died in a Chilean prison in 2010. Source: Wikipedia, Colonia Dignidad.

markers.name: Sverdlovsk (Yekaterinburg) - Compound 19 Anthrax Leak Site
markers.ctx: Compound 19 (Sverdlovsk-19), a Soviet military biological facility. An accidental release of anthrax spores in early April 1979 killed at least 68 people downwind (Meselson et al.). Soviet authorities blamed contaminated meat; Yeltsin was reported in May 1992 to have said 'our military development was the cause', though the post-Soviet government maintains the food explanation. Ken Alibek, former first deputy director of Biopreparat, defected in 1992 and described the Soviet offensive bioweapons programme run in breach of the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention. Pin at city level. Source: Wikipedia, Sverdlovsk anthrax leak; Ken Alibek.

markers.name: Stasi Headquarters (Normannenstraße), Berlin
markers.ctx: Ministry for State Security (MfS) headquarters, Lichtenberg. At its height 91,015 staff and about 174,000 unofficial informants (estimates up to 189,000). Officers shredded files as the GDR collapsed; on 15 January 1990 citizens occupied the building to stop the destruction. About 16,000 bags of shredded paper (roughly 45 million pages) are being reassembled by computer. Source: Wikipedia, Stasi.

markers.name: Kamloops Indian Residential School, British Columbia
markers.ctx: Kamloops Indian Residential School (opened 1890). In May 2021 the Tk'emlups te Secwepemc announced ground-penetrating radar results indicating about 200-215 probable unmarked burials in the orchard; the surveyor said only excavation could confirm human remains, and none has been reported. The NCTR documents 51 student deaths at the school. The residential school system (to 1996) took 150,000+ Indigenous children; the TRC (2015) found at least 4,100 died. Other 2021 GPR findings include Marieval (Cowessess First Nation, 751 graves). Source: Wikipedia, Kamloops Indian Residential School.

markers.name: Unit 731 Site, Pingfang District, Harbin, China
markers.ctx: Imperial Japanese Army biological and chemical warfare unit at Pingfang (facility 1936-1945): vivisection, plague bomb tests, frostbite experiments; over 3,000 prisoners killed in the facility and an estimated 200,000-300,000 deaths from biological warfare in China. The US granted immunity to Shiro Ishii and other key members in exchange for research data; the USSR tried twelve members at Khabarovsk in 1949. The Japanese government has never officially acknowledged the programme, though a Tokyo court recognised it in 2002. Source: Wikipedia, Unit 731.

markers.name: Roodeplaat Research Laboratories - Project Coast, Pretoria, South Africa
markers.ctx: Apartheid-era chemical and biological weapons programme (formed 1983 after a 1981 order) led by Wouter Basson, run through front companies including Roodeplaat Research Laboratories. It produced poisons and covert delivery devices; TRC testimony described research into anti-fertility agents aimed at the Black population and attempts to contaminate water with cholera. Much material was destroyed in the early 1990s. Basson was acquitted in 2002. Pin approximate. Source: Wikipedia, Project Coast.

markers.name: In Ekker Nuclear Test Site, Algeria (French underground tests)
markers.ctx: 13 underground French nuclear tests (1961-1966). 'Béryl' test (May 1, 1962) - containment failure caused radioactive cloud to irradiate soldiers and officials including ministers. Footage suppressed for decades. French military personnel ordered to walk through contaminated zone. Algerian independence (1962) did not stop French testing - they continued for 4 more years under treaty provision. The colony that gained independence but not sovereignty over its own soil.

markers.name: Tiananmen Square, Beijing - June Fourth Suppression
markers.ctx: 4 June 1989: troops cleared Tiananmen Square and surrounding streets. Death toll unknown: estimates range from several hundred (US Ambassador Lilley; an NSA cable, 180-500) to about 1,000 (Amnesty), while a disputed British cable from Ambassador Alan Donald, released 2017, relayed a 'minimum' of 10,000 from a single source. The event remains censored in China; the Tiananmen Mothers group has been suppressed. Source: Wikipedia, 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre.

markers.name: Paramount Pictures, Hollywood
markers.ctx: Founded 1912; the last major studio still headquartered in Hollywood (5555 Melrose Ave). The CIA has an entertainment liaison office; military equipment and base access come through the Pentagon's liaison. Paramount: Top Gun (1986), during whose run the Navy staffed recruitment booths at some theatres; Mission: Impossible franchise.

markers.name: Universal Studios, Universal City
markers.ctx: NBCUniversal - owned by Comcast, the largest home internet service provider in the US. The Bourne franchise: CIA assassins, mass surveillance, rogue programs. Jurassic World: InGen's plan to weaponise dinosaurs.

markers.name: Sony Pictures / Columbia, Culver City
markers.ctx: Sony Pictures Entertainment - Columbia Pictures began as CBC Film Sales (1918). Zero Dark Thirty (2012): the CIA cooperated with the filmmakers; an unreleased Defense Department Inspector General draft (reported June 2013) said CIA Director Leon Panetta disclosed classified information at a 2011 CIA ceremony attended by screenwriter Mark Boal. Sony hack (2014), attributed by the US government to North Korea, over 'The Interview'.

markers.name: Walt Disney Studios, Burbank
markers.ctx: Walt Disney testified before HUAC (1947), naming union organizers Herbert Sorrell, David Hilberman and William Pomerance as communist agitators. Made an FBI 'SAC Contact' in 1954 (the FBI calls it largely honorary). 'Man in Space' (ABC, March 1955) featured Wernher von Braun, brought to the US under Operation Paperclip. Disneyland opened the same year. Disney now owns Marvel, Lucasfilm, Pixar, ABC, ESPN and most of National Geographic.

markers.name: Warner Bros. Studios, Burbank
markers.ctx: Warner Bros. Discovery - merged with Discovery (2022). The Matrix franchise. Eyes Wide Shut (1999): Kubrick delivered his final cut on 1 March 1999 and died on 7 March; for the US release Warner digitally obscured parts of the orgy scene with added figures to secure an R rating.

markers.name: Pinewood Studios, Buckinghamshire, UK
markers.ctx: UK film studio, opened 30 September 1936; home of the James Bond franchise. Ian Fleming, Bond's creator, served in Naval Intelligence in WWII (personal assistant to the Director of Naval Intelligence, codename 17F). Also Star Wars and Marvel productions.

markers.name: Elstree Studios, Hertfordshire, UK
markers.ctx: Original Star Wars trilogy (1977-1983), Indiana Jones, The Shining. Adjacent to Elstree film history - Borehamwood was 'British Hollywood.' Also home to Big Brother UK. From Kubrick to reality TV surveillance entertainment - the arc of the panopticon as content.

markers.name: Shepperton Studios, Surrey, UK
markers.ctx: Established 1931 (as Sound City); owned by the Pinewood Group since 2001. Ridley Scott's Alien (1979), The Omen, Gandhi. About 17 miles from central London.

markers.name: Cinecittà Studios, Rome, Italy
markers.ctx: Founded 1937 by Mussolini - 'Cinema City' - as state film infrastructure. Fellini transformed it postwar. Ben-Hur (1959), Cleopatra (1963), Gangs of New York (2002). The fascist infrastructure repurposed but never demolished.

markers.name: Studio Babelsberg, Potsdam, Germany
markers.ctx: World's oldest large-scale film studio (1912). Metropolis (1927, Fritz Lang) - the film that depicted class stratification as architectural fact. UFA under Goebbels: Nazi propaganda machine. Postwar: DEFA (East German state film). Post-reunification: Hollywood productions (Inglourious Basterds, Grand Budapest Hotel). The studio that served Weimar, Nazi, Communist, and capitalist masters. Every regime needs a camera.

markers.name: Mosfilm Studios, Moscow, Russia
markers.ctx: Soviet Union's primary film studio (founded 1920). Eisenstein's 'Battleship Potemkin' (1925) - the film that taught the world montage was a weapon. Soviet cinema as state function: every film approved by Goskino (State Committee for Cinematography). Tarkovsky's 'Stalker' (1979): the Zone as forbidden knowledge territory. Mosfilm still operates. Russia's RT (state media) is the modern continuation - same state, different medium.

markers.name: Mumbai Film City (Goregaon), India
markers.ctx: Film City (Dadasaheb Phalke Chitranagari), Goregaon - production hub of Hindi cinema (Bollywood). Indian cinema as a whole is the world's largest by output - 1,986 features in 2017, of which 364 in Hindi. Content is certified by the Central Board of Film Certification under the Information and Broadcasting Ministry.

markers.name: Ramoji Film City, Hyderabad, India
markers.ctx: Guinness World Record: largest film studio complex (1,666 acres). Telugu, Tamil, Hindi, and international productions. Owned by Ramoji Group (Eenadu media conglomerate). India produces films in 20+ languages - the most linguistically diverse film industry on Earth. Cultural manufacturing at continental scale.

markers.name: Toho Studios, Setagaya, Tokyo, Japan
markers.ctx: Godzilla (1954) - the first film was not entertainment. It was Hiroshima processed through metaphor. The monster created by nuclear radiation, destroying Tokyo - 9 years after the actual nuclear destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Toho produced it. Akira Kurosawa's films also Toho. Japanese cinema's postwar output is atomic trauma rendered as genre. The bomb became a monster. The monster became a franchise.

markers.name: CJ ENM / Korean Film Studios, Seoul
markers.ctx: CJ ENM (entertainment division at Sangam DMC, Mapo-gu) - South Korean cultural export machine, 'Hallyu'. Distributed Parasite (2019, Bong Joon-ho), the first non-English-language Best Picture Oscar winner. The South Korean Ministry of Culture invests directly in cultural export. CJ Group is a Samsung family offshoot.

markers.name: Hengdian World Studios, Zhejiang, China
markers.ctx: One of the largest outdoor film studios in the world - about 331 ha (820 acres), developed from the mid-1990s by the private Hengdian Group. Replicas of the Forbidden City and historical Chinese cities. Films released in China require approval under the CCP Central Propaganda Department's film administration; foreign imports are limited by quota.

markers.name: China Film Group / Beijing Studios
markers.ctx: Party-owned enterprise under the CCP Central Propaganda Department; described as a state monopoly that produces, distributes and regulates imported films (34 revenue-sharing imports a year under the 2012 quota). Hollywood studios have altered content for Chinese market access. Studio base in Huairou District.

markers.name: Nollywood - Lagos Film District, Nigeria
markers.ctx: World's second largest film industry by volume (~2,500 films/year). $6.4B industry. Nollywood emerged from video parlor culture in the 1990s - no state funding, no studio system, pure market-driven production. Films distributed via VCD/DVD/streaming across Africa. Cultural influence: 300M+ viewers across the continent. The film industry that was never designed, never funded, and outproduces Hollywood. Organic cultural manufacturing.

markers.name: Disney Studios Australia (formerly Fox Studios Australia), Sydney
markers.ctx: Owned by The Walt Disney Company (via its 21st Century Fox acquisition) on a 99-year lease from NSW; renamed from Fox Studios Australia in 2022. The Matrix, Moulin Rouge!, Star Wars Episodes II and III, Superman Returns.

markers.name: Weta Workshop / Stone Street Studios, Wellington, NZ
markers.ctx: Weta Workshop (founded 1987 by Richard Taylor and Tania Rodger) and Peter Jackson's Stone Street Studios, both in Miramar, Wellington. Lord of the Rings, King Kong, Avatar.

markers.name: Spring Grove State Hospital, Catonsville, MD
markers.ctx: Spring Grove Hospital Center, Catonsville, Maryland - founded 1797, the second-oldest continuously operating psychiatric hospital in the US. From 1963 to 1976 researchers including Stanislav Grof and Walter Pahnke gave LSD and other psychedelics to patients, including terminally ill cancer patients, in state and federally funded clinical research. No document links this research to the CIA's MKUltra. Source: Wikipedia, Spring Grove Hospital Center.

markers.name: Ionia State Hospital, Michigan
markers.ctx: MKUltra Subproject 53. Dr. James Hamilton conducted experiments on prisoners at the adjacent Ionia State Reformatory - and psychiatric patients at the hospital. LSD, mescaline, scopolamine administered to incarcerated populations who could not leave. Ionia closed 1968. Records largely destroyed. The hospital that experimented on prisoners and called it psychiatry.

markers.name: St. Elizabeths Hospital, Washington D.C.
markers.ctx: St. Elizabeths Hospital, opened 1855 as the Government Hospital for the Insane, the first federally operated psychiatric hospital in the US. Patients included John Hinckley Jr. (1982-2016) and Ezra Pound (1946-1958, found unfit to stand trial for treason). Walter Freeman was its director of laboratories before he developed the transorbital ('ice-pick') lobotomy. The West Campus is now headquarters of the Department of Homeland Security and the Coast Guard. Source: Wikipedia, St. Elizabeths Hospital; Walter Jackson Freeman II.

markers.name: Creedmoor Psychiatric Center, Queens, NY
markers.ctx: MKUltra Subproject 26. Dr. Paul Hoch administered mescaline and LSD to patients. Harold Blauer - tennis professional, admitted for depression - died December 1952 after injection of a mescaline derivative (EA-1298) in Army-funded experiments conducted at New York State Psychiatric Institute (Creedmoor network). Army contract W-18-064-CML-2397. Blauer's family didn't learn the truth for 23 years. The depressed tennis player killed by the Army in a hospital.

markers.name: New York State Psychiatric Institute, Manhattan
markers.ctx: New York State Psychiatric Institute (Columbia University affiliate). Tennis professional Harold Blauer, admitted for depression in late 1952, died on 8 January 1953 after injections of a mescaline derivative (EA-1298, MDA) in an Army Chemical Corps-contracted experiment run by Paul Hoch and James Cattell. His family learned the truth only in 1975. Source: Wikipedia, Harold Blauer; MKUltra.

markers.name: Riverview Hospital (Essondale), Coquitlam, BC, Canada
markers.ctx: British Columbia's psychiatric hospital. LSD experiments on patients (1950s-1960s) parallel to Allan Memorial. Dr. Hollywood (actual name: Dr. J.G. Chicken worked under pseudonym), BC government-funded. Canada's MKUltra participation extended beyond Cameron's Montreal - multiple provincial facilities participated. The Canadian government acknowledged these experiments in 2017. The apology came 60 years after the injury.

markers.name: Oak Ridge - Penetanguishene Mental Health Centre, Ontario
markers.ctx: Maximum security psychiatric facility. Dr. Elliott Barker's 'total encounter capsule' program (1960s-1970s): patients locked naked in a room together for weeks under LSD, forced to undergo 'psychic driving' (borrowed from Cameron at Allan Memorial). Defense Research Board funded. Barker believed he could 'cure' psychopathy through forced intimacy under hallucinogens. The experiment that used one MKUltra technique to treat the damage caused by another.

markers.name: Bethlem Royal Hospital (Bedlam), London, UK
markers.ctx: Bethlem Royal Hospital, founded 1247 as the Priory of St Mary of Bethlehem and among the oldest psychiatric institutions in Europe; its name gave English the word 'bedlam'. In the 17th-18th centuries visitors paid to view patients. On its present Beckenham site since 1930. Source: Wikipedia, Bethlem Royal Hospital.

markers.name: Chelmsford Private Hospital, Sydney, Australia
markers.ctx: Chelmsford Private Hospital, Pennant Hills, Sydney. Harry Bailey's deep sleep therapy (1963-1979): patients kept unconscious for days or weeks with barbiturates, often with ECT. Between 24 and 26 patients died at the hospital; the treatment has been linked to 85 deaths including 19 suicides. Bailey had observed Ewen Cameron's and William Sargant's methods on a WHO fellowship. He died by suicide in 1985 while facing committal proceedings; the Chelmsford Royal Commission followed. Source: Wikipedia, Harry Bailey; Deep sleep therapy.

markers.name: Vipeholm Experiments - Lund, Sweden
markers.ctx: Vipeholm Hospital, Lund (1945-1955): residents with intellectual disabilities were fed large amounts of sticky sweets to provoke tooth decay and study how carbohydrates cause cavities. The study was sponsored by the sugar industry and the dental community, with state involvement; its findings shaped Swedish advice on limiting sweets. Source: Wikipedia, Vipeholm experiments.

markers.name: Pavlov Institute of Physiology, St. Petersburg, Russia
markers.ctx: Pavlov Institute of Physiology (Russian Academy of Sciences), St Petersburg - named for Ivan Pavlov, whose work on conditioned reflexes became foundational to behavioural science. Soviet punitive psychiatry is a separate history (see Serbsky Center).

markers.name: Serbsky State Scientific Center, Moscow, Russia
markers.ctx: Serbsky Center, Moscow - the Soviet Union's central forensic psychiatry institute and a centre of punitive psychiatry. Dissidents were diagnosed with 'sluggish schizophrenia', a diagnosis used almost only in Soviet psychiatry. Gen. Pyotr Grigorenko was declared insane there because he 'was unshakably convinced of the rightness of his actions'. The number of political detainees committed is uncertain. Source: Wikipedia, Serbsky Center; Sluggish schizophrenia.

markers.name: Kasr El Aini Hospital, Cairo, Egypt
markers.ctx: Egypt's oldest hospital (founded 1837). Under Mubarak regime (1981-2011) and el-Sisi (2014-present): psychiatric commitment as political tool. Human Rights Watch documented forced psychiatric evaluations of activists, bloggers, LGBTQ individuals. The pattern: dissident → arrested → 'psychiatric evaluation' → commitment → disappeared from legal system. Same architecture as Soviet punitive psychiatry, different flag. The Cairo version has never been formally investigated.

markers.name: Ankang Institutions - Beijing, China
markers.ctx: Ankang ('Peace and Health'): China's police-run forensic psychiatric hospitals, administered by the Ministry of Public Security. Robin Munro (Human Rights Watch / Geneva Initiative, 2002) documented the committal of political petitioners, Falun Gong practitioners and labour activists, with forced medication. About 20-25 Ankang facilities were reported. Pin approximate (Beijing). Source: Human Rights Watch, Dangerous Minds (2002).

markers.name: Topeka State Hospital, Kansas
markers.ctx: MKUltra Subproject 43 - Dr. Robert Hyde. Connected to Boston Psychopathic Hospital network. Menninger Foundation in Topeka was CIA's preferred psychiatric training ground - Dr. William Menninger served as Army's chief psychiatrist (WWII). Karl Menninger Foundation trained CIA-affiliated psychiatrists who later conducted behavioral experiments across the MKUltra network. The hospital that trained the psychiatrists who ran the other hospitals.

markers.name: Vacaville - California Medical Facility
markers.ctx: California Medical Facility, Vacaville - state prison medical facility. In the late 1960s inmates were reportedly given succinylcholine (Anectine), a paralytic that halts breathing while the subject is conscious, as 'aversion therapy'. A CIA role is not established in the sources read. Source: Wikipedia, California Medical Facility; press reports.

markers.name: MIT - Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA
markers.ctx: MIT Radiation Laboratory (WWII): radar. Lincoln Laboratory (1951): SAGE air defence, missile defence, space surveillance - DoD-funded. Instrumentation Lab (now Draper): Apollo, ICBM and Trident guidance. Epstein gave MIT 10 gifts totalling $850,000 (2002-2017); the nine after his 2008 conviction included $525,000 to the Media Lab (Goodwin Procter report, Jan 2020).

markers.name: Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA
markers.ctx: Stanford Research Institute (1946) formally separated from Stanford in 1970 and kept defence contracts; SRI ran CIA/DIA-funded remote-viewing research in the 1970s-80s. SAIL: DARPA-funded AI research. Ken Kesey volunteered for a CIA-financed MKUltra drug study at the Menlo Park Veterans' Hospital (1959-60), an experience he wrote and lived out with the Merry Pranksters. Stanford alumni founded HP, Cisco, Yahoo and Google.

markers.name: Yale University, New Haven, CT
markers.ctx: Skull and Bones (founded 1832): members include George H.W. Bush (later CIA Director), George W. Bush, John Kerry and William F. Buckley Jr. Yale also produced James Jesus Angleton, CIA counterintelligence chief 1954-1975 (not a Bonesman). Yale's José Delgado implanted radio-controlled brain electrodes - his 1963 bull demonstration was filmed in Córdoba, Spain.

markers.name: Harvard University, Cambridge, MA
markers.ctx: Henry Murray (OSS assessment veteran) ran stress experiments on undergraduates in 1959-62, recognised as purposefully abusive; Ted Kaczynski spent ~200 hours in the study (CIA funding alleged, not established). Timothy Leary and Richard Alpert's Harvard Psilocybin Project, 1960-62. Henry Kissinger: Harvard professor, then National Security Advisor and Secretary of State.

markers.name: Johns Hopkins University / APL, Laurel, MD
markers.ctx: Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (1942): university-affiliated DoD research centre, budget ~$2.09B, 8,800 staff. Missile defence, Aegis, space systems, cyber. APL developed the WWII variable-time proximity fuze. Separately, Johns Hopkins Medicine's psilocybin research under Roland Griffiths (2006-2023).

markers.name: University of Chicago, IL
markers.ctx: Chicago Pile-1: Fermi's team achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction on 2 December 1942 in a rackets court under the west stands of Stagg Field. Separately, the 'Chicago Boys' - Chilean economists trained under Milton Friedman and Arnold Harberger - ran economic policy for Pinochet's junta after the 1973 coup.

markers.name: Columbia University, New York, NY
markers.ctx: Early Manhattan Project research at Columbia (Pupin Hall, 1939-42; later SAM Laboratories). New York State Psychiatric Institute, a Columbia affiliate: tennis player Harold Blauer died there in January 1953 after injections of a mescaline derivative in an Army Chemical Corps experiment. Zbigniew Brzezinski: Columbia professor, then Carter's National Security Advisor during the covert aid to the Afghan mujahideen.

markers.name: Georgetown University, Washington D.C.
markers.ctx: Georgetown's Walsh School of Foreign Service: training ground for U.S. diplomats and national-security officials. Center for Security and Emerging Technology (2019): AI and security think tank funded by Open Philanthropy and others. Alumnus Bill Clinton (SFS '68).

markers.name: University of California, Berkeley
markers.ctx: Ernest Lawrence's Radiation Laboratory: cyclotron, plutonium work, Manhattan Project. UC ran Los Alamos and Livermore for decades and remains a partner in the LLCs that now hold both NNSA contracts. The FBI kept files on UC President Clark Kerr and Free Speech Movement leader Mario Savio and interfered with them under COINTELPRO.

markers.name: Caltech - California Institute of Technology, Pasadena
markers.ctx: Caltech manages JPL, a NASA FFRDC. Jack Parsons, a principal founder of JPL and Aerojet, led the Agape Lodge of Crowley's Thelema in Pasadena and performed the 'Babalon Working' with L. Ron Hubbard (1946); he died in a 1952 explosion ruled accidental. JPL later built the Ranger and Surveyor probes that scouted the Moon for Apollo.

markers.name: Princeton University / IDA, Princeton, NJ
markers.ctx: Institute for Defense Analyses (1956), founded under a university consortium that Princeton joined (oversight ended 1968); its Center for Communications Research, working for the NSA, has been in Princeton since 1959. JASON was first administered through IDA (1960). The separate Institute for Advanced Study hosted Einstein, Oppenheimer and von Neumann.

markers.name: University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia
markers.ctx: Holmesburg Prison experiments (1951-1974): UPenn dermatologist Albert Kligman ran non-therapeutic tests on inmates, including dioxin, drugs and other agents, for the Army and industry (documented in Hornblum, 'Acres of Skin'). ENIAC, the first programmable general-purpose electronic computer, was built at Penn under a WWII Army contract (1945).

markers.name: RAND Corporation, Santa Monica, CA
markers.ctx: Spun off from Project RAND (Douglas Aircraft/USAF) on 14 May 1948. Nuclear strategy and game theory; Herman Kahn's 'On Thermonuclear War'. Daniel Ellsberg worked here before leaking the Pentagon Papers. Paul Baran's 1964 work at RAND on distributed communications was one of the two independent origins of packet switching.

markers.name: Tavistock Institute, London, UK
markers.ctx: Tavistock Institute of Human Relations, founded 20 Sept 1947 out of the Tavistock Clinic by staff including John Rawlings Rees and Wilfred Bion, after their WWII work on Army officer selection and morale. Work on group dynamics and sociotechnical systems (Eric Trist). Rees's 1945 call for psychiatric 'shock troops' is quoted from a lecture (attributed).

markers.name: École Polytechnique, Palaiseau, France
markers.ctx: Founded 1794 during the Revolution; militarised by Napoleon in 1804 and still under the Ministry of the Armed Forces. Its graduates staff the French state's technical corps, the nuclear and aerospace sector and senior government.

markers.name: Technion - Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa
markers.ctx: Israel's premier STEM university. Unit 8200 (SIGINT) recruits heavily from Technion and produces founders: Check Point Software, NSO Group (Pegasus spyware), Cellebrite (phone forensics). The Technion→8200→startup pipeline: military surveillance training → commercial surveillance products. Pegasus zero-click spyware sold to governments that used it on journalists (Jamal Khashoggi's associates, Mexican reporters, Indian activists). The university that trains the coders who build the spyware that surveils the journalists.

markers.name: Moscow State University (MSU), Russia
markers.ctx: Russia's flagship university; its main building (1953, 239 m spire) is the tallest of Stalin's 'Seven Sisters'.

markers.name: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
markers.ctx: China's premier engineering university. Alumni include Xi Jinping (chemical engineering, 1979) and Hu Jintao (hydraulic engineering, 1964).

markers.name: JASON - IDA / MITRE, McLean, VA
markers.ctx: JASON: independent scientific advisory group founded 1960, 30-60 members, mostly physicists, meeting in an annual summer study. Known work: the Vietnam-era McNamara Line, nuclear-weapons issues, early global-warming and acid-rain studies. Administered through the MITRE Corporation; DoD ended the contract in April 2019, then reinstated it.

markers.name: JASON Summer Study - La Jolla, CA
markers.ctx: JASON holds an annual summer study, historically in La Jolla, where its members - academics holding clearances - review problems for DoD, DOE and other sponsors.

markers.name: MITRE Corporation, Bedford, MA
markers.ctx: Not-for-profit spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1958 (SAGE engineers). Manages six federally funded R&D centres serving DoD, the FAA, the IRS and VA, DHS and others. Revenue $2.37B (2023). Administers the JASON advisory group.

markers.name: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, CA
markers.ctx: Nuclear-weapons laboratory founded 2 Sept 1952 (Lawrence and Teller). Designed the W87 (Minuteman III) and later W80 variants. Its National Ignition Facility achieved fusion ignition on 5 Dec 2022: 3.15 MJ out from 2.05 MJ of laser energy. Run by UC until 2007, then by Lawrence Livermore National Security LLC.

markers.name: Los Alamos National Laboratory, NM
markers.ctx: Manhattan Project laboratory (1943) under Oppenheimer; designed both Little Boy and Fat Man. The Trinity site is ~150 miles south. Still one of the two U.S. nuclear-weapons design laboratories. Los Alamos town: ~13,200 people (2020).

markers.name: Psychiatrisch Ziekenhuis Wolfheze (Pro Persona), Netherlands
markers.ctx: Psychiatric hospital founded 1906 on 86 hectares of woodland bought by a Christian care association; merged into De Gelderse Roos (1996), now part of Pro Persona (2009). On 17 Sept 1944, at the opening of Operation Market Garden, English bombers struck the hospital buildings - the Allies suspected German troops there - killing 81; the gliders landed on the nearby Reijerscamp heath. Its 1907 water tower (architect E. Knevel) and other buildings are municipal monuments.

markers.name: Deelen Air Base (Fliegerhorst Deelen), Netherlands
markers.ctx: Luftwaffe Fliegerhorst Deelen (1940-45): night fighters (Bf 110, Ju 88) flew from here; south-west of the field the Diogenes bunker housed the fighter-control centre for the Netherlands, Belgium and northern France. From 1942 a standard-gauge spur (the 'bommenlijntje') ran from Wolfheze station to the base, also used to build the bunker. Post-war a Dutch military airfield. About 9 km north-east of the Hotel de Bilderberg.

markers.name: Hotel Hartenstein / Airborne Museum, Oosterbeek
markers.ctx: Headquarters of the British 1st Airborne Division in the Battle of Arnhem (17-25 Sept 1944); Maj-Gen Roy Urquhart commanded from here. Of 10,095 men landed by parachute and glider, about 2,400 (2,163 British, 160 Poles, 75 Dorsets) were evacuated across the Rhine on 25-26 Sept. Now the Airborne Museum Hartenstein, on the Utrechtseweg about 1 km east of the Hotel de Bilderberg.

markers.name: Laag Wolfheze Estate, Doorwerth
markers.ctx: Rijksmonument (523653-523655): country house built 1919 to designs by ir. Samuel de Clercq, park laid out by Samuel Voorhoeve (1920), and entrance gate (1920), on the Utrechtseweg in Doorwerth, Renkum municipality - about 1.2 km west of the Hotel de Bilderberg.

markers.name: Bilderberg Estate Boundary Post, Oosterbeek
markers.ctx: Municipal monument: boundary post of the former Bilderberg estate (landgoed de Bilderberg), at the Utrechtseweg/Wolfhezerweg junction, Oosterbeek - about 300 m west of the Hotel de Bilderberg, which stands on the former estate and gave the Bilderberg Meeting its name (1954).

markers.name: De Witte Poort (The White Gate), Oosterbeek
markers.ctx: Villa 'De Witte Poort' - The White Gate - Utrechtseweg, Oosterbeek. Built circa 1850. Municipal monument. Part of the 19th-century villa corridor along Utrechtseweg where wealthy Dutch families built estates. White-painted gate/entrance structure. White paint = wealth signal (expensive lead white/titanium dioxide vs. cheap red iron oxide barnpaint). The white gate on the road to the Bilderberg.

markers.name: Kasteel Doorwerth, Renkum
markers.ctx: Water castle on the Rhine floodplain at Doorwerth, Renkum municipality; Rijksmonument 32429. First mentioned in 1260, when it was besieged and burned; rebuilt in stone and enlarged from 1435 under Reinald van Homoet.

markers.name: Howard Lutnick / Cantor Fitzgerald, NYC
markers.ctx: Born 1961. Chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald until Feb 2025, when his sons took over; on 9/11 the firm, in the North Tower, lost all 658 of its 960 New York employees who were in the office, including his brother Gary - he was taking his son to kindergarten. 41st US Secretary of Commerce (sworn in 21 Feb 2025); co-chaired Trump's 2024 transition. Cantor manages Tether's reserves, including over $80bn in Treasuries (attributed). His Manhattan house on East 71st Street, owned since 1998, is next door to Epstein's former townhouse. Before the Senate Appropriations Committee (10 Feb 2026) he acknowledged a December 2012 family lunch with Epstein on Little St. James; in a May 2026 House Oversight interview he described a 2011 visit to Epstein's house about scaffolding and said he saw no improper conduct. Disclosed assets of at least $806M (Jan 2025).

markers.name: Hunneschans (Duno ring-fort), Heveadorp
markers.ctx: Rijksmonument 45966: early-medieval fortification with earthen rampart and moat (Carolingian, c.1000 AD) on the Duno hill at Heveadorp, Renkum municipality. Neolithic/Bronze Age burial mounds lie nearby (rijksmonument 45964).

markers.name: Black Wall Street - Greenwood District, Tulsa OK
markers.ctx: Greenwood District, Tulsa - 'Black Wall Street', one of the wealthiest Black communities in the US. On 31 May-1 June 1921 white mobs, many deputised by city officials, burned more than 35 square blocks. Eyewitnesses describe private aircraft firing on and firebombing the district (attributed). Deaths: official count 36, estimates up to ~300; about 10,000 left homeless; property losses of ~$2.25M (1921). The National Guard interned up to 6,000 Black residents. A grand jury indicted more than 85 people but no one was convicted for the killings or destruction. The survivors' lawsuit was dismissed in 2024; in 2025 the city announced a $105M private trust for descendants.

markers.name: Tulsa Mass Graves - Oaklawn Cemetery
markers.ctx: Oaklawn Cemetery, Tulsa. Eyewitness accounts describe victims of the 1921 massacre buried in unmarked graves, dumped in the river or burned (attributed). The official death toll was 36 (26 Black, 10 white); estimates run to ~300. In October 2020 a forensic team unearthed 11 coffins in a suspected mass grave; later excavations recovered remains with gunshot wounds. Identification continues more than a century later.

markers.name: Tulsa Convention Hall - 1921 Detention Camp
markers.ctx: Convention Hall (now the Tulsa Theater), McNulty Park and the fairgrounds were used to intern up to 6,000 Black residents of Greenwood during the 1921 massacre. Under martial law detainees needed identification cards and release required a white person to vouch for them; meanwhile homes were looted and burned. Guardsmen fired on Black neighbourhoods, including with a machine gun (attributed).

markers.name: Flamingo Hotel - Bugsy Siegel / Meyer Lansky
markers.ctx: Casino opened Dec 26, 1946 (hotel March 1947); the third resort on the Strip and the oldest still operating. Bugsy Siegel took over the project from Billy Wilkerson, with Meyer Lansky's approval as an off-the-books financier. Siegel was shot dead by an unknown gunman at a Beverly Hills home on June 20, 1947; the killing is unsolved.

markers.name: Stardust Casino - Frank Rosenthal / Chicago Outfit
markers.ctx: Argent Corporation (Allen Glick) bought the Stardust in 1974 with Teamsters pension-fund loans; executive Frank 'Lefty' Rosenthal ran casino operations at the Stardust and other Argent properties. A skimming operation was uncovered from 1976; members of organized crime were later convicted over the Las Vegas skim, but Rosenthal was never charged in connection with it. Rosenthal survived a car bomb on Oct 4, 1982. Depicted in 'Casino' (1995). The Stardust closed Nov 1, 2006; its towers were imploded March 13, 2007.

markers.name: Caesars Palace - Jay Sarno / Teamsters Loans
markers.ctx: Opened Aug 5, 1966. Jay Sarno and Stanley Mallin built it with a $10.6M loan (1962) from the Teamsters Central States Pension Fund. Allen Dorfman, the fund's insurance administrator and a close associate of Jimmy Hoffa, was convicted in Dec 1982 of conspiring to bribe U.S. Senator Howard Cannon and was shot dead in a Lincolnwood, Illinois hotel parking lot on Jan 20, 1983, three days before sentencing; the killing is unsolved. Hoffa disappeared in 1975.

markers.name: Havana Casinos - Lansky/Trafficante Pre-Revolution
markers.ctx: Meyer Lansky was associated with the casinos at the Hotel Nacional and the Hotel Riviera in Havana; Santo Trafficante Jr. with the Sans Souci and others. The revolution (Jan 1, 1959) closed the mob-linked casino trade. Where that capital and expertise went after 1959 is a question, not a finding.

markers.name: T-Mobile Arena / Las Vegas Strip - Sports Capital
markers.ctx: Opened Apr 6, 2016 - home of the Vegas Golden Knights (NHL, from 2017). Las Vegas now also hosts the Raiders (NFL, 2020, Allegiant Stadium), the Aces (WNBA), NBA Summer League, the F1 Grand Prix, Super Bowl LVIII (2024), and the planned relocation of the Athletics (MLB). The leagues that long kept away from Las Vegas now hold sports-betting partnerships.

markers.name: Allegiant Stadium - Las Vegas Raiders
markers.ctx: $1.9 billion stadium; $750M of public money raised through a Clark County hotel-room tax (SB1, signed Oct 17, 2016). The Raiders moved from Oakland in 2020; owner Mark Davis, son of Al Davis. Sheldon Adelson (d. 2021) of Las Vegas Sands first backed the project and pledged $650M of his own money, then pulled out in early 2017. The NFL, which suspended players for gambling, relocated a franchise to the gambling capital, with the public paying the largest single share of the stadium.

markers.name: NBA HQ - 645 Fifth Ave, New York
markers.ctx: National Basketball Association headquarters (also Secaucus, NJ). Commissioner Adam Silver (since Feb 2014) wrote a 2014 New York Times op-ed advocating legal, regulated sports betting. Referee Tim Donaghy pleaded guilty in 2007 to federal charges for betting on games and passing information to gamblers; reports of mob involvement were later discounted. The league now has official betting partnerships with sportsbooks. Silver's position: regulate what happens anyway.

markers.name: Tim Donaghy - West Chester, Pennsylvania
markers.ctx: FBI investigation (2007): NBA referee Tim Donaghy bet on games he officiated (2003-07) and passed information to gamblers James Battista and Thomas Martino, high-school classmates. Pleaded guilty Aug 15, 2007; sentenced to 15 months (July 29, 2008). Early reports of mob ties were later discounted; Donaghy alleged other referees and the league office influenced outcomes - the NBA denied it. Question, not finding: one referee went undetected for years.

markers.name: Boston College - 1978-79 Point Shaving
markers.ctx: 1978-79 season: Pittsburgh gamblers Rocco and Tony Perla recruited Boston College player Rick Kuhn; Paul Mazzei brought in Henry Hill and Jimmy Burke of the Lucchese crime family. Gamblers bet against BC on fixed games - the team often still won, just not by the spread. Convicted in 1981: Burke (12 years), Kuhn (10 years, reduced), Mazzei and Tony Perla (10 years), Rocco Perla (4 years); Hill testified. Retold in 'Goodfellas'.

markers.name: Tulane University - 1985 Point Shaving
markers.ctx: Feb 1985: Tulane players shaved points in two home games (Southern Miss Feb 6, Memphis State Feb 20) after student Gary Kranz, who had supplied some of them with cocaine, offered cash; several thousand dollars changed hands. Kranz and others pleaded guilty; star John 'Hot Rod' Williams was acquitted at trial. President Eamon Kelly disbanded the program on April 4, 1985; it returned in 1989.
