markers.name: Arizona State - 1994 Point Shaving
markers.ctx: Former ASU student and campus bookmaker Benny Silman paid guards Stevin 'Hedake' Smith and Isaac Burton to shave points in four games in the 1993-94 season; the team won but failed to cover. Chicago-area bettors were also convicted; Silman says organized-crime figures pressured him to continue. Silman was sentenced to 46 months; Smith to a year and a day.

markers.name: NFL HQ - 345 Park Ave, New York
markers.ctx: National Football League headquarters. Commissioner Roger Goodell repeatedly opposed sports betting until the revenue opportunity became clear. The NFL suspended players for gambling (Paul Hornung 1963, Alex Karras 1963, Art Schlichter, Josh Shaw, Calvin Ridley, etc.) while simultaneously accepting $1B+ annually in gambling advertising revenue. FanDuel, DraftKings, Caesars are all 'official partners.' The league that suspends players for betting profits from the betting industry. $20.2B league revenue (2023).

markers.name: 1958 NFL Championship - 'Greatest Game Ever Played'
markers.ctx: Yankee Stadium, Dec 28, 1958. Baltimore Colts 23, New York Giants 17 (OT) - the game that made the NFL a television product. Colts owner Carroll Rosenbloom was a known gambler; it has been alleged, never established, that he bet on the game. He drowned off Golden Beach, Florida on April 2, 1979 - ruled an accident; a PBS Frontline documentary later suggested he may have been murdered.

markers.name: Art Schlichter - Gambling / Organized Crime
markers.ctx: Ohio State quarterback, 4th overall pick (1982, Baltimore Colts). Lost hundreds of thousands betting; went to the FBI about his bookies in 1983 and was suspended by the NFL (1983). Arrested in New York in 1987 over a sports-betting operation (probation). In 2011 pleaded guilty to state theft/corrupt-activity charges (10 years) and to federal wire-fraud charges over a ticket scheme; federal sentence 10 years 7 months (May 2012), concurrent.

markers.name: Calvin Ridley - NFL Gambling Suspension
markers.ctx: Atlanta Falcons WR suspended indefinitely, through at least the 2022 season, for betting on NFL games in 2021, including on his own team (reported as ~$1,500 in parlays); not accused of fixing anything. Forfeited his $11.1M 2022 salary. The league that suspended him holds sportsbook partnerships.

markers.name: Jerry Jones - Dallas Cowboys / Comstock Resources
markers.ctx: AT&T Stadium, Arlington TX. Jones bought the Cowboys for $140M (Feb 1989); Forbes has since valued them as the world's most valuable sports team (~$10.1B). Jones is also the controlling shareholder of Comstock Resources (oil/gas) through entities he solely owns (~70.9%, 2026 proxy). Pattern: NFL ownership as one holding among energy, real estate, finance and media wealth.

markers.name: Robert Kraft - New England Patriots / Kraft Group
markers.ctx: Gillette Stadium, Foxborough MA. Kraft bought the Patriots for $172M (1994). Kraft Group: paper, packaging, real estate, private equity. Feb 2019: charged with two misdemeanor counts of soliciting prostitution at Orchids of Asia Day Spa, Jupiter FL; police had entered the spa under the banner of a human-trafficking investigation, but prosecutors said in April 2019 there was no evidence of trafficking. Charges dropped in 2020 after Florida courts suppressed the hidden-camera video.

markers.name: Stan Kroenke - LA Rams / Arsenal / KSE
markers.ctx: SoFi Stadium, Inglewood CA. Kroenke owns the LA Rams, Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche, Colorado Rapids, Colorado Mammoth and Arsenal FC; KSE agreed in Sept 2026 to buy the Los Angeles Angels (reported; close expected 2027, pending MLB approval). Married to Ann Walton Kroenke, a Walmart heiress. Cross-border sports ownership as financial network mapping.

markers.name: Comiskey Park - 1919 Black Sox Scandal
markers.ctx: 1919 World Series: eight Chicago White Sox players were accused of losing to the Cincinnati Reds for gamblers' money. Arnold Rothstein's involvement is contested - there is evidence both for and against it. The players were acquitted in court (1921) but banned for life by Commissioner Landis. Rothstein was shot at the Park Central Hotel, NYC, on Nov 4, 1928.

markers.name: Arnold Rothstein - Park Central Hotel, NYC
markers.ctx: Arnold Rothstein, widely reputed to have organized the fix of the 1919 World Series, was shot at the Park Central Hotel on Nov 4, 1928 and died Nov 6. A mentor to Lucky Luciano, Meyer Lansky, Frank Costello and Bugsy Siegel, he is credited with turning organized crime into a business run like a corporation.

markers.name: Pete Rose - Gambling Ban / Hit King
markers.ctx: Riverfront Stadium / Great American Ball Park, Cincinnati. Rose - MLB's all-time hits leader (4,256) - was banned for life by Commissioner Giamatti on Aug 24, 1989 for betting on baseball, including games he managed. He denied it until 2004. Giamatti died of a heart attack on Sept 1, 1989. Rose died Sept 30, 2024; on May 13, 2025 MLB ended permanent bans at death, reinstating him posthumously. MLB now has official partnerships with legal sportsbooks.

markers.name: BALCO Labs - Burlingame, California
markers.ctx: Bay Area Laboratory Co-Operative. Founder Victor Conte distributed the designer steroid THG ('the Clear') and other drugs to athletes; the 2003 federal investigation reached MLB, NFL and Olympic sports, and several athletes, including Marion Jones, later admitted use. Barry Bonds testified to the 2003 grand jury and denied knowingly using steroids; his obstruction conviction was overturned.

markers.name: MLB HQ - 1271 Ave of the Americas, NYC
markers.ctx: Major League Baseball headquarters. MLB has official sports-betting partnerships with several sportsbooks (incl. DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM). Commissioner Rob Manfred. The league that banned Pete Rose for life for betting now earns partnership revenue from legal betting.

markers.name: Houston Astros - Sign Stealing Scandal
markers.ctx: Daikin Park (formerly Minute Maid Park), Houston. MLB found (Jan 13, 2020) the Astros used a camera system to steal signs in 2017 and part of 2018, relaying them by banging a trash can. They won the 2017 World Series. Manager AJ Hinch and GM Jeff Luhnow were suspended one year and fired; players received immunity for cooperating. The title stands.

markers.name: NCAA HQ - Indianapolis, Indiana
markers.ctx: National Collegiate Athletic Association headquarters. Walter Byers, the NCAA's first executive director, wrote that the NCAA developed the term 'student-athlete' to insulate colleges from injured players' disability claims. NCAA v. Alston (2021, unanimous) held that NCAA limits on education-related benefits violate antitrust law; Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence said the NCAA's business model would be flatly illegal in almost any other industry.

markers.name: CCNY - 1950-51 Point Shaving Scandal
markers.ctx: City College of New York. The 1950-51 investigation exposed point shaving at at least seven schools: CCNY, LIU, NYU, Manhattan, Kentucky, Bradley, Toledo. Gamblers included Salvatore Sollazzo and Eli 'Kaye' Klukofsky. CCNY had won both the NIT and NCAA tournament in 1950 - the only team ever to do so. Kentucky's program was suspended for the 1952-53 season.

markers.name: University of Kentucky - Rupp Arena
markers.ctx: UK basketball — the most storied program in college basketball history — was implicated in the 1951 point-shaving scandal. Coach Adolph Rupp initially claimed the fixers 'couldn't touch my boys with a ten-foot pole.' Three players were arrested. The NCAA suspended the program for the entire 1952-53 season. Judge Saul Streit called UK's program 'the acme of commercialism and overemphasis' — in 1951. 75 years later, UK basketball generates $50M+ in annual revenue. The commercialism the judge identified has been formalized, not reformed.

markers.name: Northwestern University - 1995 Point Shaving
markers.ctx: Evanston, IL. In 1995 former Notre Dame kicker Kevin Pendergast, deep in gambling debt, persuaded Northwestern players Kenneth Dion Lee and Dewey Williams to shave points; Pendergast pleaded guilty (1998) to conspiring to fix three games.

markers.name: University of San Diego - Gambling Ring (2011)
markers.ctx: April 2011 federal indictment: former USD assistant coach Thaddeus 'T.J.' Brown (on staff 2006-07), former star Brandon Johnson and others were charged with sports bribery over games in the 2009-10 season. Johnson was sentenced to six months. Point shaving did not stop after each decade's scandal.

markers.name: FIFA HQ - Zurich, Switzerland
markers.ctx: Federation Internationale de Football Association. May 27, 2015: the DOJ indicted 14 FIFA officials and associates on 47 counts including racketeering, wire fraud and money laundering; Swiss police arrested seven officials at the Baur au Lac hotel. The indictment described corruption 'rampant, systemic, and deep-rooted' spanning 24 years, prosecuted under RICO - the statute written for the Mafia. FIFA is a private association under Swiss law.

markers.name: Baur au Lac Hotel - FIFA Arrests, Zurich
markers.ctx: May 27, 2015: Swiss police arrested seven FIFA officials at dawn on U.S. corruption charges as they gathered for the 65th FIFA Congress and presidential election; the U.S. alleged more than $150M in bribes. Hotel staff reportedly held up sheets to shield them from cameras.

markers.name: CONMEBOL HQ - Luque, Paraguay
markers.ctx: South American football confederation. Three successive presidents were indicted in the 2015 U.S. case: Nicolas Leoz (charged 2015, died 2019 in Paraguay without being extradited), Eugenio Figueredo, and Juan Angel Napout (convicted Dec 2017 of racketeering and wire-fraud conspiracy, sentenced 2018 to 9 years). Copa America and Copa Libertadores media rights were sold through bribe-mediated deals.

markers.name: CONCACAF HQ - Miami, Florida
markers.ctx: North/Central American football confederation. Jack Warner (president 1990-2011, Trinidad) and Chuck Blazer (general secretary 1990-2011, USA). Warner was indicted in 2015 and has been fighting extradition from Trinidad; a U.S. court ordered him to repay CONCACAF US$79M in a 2019 default judgment. Blazer became an FBI cooperating witness, pleaded guilty to racketeering, wire fraud, tax evasion and money laundering, and died in 2017 before sentencing. Its top two officials for 21 years: one indicted and abroad, the other a federal informant.

markers.name: Trump Tower - Chuck Blazer's Apartment
markers.ctx: Fifth Avenue, NYC. Chuck Blazer (CONCACAF general secretary, FIFA executive committee) kept two apartments on the 49th floor - one reportedly for his cats. He failed to file U.S. tax returns for years, became an FBI cooperating witness (from 2011) and pleaded guilty to tax evasion, racketeering, wire fraud and money laundering; he died in 2017.

markers.name: Qatar - 2022 FIFA World Cup
markers.ctx: FIFA awarded Qatar the 2022 World Cup on Dec 2, 2010. A 2020 U.S. indictment alleged bribes to FIFA executive-committee members to vote for Qatar. The Guardian (Feb 2021) found 6,500+ migrant workers from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka died in Qatar since 2010 - across all sectors, during a building programme largely for the tournament; 37 deaths were directly linked to stadium construction. 69% of Indian, Nepali and Bangladeshi deaths were recorded as 'natural'. Workers were bound by the kafala sponsorship system.

markers.name: Russia - 2018 FIFA World Cup
markers.ctx: FIFA awarded Russia the 2018 World Cup on Dec 2, 2010, in the same vote as Qatar. A 2020 U.S. indictment alleged Jack Warner received $5M in wire transfers to vote for Russia. FIFA's own inquiry, the Garcia Report (2014), was kept secret and summarized in a way Garcia called 'materially incomplete' with 'erroneous representations'. Russia hosted the tournament four years after annexing Crimea, with the Donbas war ongoing.

markers.name: Bochum, Germany - Match Fixing Hub
markers.ctx: Nov 2009: Bochum prosecutors and German police exposed a match-fixing network covering about 200 fixtures in nine European countries, including UEFA Europa League and Champions League qualifiers - 'the biggest match-fixing scandal ever to hit Europe' (UEFA). Croatian brothers Ante and Milan Sapina were arrested on Nov 19, 2009; Ante Sapina was sentenced to five and a half years (May 2011). Bets were placed with Asian bookmakers.

markers.name: Singapore - Dan Tan / Global Match Fixing
markers.ctx: Dan Tan Seet Eng - charged in Italy (2011) and Hungary over match fixing; Interpol called him the 'boss' of the world's largest and most aggressive match-fixing syndicate. Singapore, which has no extradition treaty with the EU, detained him without trial in 2013; its Court of Appeal ordered his release in Nov 2015.

markers.name: Calciopoli - Rome / Italian Football Fixing
markers.ctx: 2006 Italian football scandal: wiretaps showed Juventus general manager Luciano Moggi working FIGC and referee-designator contacts to influence referee selection. Juventus was stripped of two Serie A titles and relegated; AC Milan, Fiorentina, Lazio, Reggina and Arezzo were penalized. Moggi was banned by sporting courts; his criminal case ended in 2015 with the main charge time-barred.

markers.name: IOC HQ - Lausanne, Switzerland
markers.ctx: International Olympic Committee headquarters. A private association under Swiss law with special recognized status - the same Swiss-seat pattern as FIFA and the BIS. IOC members are a self-electing body. The IOC chooses host cities and its 'official partners'.

markers.name: Salt Lake City - 2002 Olympic Bribery Scandal
markers.ctx: Late 1998: it emerged that Salt Lake's bid committee had given IOC members and relatives cash, scholarships and gifts to win the 2002 Winter Games. The IOC recommended expelling six members. Bid leaders Tom Welch and Dave Johnson were charged with 15 counts of bribery and fraud and acquitted of all charges in December 2003.

markers.name: Rio de Janeiro - 2016 Olympics / Corruption
markers.ctx: 2016 Summer Olympics. Brazilian authorities say Brazilian Olympic Committee president Carlos Nuzman was central to channelling $2M to IOC member Lamine Diack to buy votes for Rio's 2009 selection. Arrested Oct 2017 (released to house arrest after 15 days); sentenced Nov 2021 to 30 years 11 months for corruption, organized crime, money laundering and currency evasion.

markers.name: Sochi - 2014 Winter Olympics / $51 Billion
markers.ctx: Most expensive Olympics in history: ~$51 billion including regional infrastructure, against a $12B budget. Opposition politician Boris Nemtsov, a Sochi native, published reports estimating that $25-30B was embezzled; he was shot four times on a bridge near the Kremlin on Feb 27, 2015. Russia's state doping programme was exposed by Grigory Rodchenkov, former Moscow anti-doping lab director, now under U.S. witness protection.

markers.name: Beijing - 2008/2022 Olympics / Dual Host
markers.ctx: Beijing is the only city to host both Summer (2008) and Winter (2022) Olympics. Estimates put the 2008 Games at $40-44B (official figure about $15B) - the most expensive Summer Olympics. Rights groups documented evictions, surveillance expansion and press restrictions. The 2022 Games went ahead amid UN and satellite-imagery documentation of mass detention in Xinjiang.

markers.name: Berlin - 1936 Olympics / Nazi Propaganda
markers.ctx: Olympiastadion. Hitler's Olympics - the template for international sport as state propaganda. Leni Riefenstahl's 'Olympia' (1938) set the look of sports filmmaking. Jesse Owens won four gold medals and returned to a segregated America. Coca-Cola's German subsidiary supplied and promoted the drink at the Games. The IOC kept the Games in Nazi Germany and the U.S. took part.

markers.name: Munich - 1972 Olympics / Black September
markers.ctx: Olympiapark. Sept 5, 1972: Black September killed two members of the Israeli team and took nine hostage; the West German rescue attempt at Fuerstenfeldbruck airbase failed - all nine hostages, five attackers and one police officer died (11 Israelis in all: 6 coaches, 5 athletes). Israel followed with Mossad's Operation Wrath of God. IOC President Avery Brundage, who had been involved with the 1936 Games, kept the Olympics going.

markers.name: Atlanta - 1996 Olympics / Centennial Park Bombing
markers.ctx: Centennial Olympic Park bombing, July 27, 1996. Pipe bomb killed Alice Hawthorne, injured 111. Eric Robert Rudolph was the bomber — domestic terrorist who also bombed abortion clinics and a lesbian nightclub. Security guard Richard Jewell, who discovered the bomb and saved lives, was falsely accused by the FBI and destroyed by media coverage. The FBI's incorrect investigation ruined an innocent man while the actual bomber evaded capture for 5 years. The Olympics as a target, the investigation as a pattern of institutional failure.

markers.name: Tilman Fertitta - Toyota Center, Houston
markers.ctx: Owns the Houston Rockets (bought for $2.2B, 2017) and Landry's (Golden Nugget casinos, restaurants). Reported lead shareholder in Wynn Resorts (2025). U.S. Ambassador to Italy since May 2025. An NBA team owner who also owns casinos, in a league whose integrity rules bar players from betting.

markers.name: MGM Resorts HQ - Las Vegas
markers.ctx: MGM Resorts International (founded by Kirk Kerkorian). Official gaming partner of major U.S. leagues; BetMGM is a 50/50 joint venture with Entain (formerly GVC Holdings), formed 2018. Revenue $17.5B (2025). Its Strip portfolio came largely from the 2000 Mirage Resorts merger (Bellagio, Mirage - sold to Hard Rock in 2022) and the 2005 Mandalay merger.

markers.name: FanDuel HQ - New York
markers.ctx: Parent company: Flutter Entertainment (registered in Dublin, operational headquarters New York; NYSE-listed), the world's largest online betting company - owner of FanDuel, Paddy Power, Betfair, PokerStars, Sky Betting & Gaming and Sportsbet. FanDuel is an official partner of U.S. leagues.

markers.name: DraftKings HQ - Boston
markers.ctx: Founded 2012 in Boston as a daily fantasy sports operator under the fantasy-sports carve-out in the Unlawful Internet Gambling Enforcement Act; moved into sportsbooks after Murphy v. NCAA (2018). Official partner of major U.S. leagues.

markers.name: Kroenke Sports & Entertainment - Denver
markers.ctx: Ball Arena, Denver. Stan Kroenke (married to Walmart heiress Ann Walton Kroenke) owns the LA Rams (NFL), Denver Nuggets (NBA), Colorado Avalanche (NHL), Colorado Rapids (MLS), Colorado Mammoth (NLL) and Arsenal FC; KSE agreed in Sept 2026 to buy the Los Angeles Angels (MLB), pending approval. One family's franchises across sports and two countries.

markers.name: Madison Square Garden - Dolan / MSG Networks
markers.ctx: Home of the NY Knicks (NBA) and NY Rangers (NHL), owned by Madison Square Garden Sports. James Dolan, son of Cablevision founder Charles Dolan and former Cablevision CEO, runs MSG Sports and MSG Entertainment (the venue) and chairs Sphere Entertainment and MSG Networks (regional sports broadcasting). The family's companies take revenue at venue, broadcast, advertising and tickets.

markers.name: Crypto.com Arena - AEG / Philip Anschutz
markers.ctx: Formerly Staples Center. Philip Anschutz's AEG owns the LA Kings (NHL) and LA Galaxy (MLS) and operates venues worldwide. Anschutz also owns the Washington Examiner, owned The Weekly Standard (bought 2009, closed 2018) and the San Francisco Examiner (2004-2011); previously Regal Cinemas and Qwest; oil and gas. Sports, venues and conservative media under one private owner.

markers.name: Chase Center - San Francisco / Lacob-Guber
markers.ctx: Golden State Warriors arena. Principal owner Joe Lacob is a former partner at Kleiner Perkins; co-owner Peter Guber is a former chairman of Sony Pictures (Mandalay Entertainment). Venture capital and Hollywood money in NBA ownership.

markers.name: Barclays Center - Brooklyn / Joe Tsai
markers.ctx: Brooklyn Nets arena. Joe Tsai - Alibaba co-founder and chairman (since 2023) - bought 49% of the Nets in 2017 (team valued at $2.3B) and the rest in 2019, buying the arena for nearly $1B separately. Also owns the New York Liberty (WNBA), San Diego Seals and Las Vegas Desert Dogs (NLL). China's 2017 National Intelligence Law obliges companies there to assist state intelligence work - a fact about the jurisdiction, not about the owner.

markers.name: U.S. Supreme Court - Murphy v. NCAA (2018)
markers.ctx: May 14, 2018: the Supreme Court held that PASPA (1992) violated the anti-commandeering doctrine (7-2) and struck the whole law (6-3); Justice Alito wrote for the majority. State-by-state legalization followed rapidly.

markers.name: Calabasas Crash Site - N72EX / Kobe Bryant
markers.ctx: Jan 26, 2020. Sikorsky S-76B (N72EX, built 1991), 9 killed including Kobe Bryant. Formerly the State of Illinois' N761LL (2007-2015). Island Express removed the cockpit voice recorder shortly after acquiring it (March 2016); no flight data recorder and no terrain warning system (not required). The operator's certificate was VFR-only. Pilot Ara Zobayan: 8,577 hours, ~75 IFR. NTSB probable cause (Feb 2021): the pilot's decision to continue VFR flight into instrument conditions, leading to spatial disorientation and loss of control; self-induced pressure contributed.

markers.name: Island Express Helicopters - Long Beach, CA
markers.ctx: Operator of N72EX. Removed the cockpit voice recorder after acquiring the helicopter (March 2016). Its Part 135 certificate allowed VFR-only flights. After the crash it called it 'an act of God' and cross-claimed against FAA controllers. The NTSB nonetheless determined probable cause: pilot continued VFR flight into cloud.

markers.name: Sikorsky / Lockheed Martin - Stratford, CT
markers.ctx: Manufacturer of the S-76 and UH-60 Black Hawk; owned by United Aircraft/United Technologies 1929-2015 and by Lockheed Martin since Nov 2015. Its MATRIX autonomy technology (from DARPA's ALIAS program) flies the optionally piloted Black Hawk. The 1991 S-76B N72EX had no such system; the NTSB found pilot disorientation in cloud.

markers.name: Colosseum - Rome (The Original 'Baal Game')
markers.ctx: Opened 80 AD under Emperor Titus. Capacity 50,000-80,000. Gladiatorial combat, animal hunts, executions, naval battles. Free admission — funded by the state (et circenses). The operational template: spectacle as social control. The population is fed and entertained; the rulers govern without resistance. The Colosseum was not entertainment — it was governance infrastructure. Bread and circuses is not a metaphor. It is an engineering specification. Every modern stadium is an iteration of this design: public subsidy, private profit, mass distraction, political utility.

markers.name: Circus Maximus - Rome
markers.ctx: Chariot-racing venue; probably ~150,000 seats (Pliny's 250,000 is considered too high). Used from Rome's regal era until the last recorded races in 549 AD. Racing factions (Blues, Greens, Reds, Whites) worked like franchises with patrons and betting. The same factions drove the Nika riots of 532 AD at the Hippodrome of Constantinople, which nearly toppled Justinian - about 30,000 killed.

markers.name: Olympia, Greece - Ancient Olympic Games
markers.ctx: The Olympic Games were traditionally founded here in 776 BC as a religious festival to Zeus, with a sacred truce (ekecheiria) between city-states. Athletes competed nude; married women were excluded (per Pausanias). The last recorded games were in 393 AD under Theodosius I; they likely ended under Theodosius II. The IOC (founded 1894) revived the Games in 1896 without the religious content.

markers.name: Musée du Louvre, Paris
markers.ctx: 615,000+ objects, 35,000 on display. Originally a royal palace. Under Napoleon it became the Musée Napoléon, filled with art seized from conquered states; Vivant Denon, who accompanied Napoleon to Egypt, directed it. The Mona Lisa was brought to France by Leonardo and acquired by Francis I after his death in 1519. The museum as empire.

markers.name: Getty Museum / Getty Villa, Los Angeles
markers.ctx: J. Paul Getty - oil fortune (Getty Oil, later Texaco then Chevron). Getty Villa: 44,000 Greek, Roman and Etruscan antiquities. Curator Marion True (1986-2005) was charged in Italy and Greece over looted antiquities; the cases ended without conviction (statute of limitations), and the Getty returned 40 objects to Italy and others to Greece. Endowment ~$9.4bn (2025), the largest of any art institution.

markers.name: Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Bentonville, AR
markers.ctx: Alice Walton - Walmart heir (net worth ~$134bn, 2026). The Walton Family Foundation endowed Crystal Bridges with ~$800M for construction, acquisitions and operations, in Walmart's home town. Collection includes Durand, Rockwell, Warhol, Rothko. Walmart is the largest private US employer; studies have counted many of its workers on public assistance (attributed). Retail fortune converted into a tax-advantaged philanthropic institution.

markers.name: National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City
markers.ctx: Aztec Sun Stone, Olmec colossal heads, Maya jade masks; 600,000+ artefacts. Built 1964 by the modern Mexican state to present a pre-Hispanic heritage destroyed by the Spanish conquest. On 25 Dec 1985 two students stole 124 artefacts; most were recovered in 1989. The museum as the state's claim to a heritage it inherited from conquest.

markers.name: Acropolis Museum, Athens
markers.ctx: Built 2009, €130M. Entire floor designed with empty spaces — reserved for the Parthenon Marbles currently in the British Museum. Lord Elgin removed them 1801-1812 from the Parthenon under an Ottoman permit of questionable validity. Greece has demanded return since independence (1832). The museum that was architecturally designed around its own absence — the building is a repatriation argument.

markers.name: Royal Museum for Central Africa, Tervuren, Belgium
markers.ctx: Built to showcase Leopold II's Congo Free State at the 1897 International Exposition, financed by profits from a forced-labour rubber regime under which millions died (estimates range widely, up to ~10 million - contested). For a century it presented the colonial 'civilising mission'. Reopened 2018 as the AfricaMuseum; the building itself is the artefact.

markers.name: National Museum of Brazil, Rio de Janeiro
markers.ctx: Brazil's oldest scientific institution (1818), in the former Imperial Palace; ~20 million items. Fire on 2 Sept 2018 destroyed most of the collection (reported 92.5%), after years of budget cuts (maintenance reportedly ~$13,000/year - attributed). Luzia, an 11,500-year-old skeleton, was fragmented in the fire; most of her remains were recovered.

markers.name: National Museum of China, Beijing
markers.ctx: East side of Tiananmen Square. 1.3 million objects. Formed 2003 from the Museum of the Revolution and the Museum of Chinese History. Its permanent exhibitions frame 5,000 years of history as leading to Communist Party rule, on the square where the 1989 protests were crushed.

markers.name: Topkapi Palace Museum, Istanbul
markers.ctx: Ottoman imperial residence (1478-1853). Holds relics attributed to Muhammad (sword, cloak) and claimed relics of Moses and Joseph. The Harem: some 300-400 rooms. After the sultanate was abolished (1922), the palace became a museum in 1924. The seat of an empire spanning Europe and Asia, now a tourist site.

markers.name: Frick Collection, New York
markers.ctx: Henry Clay Frick: chairman of Carnegie Steel during the Homestead Strike (1892) - hired Pinkerton agents; seven strikers and three Pinkertons were killed. Anarchist Alexander Berkman tried to assassinate Frick; Frick survived and broke the union. The fortune built this Fifth Avenue mansion-museum: Vermeer, Rembrandt, Bellini, Holbein. The Pinkerton budget became the Vermeer budget.

markers.name: National Palace Museum, Taipei
markers.ctx: 696,000+ objects — Chinese imperial collection spanning 8,000 years. Chiang Kai-shek evacuated the collection from Beijing's Forbidden City (1948-49) during the Chinese Civil War — 2,972 crates shipped to Taiwan in three shipments. The mainland government calls it theft. Taiwan calls it preservation. The museum whose entire collection is a political argument about which China is the real one.

markers.name: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam
markers.ctx: Dutch Golden Age collection. Rembrandt's Night Watch. Vermeer's Milkmaid. The 'Golden Age' was funded by the VOC (Dutch East India Company) — the world's first multinational corporation, first to issue stock, and the organization that colonized Indonesia, South Africa, and controlled the global spice trade through military force. The museum celebrates the art produced by the profits of the first corporate empire.

markers.name: Museo del Prado, Madrid
markers.ctx: Opened 1819 from the Spanish royal collection: Velázquez, Goya, El Greco, Bosch. The Habsburg and Bourbon crowns that assembled it drew silver from Potosí, worked by forced indigenous (mita) and enslaved labour, and ruled one of the largest empires in history. Las Meninas was painted while Potosí's silver was arriving in Seville.

markers.name: Natural History Museum, London
markers.ctx: 80 million specimens. Founded 1881 from British Museum's natural history collection. Darwin's specimens. Colonial-era botanical, zoological, and geological specimens collected from every continent Britain controlled. Specimen collecting was mapping for extraction — catalogue the resources, then send the companies. The museum as inventory ledger for the empire's resource base.

markers.name: Art Institute of Chicago
markers.ctx: Founded 1879. One of the largest Impressionist collections outside Paris; Seurat's Sunday Afternoon, Wood's American Gothic. Board historically drawn from Chicago's industrial fortunes (Armour meat-packing, railroads, real estate), the same circle behind the 1893 World's Fair that also founded the nearby Field Museum.

markers.name: Deutsches Museum, Munich
markers.ctx: World's largest museum of science and technology. 28,000+ objects. V-2 rocket on display — the weapon built by slave labor at Mittelbau-Dora (20,000 deaths). Werner von Braun artifacts. Enigma machines. The museum that displays the technology without the slaves who built it. Science and technology museums worldwide follow this template: celebrate the invention, omit the human cost.

markers.name: International Spy Museum, Washington D.C.
markers.ctx: Founded by Milton Maltz (Malrite Communications), opened 19 July 2002; now an independent non-profit, at L'Enfant Plaza since 2019. Large public collection of espionage artefacts; advisers have included former intelligence directors. The public version of the story, told while the classified one continues.

markers.name: Potosí (Cerro Rico), Bolivia - Colonial Silver
markers.ctx: Cerro Rico, 'the mountain that eats men'. Mined for silver from 1545, the richest silver source in history; its output financed the Spanish Empire. Deaths under colonial forced labour are contested - estimates run from hundreds of thousands to eight million, the latter possibly for the whole Viceroyalty of Peru. Mining continues today.

markers.name: Kimberley, South Africa - De Beers 'Big Hole'
markers.ctx: Cecil Rhodes founded De Beers in 1888. The Big Hole was long considered the largest hand-dug excavation on Earth (a 2005 re-examination suggests Jagersfontein or Bultfontein may be larger). Diamonds -> De Beers monopoly -> 'A Diamond Is Forever' (1947) -> managed scarcity. Rhodes' fortune funds the Rhodes Scholarships (Bill Clinton, Pete Buttigieg, Susan Rice, Rachel Maddow) and financed the Round Table movement, which is credited with influencing the Council on Foreign Relations (attributed; Section VII).

markers.name: Witwatersrand Basin, South Africa - Gold
markers.ctx: World's largest known gold reserves; over 40,000 tonnes produced, about 22% of all gold ever mined. Anglo American, founded by Ernest Oppenheimer, came to control much of its gold and, through De Beers, diamonds (attributed). The mines ran on migrant labour - single-sex hostels, families left behind, a fraction of white wages - begun under colonial rule and entrenched under apartheid. South African gold underpinned the gold-backed Bretton Woods order.

markers.name: Marikana, South Africa - Lonmin Platinum Massacre
markers.ctx: 16 August 2012: South African Police Service shot dead 34 striking Lonmin rock-drill operators and wounded 78; ten others, including police and guards, had died in the days before. The strikers wanted R12,500 a month. Cyril Ramaphosa, then a Lonmin board member, emailed that the events were 'dastardly criminal' and needed 'concomitant action'; he apologised for the phrasing in 2017. The Farlam Commission absolved him of wrongdoing and found police commanders had tried to mislead the public and the inquiry. Lonmin was acquired by Sibanye-Stillwater (2019).

markers.name: Bingham Canyon Mine, Utah - Kennecott/Rio Tinto
markers.ctx: The largest human-made excavation and deepest open-pit mine in the world: over 1.2 km deep and 4 km wide, mined since 1906, now by Rio Tinto's Kennecott subsidiary. It has produced more copper than any mine in history - over 17 million tonnes. In April 2013 a slide inside the pit, possibly the largest non-volcanic landslide in North American history, buried part of the pit. Mining continued.

markers.name: Panguna Mine, Bougainville, PNG - Rio Tinto Civil War
markers.ctx: Open-pit copper-gold mine run 1972-1989 by Bougainville Copper Ltd, a Rio Tinto (CRA) subsidiary. Landowner anger over pollution and revenue fed the Bougainville Civil War (1988-1998); estimates of Bougainvillean dead run from 15,000 to 20,000. After the rebels declared independence in May 1990, PNG blockaded the island with UH-1 helicopters and patrol boats Australia had supplied as aid. Closed since 1989.

markers.name: Ok Tedi Mine, Papua New Guinea - BHP Environmental Disaster
markers.ctx: Ok Tedi copper-gold mine, operated by BHP until 2002. In 1999 BHP reported that about 90 million tonnes of mine waste a year had been discharged into the Ok Tedi and Fly rivers for over a decade, destroying downstream villages, farms and fisheries; about 1,588 km2 of forest has died or is under stress. BHP's CEO said the mine was 'not compatible with our environmental values'. BHP left in 2002 by transferring its stake to the PNG Sustainable Development Program.

markers.name: Morenci Mine, Arizona - Freeport-McMoRan
markers.ctx: One of the largest copper mines in North America, now Freeport-McMoRan's (which absorbed Phelps Dodge in 2007). The 1903 Morenci strike by mostly Mexican-American miners ended when a flash flood killed 40-50 people before an expected clash with troops. In the 1917 Bisbee Deportation, Phelps Dodge and sheriff's deputies loaded about 1,300 striking miners onto cattle cars and left them in the New Mexico desert.

markers.name: Yanacocha Mine, Peru - Newmont Gold
markers.ctx: Largest gold mine in South America, wholly owned by Newmont since 2022. On 2 June 2000 a contractor's truck spilled 151 kg of the mine's mercury in Choropampa; government estimates put the poisoned at more than 900. The Conga expansion was stalled by mass protests (2011-12); subsistence farmer Máxima Acuña refused to leave her land and won the Goldman Environmental Prize (2016).

markers.name: Chuquicamata, Chile - World's Largest Copper Open-Pit
markers.ctx: Codelco's open pit, among the largest by excavated volume; mined industrially since 1915 under the Guggenheims and then Anaconda. Allende's government nationalised copper in 1971 ('copper is Chile's wage'), taking Anaconda's and Kennecott's mines; ITT had offered the CIA $1 million in 1970 to stop Allende (attributed). The CIA funded his opponents; its role in the 11 September 1973 coup itself is contested. Nationalisation and coup share a timeline - that is not a chain.

markers.name: Mountain Pass Mine, California - U.S. Rare Earths
markers.ctx: The only rare-earth mining and processing site in the United States (15.8% of world output in 2020), owned since 2017 by MP Materials, whose largest holders were JHL Capital, QVT Financial and CEO James Litinsky, with China's Shenghe Resources holding about 7.7%. In July 2025 the Department of Defense agreed a deal making it MP's largest shareholder. China mined about 69% of the world's rare earths in 2025 (USGS) and dominates processing.

markers.name: Broken Hill, Australia - Origin of BHP
markers.ctx: BHP - the Broken Hill Proprietary Company - was founded here in 1885 by Charles Rasp and six partners to mine silver, lead and zinc. Now BHP Group, the world's largest mining company by market capitalisation (2025), operating worldwide. The company still carries the name of its first mine.

markers.name: Olympic Dam, South Australia - BHP Uranium
markers.ctx: BHP's underground copper-uranium-gold-silver mine (since 1988): the world's largest known single uranium deposit. A planned open-pit expansion was postponed indefinitely in August 2012. The Roxby Downs (Indenture Ratification) Act 1982 set the mine's legal framework; Aboriginal elders, including Arabana elder Kevin Buzzacott, have challenged its approvals.

markers.name: Rössing Mine, Namibia - Uranium
markers.ctx: The longest-running and one of the largest open-pit uranium mines (Namib Desert, since 1976). Run by Rio Tinto through South Africa's occupation of Namibia until independence in 1990, drawing anti-apartheid protests. Rio sold its 68.6% to China National Uranium Corporation in 2018-19. Iran's government has held 15% since 1976; reports of uranium diversion to Iran have been denied by the mine and by Namibia.

markers.name: Tenke Fungurume, DRC - CMOC Cobalt/Copper
markers.ctx: Copper-cobalt mine in Lualaba. China Molybdenum (CMOC) bought Freeport-McMoRan's stake for US$2.65 billion in 2016 and holds 80%. In 2022 state miner Gécamines claimed CMOC owed it up to $5 billion and a court-appointed administrator suspended exports. The DRC mined about 73% of the world's cobalt in 2025 (USGS). Same belt as Kolwezi and Lubumbashi.

markers.name: Serra Pelada, Pará, Brazil - Open-Pit Gold Rush
markers.ctx: 1980s gold rush. 100,000+ garimpeiros (artisanal miners) in a single open pit. Sebastião Salgado's photographs documented the scene: ant-like columns of mud-covered men carrying sacks up vertical ladders. No machines — pure human labor extraction. The images are indistinguishable from ancient slave mining. Mercury contamination destroyed the surrounding ecosystem. The mine is now a lake. The gold is in bank vaults; the mercury is in the water table.

markers.name: Mt. Shasta, Siskiyou County, California
markers.ctx: 14,179 ft stratovolcano. Subject of a Lemuria legend that grew from an 1880s mention to a hidden-city story by 1925-31 (Cerve). Lava tubes on its flanks. Sacred to Native peoples. Marked as an 'entrance' on a 1978 'Inner-Earth' map (a private map, not a government one).

markers.name: Mt. Rainier, Washington
markers.ctx: 14,411 ft, highest peak of the Cascades; summit steam caves. Kenneth Arnold's 1947 sighting near the mountain gave rise to the term 'flying saucers'. Paradise Ice Caves documented from 1908. Marked on a 1978 'Inner-Earth' map.

markers.name: Carlsbad Caverns, New Mexico
markers.ctx: 119 known caves in a Permian reef (~265 million years). The Big Room - almost 4,000 ft long, 255 ft high - is the largest cave chamber in North America. Nearby Lechuguilla Cave is 1,588 ft deep, seventh-deepest in the U.S. Marked on a 1978 'Inner-Earth' map.

markers.name: Mammoth Cave, Kentucky
markers.ctx: Longest known cave system in the world: more than 426 miles surveyed (2025). Several levels, underground rivers. Prehistoric Native mining; saltpeter mining for gunpowder in the War of 1812; tuberculosis hospital in the cave (1840s). Marked on a 1978 'Inner-Earth' map.

markers.name: Lava Beds National Monument, California
markers.ctx: Hundreds of lava-tube caves on the flank of Medicine Lake Volcano, ~40 miles NE of Mount Shasta. In the Modoc War (1872-73) Kintpuash (Captain Jack)'s band held the lava beds against the U.S. Army for months before defeat. Marked on a 1978 'Inner-Earth' map.

markers.name: Yucca Mountain, Nevada
markers.ctx: Proposed high-level waste repository; ~5 miles of exploratory tunnel in volcanic tuff ~1,000 ft down. Funding ended April 2011 under Obama. Designed for 70,000 metric tons; U.S. spent fuel instead sits at 76 reactor sites in 34 states. ~45 miles SW of Area 51; on land claimed by the Western Shoshone under the 1863 Ruby Valley treaty.

markers.name: China Lake NAWS, Ridgecrest, California
markers.ctx: 1.1 million acres - the U.S. Navy's largest single landholding (85% of its land for weapons R&D). Navy since 1943. The July 2019 Ridgecrest earthquakes (M6.4, M7.1) struck largely within the base; the M7.1 was California's strongest since 1999. Marked on 1978 and 1996 'underground base' maps.

markers.name: Tonopah Test Range, Nevada
markers.ctx: DOE range managed by Sandia within the Nevada Test and Training Range. The F-117 Nighthawk wing operated secretly from its airfield from 1983, was acknowledged in November 1988, and moved to Holloman AFB around 1992. ~70 miles NW of Area 51.

markers.name: Dugway Proving Ground, Utah
markers.ctx: Army chemical and biological test range since 1942, 801,505 acres. 1968 Dugway sheep incident. Project SHAD-era open-air tests in the 1960s. On 26 Jan 2011 the base locked down when a vial of VX was temporarily lost; it was recovered the next day.

markers.name: Chaco Canyon, New Mexico
markers.ctx: UNESCO World Heritage. Ancestral Puebloan centre (c. 850-1250 CE): great houses with subterranean kivas, some aligned to solstices; prehistoric roads radiate to outlying sites. Labeled a 'suspected ancient tunnel site' on a Four Corners map.

markers.name: Mt. Taylor, New Mexico
markers.ctx: 11,301 ft; sacred to the Navajo (Tsoodził), Acoma, Laguna, Zuni and Hopi. The surrounding Grants belt was mined for uranium 1951-1989; Laguna Pueblo's Jackpile Mine (1953-1982) was then the world's largest open-pit uranium mine. Marked on a Four Corners map.

markers.name: Socorro, New Mexico
markers.ctx: New Mexico Tech and its Energetic Materials Research and Testing Center (explosives research). Trinity Site (first atomic test, 16 July 1945) ~35 miles SE; the Very Large Array ~40 miles W. Marked on a Four Corners map.

markers.name: Paris Catacombs, France
markers.ctx: Ossuary holding remains of more than six million people, moved from overflowing cemeteries from 1786, in a fraction of Paris's ~300 km of old limestone quarries. Used in WWII by the Resistance and by German forces. Only a short stretch is open to visitors; cataphiles enter the rest illegally.

markers.name: Edinburgh Vaults, Scotland
markers.ctx: South Bridge Vaults: about 120 rooms in the nineteen arches of South Bridge (completed 1788), used for taverns, workshops and lodgings for about 30 years, then abandoned. Nearby Mary King's Close, a 17th-century street, lies beneath the former Royal Exchange (City Chambers).

markers.name: Kaymakli Underground City, Cappadocia, Turkey
markers.ctx: Eight levels (four open). Connected to Derinkuyu by 8-9 km of tunnels. Used by Byzantine Christians as a refuge from Arab raids (780-1180); abandoned after the 1923 population exchange. Nearly a hundred tunnels still serve the village above.

markers.name: Wieliczka Salt Mine, Poland
markers.ctx: UNESCO World Heritage. Mined from the 13th century until 1996; 327 m deep, over 287 km of passages and chambers. Underground chapels (St Kinga's, with rock-salt chandeliers), lakes and a sanatorium. Now a museum.

markers.name: Coober Pedy, South Australia
markers.ctx: Opal-mining town founded 1915. Many residents live in 'dugouts' below ground to escape the heat; underground churches, hotels and shops. Population 1,437 (2021). Marked on an underground-city map.

markers.name: Naica Mine, Chihuahua, Mexico
markers.ctx: Cave of the Crystals: giant selenite crystals in a chamber ~300 m down in the Naica mine; up to 58°C and 90-99% humidity - about ten minutes' exposure without protection. Discovered April 2000; flooded again after pumping stopped (2015).

markers.name: Lalibela Rock-Hewn Churches, Ethiopia
markers.ctx: Eleven monolithic churches cut down into the bedrock (12th-13th century), connected by passages; UNESCO World Heritage. Bete Giyorgis is cruciform, carved ~40 ft into a pit.

markers.name: Sines Cable Landing Station - Sines, Portugal
markers.ctx: Sines is Portugal's emerging Atlantic subsea hub: EllaLink lands here after crossing ~5,900 km from Fortaleza, Brazil, and the 8,760 km Medusa Mediterranean cable and the US-bound Nuvem system also terminate at the Sines Tech / Start Campus Sines 4.0 landing platform. It concentrates Europe–Americas–Africa traffic in one neutral facility. Source: Submarine Networks / EllaLink (submarinenetworks.com/en/stations/europe/portugal).

markers.name: Telxius Virginia Beach Cable Landing Station - Virginia Beach, USA
markers.ctx: This single station at 1900 Corporate Landing Parkway lands three transatlantic systems: Microsoft/Meta's MAREA (200 Tbps to Sopelana, Spain), Google's 250 Tbps Dunant (to Saint-Hilaire-de-Riez, France), and Telxius's ~11,000 km BRUSA (to Brazil and Puerto Rico), making it a primary US East Coast internet gateway. Source: Telxius / Submarine Networks (submarinenetworks.com/en/stations/north-america/usa-east/virginia-beach-cls).

markers.name: Melkbosstrand Cable Landing Station - Cape Town, South Africa
markers.ctx: Telkom's Melkbosstrand station north of Cape Town lands the legacy SAT-3/WASC and SAFE systems and, since 2022, Google's 144 Tbps, 12-fibre-pair Equiano cable running down Africa's west coast from Lisbon, a chokepoint for southern African connectivity. Source: News24 / Submarine Networks (submarinenetworks.com/en/stations/africa/south-africa).

markers.name: Nangan / Matsu Islands Cable Landing - Lienchiang County, Taiwan
markers.ctx: In February 2023 both undersea cables linking Taiwan's Matsu Islands to the main island were severed six days apart — Taiwan attributed the No. 2 break to a Chinese fishing vessel and No. 3 to a Chinese freighter — leaving ~13,000 residents largely offline for nearly two months, a flashpoint case in cable-sabotage concerns. Source: New Bloom Magazine / PBS NewsHour (newbloommag.net/2023/02/17/matsu-submarine-cable-cut).

markers.name: Piti Cable Landing Station - Piti, Guam
markers.ctx: Guam is a Pacific 'highway exchange' where trans-Pacific systems interconnect; GTA's typhoon-hardened GU1/GU2 stations at Piti land SEA-US, JGA North and JGA South. The steel-reinforced concrete facility is engineered to withstand 170-mph wind gusts, reflecting the cables' strategic value as the nearest US territory to Asia. Source: GTA / Popular Science / Submarine Networks (submarinenetworks.com/en/stations/north-america/usa-guam/piti).

markers.name: Mombasa Cable Landing Station - Mombasa, Kenya
markers.ctx: Mombasa is East Africa's principal cable gateway, landing SEACOM (a 17,000 km system), the 10,000 km EASSy along Africa's east coast, TEAMS, PEACE, and a planned 2Africa branch, funneling the region's international bandwidth through one coastal node. Source: Submarine Networks / WIOCC SEACOM (submarinenetworks.com/en/stations/africa/kenya).

markers.name: Chikura Cable Landing Station - Minamiboso, Japan
markers.ctx: KDDI's Chikura station in Chiba lands the 11,629 km FASTER trans-Pacific cable (a Google/KDDI/SingTel/China Mobile/China Telecom consortium, 60 Tbps design) plus Unity and other systems, making it a key eastern terminus for US–Japan internet traffic. Source: Submarine Networks / FASTER (submarinenetworks.com/en/stations/asia/japan/faster-ckikura-cls).

markers.name: Catania / Sicily Cable Landing Hub - Catania, Italy
markers.ctx: More than 20 subsea cables land on Sicily; the Catania landing station is a carrier-neutral node for SEA-ME-WE 5, and Sparkle's Sicily Hub interconnects most Mediterranean cables, positioning the island as a primary Europe–Asia–Africa transit point. Source: Telecom Italia Sparkle / Submarine Networks (submarinenetworks.com/en/stations/europe/italy/sicily).

markers.name: Jeddah Cable Landing - Red Sea Chokepoint, Saudi Arabia
markers.ctx: Jeddah anchors the Red Sea corridor, one of the world's densest cable chokepoints. In late February 2024 several Europe-Asia cables between Jeddah and Djibouti were cut; the dragging anchor of the Houthi-struck bulk carrier Rubymar is the reported cause (attributed), disrupting up to a quarter of Red Sea traffic.

markers.name: Bandon Cable Landing Station - Bandon, Oregon, USA
markers.ctx: The small Oregon coastal town of Bandon is the US landing point of Google's FASTER trans-Pacific cable to Chikura/Shima, Japan and Tanshui, Taiwan — one of several trans-Pacific systems that make the Oregon coast a major gateway between North America and Asia. Source: Submarine Networks / FASTER (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FASTER_(cable_system)).

markers.name: Sopelana Cable Landing Station - Biscay, Spain
markers.ctx: Sopelana, near Bilbao, is the European terminus of the Microsoft/Meta MAREA cable, which runs ~4,000 miles (6,600 km) from Virginia Beach and can carry 200 Tbps, one of the highest-capacity transatlantic routes into southern Europe. Source: Telxius / Data Centre Magazine (telxius.com/en/marea-2).

markers.name: Wuhan Institute of Virology (BSL-4) - Wuhan, China
markers.ctx: Wuhan Institute of Virology (Chinese Academy of Sciences, founded 1956). Its National Biosafety Laboratory - mainland China's first BSL-4 - was built in 2014-15 for ~300 million yuan (US$44 million) with French assistance and opened in 2018. A central subject of COVID-19 origin investigations.

markers.name: TSMC / Hsinchu Science Park - Hsinchu, Taiwan
markers.ctx: Hsinchu Science Park hosts TSMC's headquarters and R&D and its 2 nm Fab 20; TSMC's other leading-edge fabs are in Tainan (Fab 18) and Kaohsiung (Fab 22). Press estimates put ~90% of the world's most advanced chips in TSMC's Taiwan fabs - the basis of the 'Silicon Shield' argument (Foreign Policy, 2025).

markers.name: ITER Fusion Reactor - Saint-Paul-lès-Durance, France
markers.ctx: The 35-nation ITER tokamak at Cadarache aims to produce 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of heating (gain of 10). Initial budget close to €6 billion; construction and operation now projected at €18-22 billion, with outside estimates of $45-65 billion that ITER disputes.

markers.name: Oak Ridge National Laboratory - Oak Ridge, Tennessee, USA
markers.ctx: Established in 1943 as the Manhattan Project's plutonium-piloting 'Secret City' (population eventually ~75,000), ORNL is now the DOE's largest science and energy lab and hosts Frontier, the world's first exascale supercomputer, built with HPE Cray and AMD for about US$600 million. Source: Wikipedia / Undark / HPE (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontier_(supercomputer)).

markers.name: RIKEN Center for Computational Science (Fugaku) - Kobe, Japan
markers.ctx: RIKEN R-CCS on Kobe's Port Island houses Fugaku: 158,976 Fujitsu A64FX nodes, 442 PFLOPS on TOP500 (Rmax, after upgrade). Fastest in the world June 2020 - June 2022 and the first ARM-based #1. Successor to the K computer.

markers.name: Huawei Ox Horn Campus - Dongguan, China
markers.ctx: Huawei's ~300-acre R&D campus on Songshan Lake, opened June 2018 at a cost of ~US$1.5 billion, is built as 12 villages replicating European cities (Paris, Verona, Freiburg) linked by an imported Swiss red train, and houses tens of thousands of researchers at a company central to US–China tech-sanctions disputes. Source: Wikipedia / Yahoo Finance (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huawei_Ox_Horn_Campus).

markers.name: Integrated Joint Operations Platform (IJOP) - Xinjiang Public Security, Ürümqi
markers.ctx: The IJOP is a predictive-policing system rolled out across Xinjiang after a 2016 directive, aggregating data from Wi-Fi sniffers, ID cards, cameras and checkpoints to flag Uyghurs for questioning and detention. Human Rights Watch and Cure53 reverse-engineered its mobile app in 2019, documenting it in 'China's Algorithms of Repression.' Source: Human Rights Watch, 'China's Algorithms of Repression' (2019); ASPI Xinjiang Data Project.

markers.name: NYPD Lower Manhattan Security Coordination Center (Domain Awareness System)
markers.ctx: Opened in 2008 at 55 Broadway, this NYPD/Microsoft-built center aggregates the Domain Awareness System — as of 2014 pulling feeds from about 6,500 CCTV cameras and reading roughly 2 million license plates per day across Lower Manhattan. Source: Wikipedia (Lower Manhattan Security Initiative / Domain Awareness System); NYC.gov.

markers.name: GCHQ 'The Doughnut' - Cheltenham, UK
markers.ctx: The 200-metre-diameter ring building completed in 2003 houses Britain's signals-intelligence agency GCHQ and its roughly 5,500 staff; documents leaked by Edward Snowden in 2013 revealed its Tempora bulk-interception programme tapping transatlantic fibre cables. Source: Wikipedia (The Doughnut / GCHQ); The Guardian (Snowden disclosures).

markers.name: Clearview AI Headquarters - New York
markers.ctx: Clearview AI (Manhattan) sells facial recognition against a database of scraped web and social-media images (20 billion+ per Wikipedia; the company has since claimed 50 billion+) to law enforcement. Regulators in France, Italy, Greece, the Netherlands and the UK have fined it, and Australia's privacy regulator ordered it to stop collecting and delete data.

markers.name: BND Headquarters - Berlin, Germany
markers.ctx: Germany's foreign-intelligence service (BND) occupies the world's largest intelligence headquarters — 260,000 m2, completed 2017 at a cost of about EUR 1.09 billion — housing roughly 4,000 of its staff on Chausseestraße in central Berlin. Source: Wikipedia (Headquarters of the Federal Intelligence Service); Daily Sabah.

markers.name: Moscow 'Safe City' Facial-Recognition Network - Moscow, Russia
markers.ctx: Moscow's Department of Information Technology runs a live facial-recognition network — powered by NtechLab's FindFace — across roughly 175,000+ street and metro cameras, launched at scale on 1 January 2020; it has been used to identify and detain protesters and draft evaders. Source: Biometric Update; TASS; VSquare (Kremlin Leaks).

markers.name: Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex - Fort Irwin, California
markers.ctx: Operated by NASA's JPL on the US Army's Fort Irwin reservation, Goldstone is the US node of the three-station Deep Space Network; its DSS-14 'Mars' antenna (64 m from 1966, 70 m since 1988) tracks interplanetary spacecraft.

markers.name: Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex - Robledo de Chavela, Spain
markers.ctx: One of three NASA Deep Space Network complexes spaced ~120 degrees apart in longitude, this site ~65 km west of Madrid has operated since 1965 and hosts a 70-metre antenna; it is run by JPL with Spain's INTA. Source: Wikipedia (Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex); NASA.

markers.name: Guiana Space Centre - Kourou, French Guiana
markers.ctx: Europe's primary spaceport, operated by France's CNES and ESA near the equator at Kourou, launches Ariane and Vega rockets; its near-equatorial location gives a fuel-saving boost for placing satellites into geostationary orbit. Source: Wikipedia (Guiana Space Centre); ESA/CNES.

markers.name: Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SHAR) - Sriharikota, India
markers.ctx: ISRO's orbital launch site on Sriharikota island, launching PSLV, GSLV and LVM3; departure point for Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan. A second spaceport at Kulasekarapattinam (SSLV) is due to open around end-2026.

markers.name: Cavalier Space Force Station (PARCS) - North Dakota
markers.ctx: Home to the AN/FPQ-16 PARCS UHF phased-array radar (6,888 elements; originally 6,144 dipoles) run by the 10th Space Warning Squadron; provides ICBM/SLBM warning and tracks over half of all Earth-orbiting objects.

markers.name: Tanegashima Space Center - Minamitane, Japan
markers.ctx: JAXA's primary spaceport, covering ~9.7 million m2 on the southeast coast of Tanegashima island, is Japan's largest rocket launch facility and the base for H-IIA/H-IIB and H3 launches carrying satellites and ISS resupply vehicles. Source: Wikipedia (Tanegashima Space Center); JAXA.

markers.name: New York Stock Exchange, 11 Wall Street
markers.ctx: The NYSE is the world's largest stock exchange by market capitalisation of listed companies - about US$44.7 trillion (Dec 2025). It trades from the New York Stock Exchange Building: the 1903 Beaux-Arts building at 18 Broad Street and its 11 Wall Street annex. Trading is now largely electronic but the floor remains the symbolic centre of American equity capital.

markers.name: London Stock Exchange, Paternoster Square
markers.ctx: The London Stock Exchange, founded in 1801 and now headquartered at 10 Paternoster Square beside St Paul's Cathedral, is one of the world's oldest exchanges and the primary listing venue for the City of London. Its parent LSEG is a global markets-infrastructure and data firm. Source: Wikipedia, London Stock Exchange; LSEG (lseg.com).

markers.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Gold Vault, 33 Liberty St
markers.ctx: The vault 80 feet below 33 Liberty Street held roughly 507,000 gold bars weighing about 6,331 metric tons as of 2024 — the world's largest known gold depository, larger than Fort Knox. Nearly all of it is stored on behalf of foreign central banks and international organizations such as the IMF. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York (newyorkfed.org/aboutthefed/goldvault.html).

markers.name: European Central Bank, Frankfurt
markers.ctx: The ECB, in its twin-tower headquarters completed in 2014 around the historic Grossmarkthalle, sets monetary policy for the euro area (21 member states since Bulgaria joined in January 2026) and is the primary supervisor of the eurozone's largest banks.

markers.name: Bank of England, Threadneedle Street
markers.ctx: Founded in 1694 and nicknamed 'The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street,' the Bank of England is the UK's central bank and holds one of the world's largest gold reserves in its vaults — around 400,000 bars for the UK and other nations' central banks. It sets UK monetary policy and underpins the City of London. Source: Bank of England (bankofengland.co.uk); Wikipedia, Bank of England.

markers.name: International Monetary Fund HQ, Washington D.C.
markers.ctx: The IMF, conceived at Bretton Woods in 1944 (formally in existence 1945) and headquartered in Washington near the White House, has 191 member countries and provides balance-of-payments loans whose conditions shape the economic policy of borrowing nations. Its lending capacity runs to roughly US$1 trillion.

markers.name: Blackstone HQ, 345 Park Avenue, New York
markers.ctx: Blackstone is the world's largest alternative-asset manager, with about US$1.27 trillion under management (2025) across private equity, real estate and credit, and a major owner of commercial property worldwide. Headquartered at 345 Park Avenue. Source: Blackstone 10-K FY2025; Wikipedia.

markers.name: Berkshire Hathaway HQ, Omaha
markers.ctx: From an office in Omaha's Kiewit Plaza (now Blackstone Plaza), Warren Buffett ran Berkshire Hathaway from 1970 to 2025, building a conglomerate that in Aug 2024 became the first non-tech U.S. company valued above $1 trillion; it wholly owns GEICO and BNSF and holds large stakes including Apple and American Express. Greg Abel succeeded him as CEO. Source: Wikipedia; berkshirehathaway.com.

markers.name: Renaissance Technologies, East Setauket, New York
markers.ctx: Founded by mathematician Jim Simons (d. 2024), Renaissance runs the Medallion Fund, which since 1988 averaged about 66% annual returns before fees (39% after) and more than $100 billion in trading gains - widely regarded as the most successful quantitative fund. It operates from a campus in East Setauket, Long Island. Source: Wikipedia; Institutional Investor.

markers.name: Glencore HQ, Baar, Switzerland
markers.ctx: Baar-headquartered Glencore is by many estimates the world's largest commodity trader, moving metals, minerals, coal and oil globally; in 2022 it pleaded guilty in US, UK and Brazilian courts to a multi-year bribery and market-manipulation scheme and paid roughly $1.5 billion in penalties. Its executive board and all group compliance functions sit at the Baar campus. Source: Reuters / U.S. DOJ (2022 Glencore FCPA settlement); Wikipedia: Glencore.

markers.name: Cargill HQ, Minnetonka, Minnesota
markers.ctx: Cargill is the largest privately held company in the United States, posting record revenue of about $177 billion and topping the Forbes private-company list nearly every year since 1985. The family-controlled agribusiness dominates global grain, meat and commodity supply chains with roughly 160,000 employees in 70 countries. Source: Forbes / Star Tribune (2023, 'Cargill retains top spot on Forbes list of largest U.S. private companies').

markers.name: ASML HQ, Veldhoven, Netherlands
markers.ctx: ASML's Veldhoven campus: the world's only manufacturer of extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, required for the most advanced chips. Its newest High-NA EUV systems cost about $370 million each. Dutch export controls on ASML sales to China are a core front in the chip war.

markers.name: Maersk HQ, Copenhagen, Denmark
markers.ctx: A.P. Moller-Maersk, headquartered on Copenhagen's Esplanaden, was the world's largest container-shipping line from 1996 until January 2022, when MSC overtook it; it remains the second largest. A systemic node in supply-chain and trade-chokepoint analysis.

markers.name: Rheinmetall HQ, Düsseldorf, Germany
markers.ctx: Rheinmetall is Germany's largest arms manufacturer, a leading supplier of tank guns, ammunition and armored vehicles to NATO and Ukraine; its defense sales surged to EUR 7.6 billion in 2024 as European rearmament accelerated, and its stock has risen over 1,000% since 2022. Source: Fortune (2025); Wikipedia: Rheinmetall.

markers.name: Samsung Digital City, Suwon, South Korea
markers.ctx: Samsung Electronics' principal headquarters, a roughly 390-acre 'Digital City' campus 30 km south of Seoul, houses around 37,000 employees and over half of the division's R&D workforce across five office towers up to 40 stories tall. It is the birthplace of the Galaxy line and the nerve center of the Samsung chaebol. Source: YnetNews / The Business Standard ('A peek into Samsung Digital City').

markers.name: FTX / Albany Resort, Nassau, Bahamas
markers.ctx: FTX moved its headquarters to Nassau in 2021 and collapsed in November 2022 in one of history's largest financial frauds; founder Sam Bankman-Fried ran the empire from a roughly $40 million penthouse at the gated Albany resort and was later convicted on seven counts and sentenced to 25 years. FTX left an $8 billion customer shortfall. Source: Rolling Stone / Forbes / Time (2022); U.S. v. Bankman-Fried.

markers.name: Glen Park Branch Library, San Francisco (Silk Road Arrest)
markers.ctx: In October 2013 the FBI arrested Ross Ulbricht, the 'Dread Pirate Roberts' behind the Bitcoin-powered darknet market Silk Road, at this branch library while he was logged into the site's admin panel. He was sentenced to life before receiving a full presidential pardon in January 2025. Source: KQED (2013 SF sting); NBC News; Glen Park Association.

markers.name: Ledger HQ, Paris, France
markers.ctx: Paris-based Ledger is the leading maker of hardware wallets for securing crypto private keys offline, having sold more than 7.5 million devices across 200 countries with over 20% of the world's crypto assets reportedly secured on its hardware. A 2020 data breach exposed customer emails, and for a subset names, postal addresses and phone numbers (Ledger). Source: Decrypt ('Ledger Unveils New Global Headquarters in Paris'); Ledger careers.

markers.name: Chainalysis HQ, New York
markers.ctx: Chainalysis is the leading blockchain-forensics firm, tracing crypto transactions for law enforcement and governments in over 70 countries; its clients include the FBI, DEA, IRS Criminal Investigation and the UK National Crime Agency, making it a central node in state surveillance of cryptocurrency flows. Source: Wikipedia: Chainalysis; Chainalysis Government Solutions.

markers.name: Ekibastuz Bitcoin Mining Hub, Kazakhstan
markers.ctx: After China banned crypto mining in May 2021, coal-rich Ekibastuz became a magnet for relocating miners, briefly helping push Kazakhstan to the world's second-largest Bitcoin hash rate; the local Enegix facility alone was built to power over 50,000 ASICs at 150 MW, roughly five times the town's own peak demand, straining the national grid. Source: MIT Technology Review (2023); Rest of World; Bitcoin Magazine.

markers.name: Île Longue SSBN Base - Brest, France
markers.ctx: Selected by Charles de Gaulle in 1965 and operational since 1972, Île Longue in the Brest roadstead is the main base for France's Force Océanique Stratégique — its four Triomphant-class ballistic-missile submarines — and stores the warheads and missile fuel. Around 2,400 military and civilian personnel staff one of France's most sensitive sites. Source: GlobalSecurity.org, 'l'Ile Longue'; Naval Technology.

markers.name: Nevatim Airbase - F-35I Hub, Negev, Israel
markers.ctx: Nevatim, 15 km east-southeast of Beersheba in the Negev, is one of Israel's largest air bases and the primary hub for its F-35I 'Adir' stealth fighters, hosting three squadrons (140, 116 and 117). Built 1980–1983 with joint Israeli-US funding after the Sinai withdrawal, it was struck by Iranian ballistic missiles in 2024. Source: Wikipedia, 'Nevatim Airbase'; GlobalSecurity.org.

markers.name: Berbera Airbase - UAE Military Foothold, Somaliland
markers.ctx: Under a 2017 agreement, the UAE established a military base at the Gulf of Aden port of Berbera, roughly 250 km from Yemen; its Soviet-built 2.6-mile runway can host fighters, heavy transports and drones. Satellite imagery from late 2025 shows renewed expansion including ammunition depots and around a dozen underground bunkers overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb. Source: BBC News; Middle East Eye; Sri Lanka Guardian (satellite analysis).

markers.name: Offutt AFB - U.S. Strategic Command (STRATCOM) HQ, Nebraska
markers.ctx: Offutt AFB near Omaha — home of Strategic Air Command from 1948 — is headquarters of U.S. Strategic Command, responsible for the nation's nuclear deterrent, global strike and nuclear command-and-control. A new $1.3 billion command-and-control facility, the Gen. Curtis E. LeMay Building, was dedicated there in 2019. Source: Wikipedia, 'United States Strategic Command'; Military Times; GlobalSecurity.org.

markers.name: INS Kadamba (Project Seabird) - Karwar, India
markers.ctx: INS Kadamba near Karwar on the Arabian Sea is the anchor of Project Seabird; commissioned 31 May 2005, it covers 11,200 acres (45 km2) along 26 km of coastline. On completion of Phase II-B it is planned to be the largest naval base of its kind in the Eastern Hemisphere (capacity ~50 warships), sited out of range of most strike aircraft from neighbouring countries.

markers.name: Naval Base Simon's Town - South Atlantic, South Africa
markers.ctx: Naval Base Simon's Town near Cape Town is the South African Navy's largest base and home to its frigate and submarine flotillas. A dockyard since 1743 and a Royal Navy station until handed to South Africa in 1957, it guards the strategic Cape sea route and the backdoor to the South Atlantic. Source: Wikipedia, 'Naval Base Simon's Town'; Simonstown Agreement.

markers.name: Tuol Sleng (S-21) Prison, Phnom Penh, Cambodia
markers.ctx: A former high school converted by the Khmer Rouge into Security Prison 21 (S-21), the regime's central interrogation and execution centre; an estimated 20,000 people were held there from 1976 to 1979 and only twelve known survivors are recorded. Now the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum. Source: Wikipedia, Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum; United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

markers.name: Automotores Orletti, Buenos Aires, Argentina
markers.ctx: A former auto-repair garage in the Floresta neighbourhood used in 1976 by Argentina's SIDE intelligence service as the main operational base of Operation Condor, the transnational plan to disappear dissidents; more than 300 people, many of them foreign nationals, were held there. Declared a national historic site in 2014. Source: Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), cels.org.ar; Plan Cóndor archive.

markers.name: Holmesburg Prison, Philadelphia, USA
markers.ctx: Between 1951 and 1974 University of Pennsylvania dermatologist Albert Kligman ran non-therapeutic experiments on inmates, most of them Black, exposing them to viruses, skin-blistering chemicals, radioactive isotopes, psychoactive drugs and dioxin, with sponsors including Dow Chemical and the US Army. Philadelphia formally apologised in 2022. Source: Wikipedia, Holmesburg Prison; Philadelphia Inquirer (Oct. 6, 2022).

markers.name: Evin Prison, Tehran, Iran
markers.ctx: Iran's most notorious prison, at the foot of the Alborz Mountains in northwestern Tehran, holding activists, journalists and dual nationals; its Ward 209 is controlled directly by the Ministry of Intelligence and documented by Human Rights Watch for prolonged solitary confinement and 'white torture.' Source: Human Rights Watch, 'Like the Dead in Their Coffins' (2004); Wikipedia / Evin Prison.

markers.name: Bagram Theater Internment Facility / 'Black Jail', Afghanistan
markers.ctx: The main U.S. detention site in Afghanistan, alongside a separate DIA/special-operations 'Black Jail'; a 2005 Army report obtained by the New York Times documented the 2002 homicides of detainees Habibullah and Dilawar, who were chained and beaten to death, with autopsies describing leg trauma comparable to being run over by a bus. Source: New York Times / Army CID report (2005); Wikipedia, 'Bagram torture and prisoner abuse'.

markers.name: Olsztyn-Mazury Airport (Szymany), Poland
markers.ctx: A remote airfield where a Council of Europe inquiry found at least seven CIA-linked flights landed in 2002-2003, delivering high-value detainees to the nearby Stare Kiejkuty intelligence base ~12 miles away; Gulfstream jets reportedly bypassed customs. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is said to have been held and waterboarded near here. Source: Worldcrunch, 'Inside a Secret CIA Prison in the Polish Countryside'; CBS News, 'Polish Logs Confirm CIA Rendition Flights'.

markers.name: Wenchang Space Launch Site, Hainan, China
markers.ctx: China's southernmost spaceport (19°N), operational since June 2016. Unlike the inland sites it receives rocket stages by sea from Tianjin, avoiding rail size limits; the only launch site of the Long March 5 and 7, which lifted the Tiangong modules.

markers.name: Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Inner Mongolia, China
markers.ctx: China's first launch centre (Dong Fang Hong I, 1970; Shenzhou 5, 2003), in the Gobi across Ejin Banner (Inner Mongolia) and Jinta (Gansu); all Chinese crewed launches have left from here. Operated by the PLA.

markers.name: Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, India
markers.ctx: India's primary spaceport, on a barrier island off the Bay of Bengal, from which ISRO launches its PSLV and GSLV/LVM3 rockets including the Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan interplanetary missions; the near-equatorial coastal site allows spent stages to drop safely over the sea. Source: ISRO, isro.gov.in; Wikipedia / Satish Dhawan Space Centre.

markers.name: Mittelwerk / Mittelbau-Dora Underground V-2 Factory, Nordhausen
markers.ctx: Underground factory in a former gypsum mine in the Kohnstein, built with slave labour from the Mittelbau-Dora camp to produce V-2 missiles and later V-1s. About 60,000 prisoners passed through the camp in 1943-45; around one in three (~20,000) died - more than the V-2 killed in its attacks.

markers.name: Gran Sasso National Laboratory (LNGS), Assergi
markers.ctx: INFN laboratory beside the Gran Sasso highway tunnel under ~1,400 m of rock, operational since 1987; three main halls, 180,000 m³ in total. Dark-matter and neutrino experiments; endpoint of the 2011 CERN-OPERA neutrino-speed measurement. Long the world's largest underground lab, a title China's CJPL-II now claims.

markers.name: Le Vele di Scampia - Camorra Drug Market, Naples
markers.ctx: The sail-shaped 'Vele' housing blocks in Scampia, built 1962–1975, became one of Europe's largest open-air drug markets under the Camorra and the setting for Roberto Saviano's 2006 book and the series 'Gomorrah.' The 2004–2005 Scampia feud between the Di Lauro clan and breakaway 'Scissionisti' killed dozens; authorities have estimated the Scampia–Secondigliano narcotics trade at around 100 million euros a year. Source: BBC News (bbc.co.uk), 'Naples beefs up anti-mafia forces'; France 24 (france24.com), 'After Gomorrah,' 2020.

markers.name: Sun Yee On Triad Ground - Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong
markers.ctx: Sun Yee On, founded 1919 and traced to the earlier 'Yee On' Chiu Chow trade association, is regarded as the largest triad society in the world, with estimates exceeding 55,000 members. Its influence has long been concentrated in the entertainment and nightlife districts of Tsim Sha Tsui in Kowloon, spanning extortion, loan-sharking, counterfeiting and narcotics. Source: Grey Dynamics (greydynamics.com), 'Organised Crime: The Sun Yee On Triad'; Wikipedia, 'Sun Yee On'.

markers.name: Cali - Cali Cartel Stronghold, Colombia
markers.ctx: The Cali Cartel, run 1975–1995 by brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodríguez Orejuela with José Santacruz Londoño and Hélmer Herrera, was headquartered in Cali in the Valle del Cauca and at its peak was cited as controlling some 80% of the cocaine market (estimate). It laundered profits through legitimate fronts such as the Drogas La Rebaja pharmacy chain before its leadership was dismantled in the mid-1990s. Source: InSight Crime (insightcrime.org), 'Gilberto Rodríguez Orejuela, alias The Chess Player'; TIME (time.com), 'The Cali Cartel: New Kings of Coke'.

markers.name: Guadalajara - CJNG Base of Operations, Mexico
markers.ctx: Guadalajara, capital of Jalisco, is the operational base of the Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG), founded in 2009 and one of Mexico's most powerful and fastest-growing syndicates, known for trafficking fentanyl and methamphetamine to the United States. It was led by Nemesio 'El Mencho' Oseguera Cervantes, who carried a U.S. reward of up to 15 million dollars until he was fatally wounded in a Mexican military operation in Tapalpa, Jalisco, on 22 February 2026. Source: InSight Crime (insightcrime.org), 'Jalisco Cartel New Generation (CJNG)'; NPR (npr.org), 'Mexican army kills leader of Jalisco New Generation Cartel,' 2026.

markers.name: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant - Enerhodar, Ukraine
markers.ctx: Europe's largest nuclear power plant (six VVER-1000 reactors, 5,700 MW nameplate) has been under Russian military occupation since 4 March 2022; its reactors are shut down while the site is used as a fortified base. The IAEA has repeatedly warned of shelling near the plant and loss of external power. Source: Wikipedia, Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant; Al Jazeera.

markers.name: El Fasher - North Darfur, Sudan
markers.ctx: The Rapid Support Forces besieged El Fasher, the Sudanese army's last Darfur stronghold, from May 2024 and seized it on 26 October 2025; the population, once far larger, was estimated at about 250,000 when the city fell, amid famine. Mass killings followed; the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan reported in 2026 that they bore 'the hallmarks of genocide'. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of El Fasher; El Fasher massacre; UN OHCHR.

markers.name: Mekelle - Tigray, Ethiopia
markers.ctx: Capital of Tigray and focal point of the 2020-2022 war between Ethiopia's federal government and the TPLF, during which Addis Ababa imposed a de facto siege cutting food, banking, power and telecoms. Death toll estimates range widely - Ghent University researchers 385,000-600,000; AU envoy Olusegun Obasanjo about 600,000 - much of it from starvation. Pretoria ceasefire 2 November 2022. Source: Wikipedia, Tigray war; International Crisis Group.

markers.name: Bakhmut - Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine
markers.ctx: Battle of Bakhmut, 1 August 2022 - 20 May 2023, one of the longest and bloodiest battles of the war, known as the 'meat grinder'. Wagner Group, many of its fighters recruited from Russian prisons, led the assault; Prigozhin claimed about 20,000 Wagner dead. A city of about 70,000 before the war was left in ruins. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Bakhmut; Al Jazeera.

markers.name: Marib - Yemen (Oil & Gas Frontline)
markers.ctx: Marib, the government's last northern stronghold and home to a refinery producing about 90% of Yemen's LPG, was the pivotal front of the 2021-2022 Houthi offensive. The UN warned the push threatened to displace at least 385,000 people sheltering in the governorate. Source: Washington Post; RUSI — washingtonpost.com/world/interactive/2021/yemen-war-marib-houthis/.

markers.name: The Cloister, Sea Island, Georgia (2004 G8 Summit)
markers.ctx: The private barrier-island resort hosted the 30th G8 Summit on June 8-10, 2004, gathering leaders of the U.S., UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada and Russia at The Cloister; the G8 boardroom is still shown on resort tours. Sea Island is a gated enclave of estates that has drawn dignitaries since a 1928 visit by President Calvin Coolidge. Source: New Georgia Encyclopedia; George W. Bush White House Archives (g8/2004).

markers.name: Campione d'Italia (Italian Exclave in Switzerland)
markers.ctx: Italian exclave of 2.68 km2 (1.03 sq mi) inside Swiss territory on Lake Lugano; it stayed Italian when Ticino joined the Swiss Confederation in 1798. Its economy was built on the Casinò di Campione (founded 1917). Long outside EU customs, it entered the EU customs territory on 1 January 2020 against residents' wishes; a Swiss-level VAT rate still applies.

markers.name: Cabinda Oil Exclave, Angola
markers.ctx: Angolan exclave separated from the rest of the country by a strip of the DRC. Population 903,370 (2024 census); conservative estimates put it at close to 60% of Angola's oil output, from blocks in which Chevron is a major partner (Malongo terminal). Separatists of the Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda (FLEC, founded 1963) have fought since independence in 1975, including attacks on oil workers.

markers.name: North Brother Island (Typhoid Mary Quarantine), New York
markers.ctx: This 20-acre East River island between the Bronx and Rikers held Riverside Hospital's quarantine station, where Mary Mallon ('Typhoid Mary') was confined against her will for roughly 26 years until her death in 1938. Abandoned since 1963, it is now a NYC Parks bird sanctuary closed to the public, with access only by permit and Parks escort. Source: All That's Interesting; Untapped New York.

markers.name: Cocos (Keeling) Islands - former Clunies-Ross fiefdom (ended 1978)
markers.ctx: The Clunies-Ross family ruled the atoll as a private domain from 1827, paying workers in its own Cocos rupee, redeemable only at the company store. In 1978 Australia forced the family to sell for A$6.25 million under threat of compulsory acquisition; in a UN-supervised vote on 6 April 1984, 229 of 261 islanders chose integration with Australia. Now an Australian external territory: a private sovereignty ended by purchase and a supervised vote.
