markers.name: Lyford Cay, New Providence, Bahamas
markers.ctx: Private gated community of about 450 homes on the western tip of New Providence, built around the Lyford Cay Club, which Canadian brewing magnate E.P. Taylor developed after buying the land in 1954. Often ranked among the world's wealthiest enclaves; President Kennedy met Harold Macmillan here in December 1962.

markers.name: Ceuta (Spanish Enclave in North Africa)
markers.ctx: Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city and free port on Morocco's coast at the Strait of Gibraltar, one of the European Union's only two land borders with Africa (with Melilla). Ringed by double barbed-wire fences, it is a flashpoint for migration: in one 2021 surge some 8,000 people crossed in two days, and later mass breaches drew Spanish plans for new containment fencing. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ceuta); CBS News.

markers.name: Jupiter Island, Martin County, Florida
markers.ctx: Barrier-island town of gated oceanfront estates beside Hobe Sound; population 804 (2020). Median household income was $199,167 in 2010, with family income above $250,000. Long a discreet retreat for industrialists, executives and political families.

markers.name: Greenbushes Lithium Mine, Western Australia
markers.ctx: World's largest hard-rock lithium mine by reserves, output and capacity: about 1.95 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate a year (2020), enough for a third of world demand. Run by Talison Lithium, a joint venture of China's Tianqi Lithium (51%) and Albemarle (49%), 257 km south of Perth.

markers.name: Jwaneng Diamond Mine, Botswana
markers.ctx: Nicknamed the 'Prince of Mines,' Jwaneng is the world's richest diamond mine by value, producing 12-15 million carats a year and generating 60-70% of Debswana's revenue. It is run by Debswana, a 50-50 joint venture between the Government of Botswana and the De Beers Group, and is moving underground to extend its life by 20 years. Source: Debswana / Mining Technology (debswana.com/jwaneng).

markers.name: Reko Diq Copper-Gold Project, Pakistan
markers.ctx: One of the world's largest undeveloped copper-gold deposits, with an estimated 5.9 billion tonnes of ore and a projected 40-year life, in the restive Chagai District of Balochistan. It is 50% owned by Barrick Gold and 50% by Pakistani federal and Balochistan governments, and is projected to generate roughly $70 billion in revenue amid a violent local insurgency. Source: The Diplomat / Mining.com (thediplomat.com/2025/09, mining.com).

markers.name: Mir Mine (Mirny Diamond Pipe), Russia
markers.ctx: One of the world's largest excavated diamond pipes, an open pit about 1,200 m wide and 525 m deep in Yakutia. Discovered 1955 and opened 1957; the open-pit stage ended in 2001 and Alrosa moved underground. Flooding in 2017 trapped over 140 miners; eight died.

markers.name: Sudbury Basin Nickel District, Canada
markers.ctx: One of the world's largest nickel-copper mining and smelting districts, in an impact structure formed 1.849 billion years ago; mined since ore was found during railway construction in 1883, now by Vale and Glencore. Inco's 381 m Superstack at Copper Cliff, long one of the world's tallest chimneys and now being dismantled, is the legacy of sulphur emissions that once stripped the surrounding land.

markers.name: Berkeley Pit, Butte, Montana
markers.ctx: Former open-pit copper mine (1955-1982; Anaconda, then ARCO), part of a Superfund site listed in 1983. About 1.6 km long and 0.8 km wide, filled with roughly 270 m (900 ft) of acidic, metal-laden water. Snow geese die on it: 342 carcasses were recovered in 1996, and on 28 November 2016 tens of thousands landed on the pit.

markers.name: Bohemian Grove - Monte Rio, California
markers.ctx: A 2,700-acre private redwood encampment owned by San Francisco's all-male Bohemian Club, where each July about 2,500 members and guests - including US presidents, executives and officials over the years - gather; the encampment opens with the 'Cremation of Care' ceremony. A meeting on early Manhattan Project planning (Lawrence, Oppenheimer, S-1 Committee members) was held at the Grove in September 1942.

markers.name: OECD Headquarters (Château de la Muette) - Paris
markers.ctx: The 38-member OECD is headquartered at the Château de la Muette (built for Henri de Rothschild in the 1920s) in the 16th arrondissement. In 1949 it became the headquarters of the OEEC, created in 1948 to administer US Marshall Plan aid, which became the OECD in 1961.

markers.name: Atlantic Council - Washington, D.C.
markers.ctx: The NATO-aligned foreign-policy think tank opened a new 80,000-square-foot global headquarters at 1400 L Street NW in November 2024, nearly double its previous size. Its funders have included Western governments, Gulf states and defense contractors, drawing scrutiny over donor influence on its research. Source: Atlantic Council press release (atlanticcouncil.org).

markers.name: National Endowment for Democracy (NED) - Washington, D.C.
markers.ctx: Created in 1983 as a congressionally funded grantmaking foundation, NED channels an annual congressional appropriation into more than 2,000 grants across roughly 100 countries. Co-founder Allen Weinstein famously said 'a lot of what we do today was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA.' Source: National Endowment for Democracy (ned.org) / Wikipedia.

markers.name: Wilton Park (Wiston House) - Wiston, West Sussex
markers.ctx: An executive agency of the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (formed 1946), based since 1951 at the 16th-century Wiston House, Wilton Park convenes over 70 strategic policy dialogues a year in the UK and overseas for officials and opinion-formers, in support of UK foreign policy.

markers.name: Freemasons' Hall (United Grand Lodge of England) - London
markers.ctx: Headquarters of the United Grand Lodge of England, which descends from the 1717 premier Grand Lodge and is counted among the world's oldest Grand Lodges with those of Scotland and Ireland. A Masonic meeting place since 1775; the present Art Deco building (1927-1933) is a memorial to the 3,225 Freemasons who died on active service in WWI. It administers thousands of lodges in England and Wales.

markers.name: Open Society Foundations HQ - New York
markers.ctx: George Soros's grantmaking network, founded in 1993, is headquartered at 224 West 57th Street in Manhattan. With an endowment of roughly $23 billion, it funds civil-society, human-rights and media groups worldwide and is a recurring target of political campaigns internationally. Source: Open Society Foundations — Wikipedia / GuideStar.

markers.name: Luxor Temple Standing Obelisk (Twin of the Concorde Obelisk)
markers.ctx: The ~25 m red-granite obelisk of Ramesses II still stands at the entrance pylon of Luxor Temple; its twin was gifted to France in the 1830s and now stands in Paris's Place de la Concorde. France formally renounced any claim to the remaining Luxor obelisk in 1981. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis' / obelisks.org.

markers.name: Wellington Testimonial (Wellington Monument), Phoenix Park, Dublin
markers.ctx: At 62 m (203 ft), the granite obelisk to the Duke of Wellington, begun 1817 and completed only in 1861 due to funding shortfalls, is the tallest obelisk in Europe; its bronze relief plaques were cast from cannon captured at Waterloo. Source: Wikipedia, 'Wellington Monument, Dublin' / Buildings of Ireland.

markers.name: Elephant and Obelisk (Pulcino della Minerva), Piazza della Minerva, Rome
markers.ctx: A 6th-century BC Egyptian obelisk mounted on Bernini's marble elephant, unveiled 1667 outside Santa Maria sopra Minerva beside the former seat of the Roman Inquisition and Dominican order; the Latin inscription frames the elephant as a symbol that a robust mind is needed to sustain solid wisdom. Source: Wikipedia, 'Elephant and Obelisk' / Bernini catalogue.

markers.name: Quirinal Obelisk, Piazza del Quirinale, Rome
markers.ctx: A ~14.6 m ancient Roman obelisk moved from the Mausoleum of Augustus and re-erected in 1786 by Pope Pius VI between the colossal Dioscuri statues, directly before the Quirinal Palace - former papal residence and now the official residence of the President of the Italian Republic. Source: Wikipedia, 'Obelisks of Rome' (Quirinal obelisk).

markers.name: San Jacinto Monument, La Porte, Texas
markers.ctx: At 172.92 m (567.31 ft) and topped by a 220-ton Lone Star, this 1936-39 obelisk on the Houston Ship Channel is the world's tallest masonry column, taller than the Washington Monument, commemorating the 1836 Battle of San Jacinto that secured Texan independence. Source: Wikipedia, 'San Jacinto Monument'.

markers.name: Shaheed Minar (Ochterlony Monument), Kolkata
markers.ctx: A 48 m column-obelisk built in 1828 to honor East India Company general David Ochterlony, fusing Egyptian, Syrian and Turkish motifs; independent India renamed it Shaheed Minar ('Martyrs' Tower') in 1969, converting a colonial monument into a memorial to freedom fighters. Source: Wikipedia, 'Shaheed Minar, Kolkata' / Maps of India.

markers.name: Obelisk of Montevideo (a los Constituyentes de 1830), Uruguay
markers.ctx: A 40 m three-sided pink-granite obelisk by sculptor Jose Luis Zorrilla de San Martin, inaugurated 1938 at the entrance to Parque Batlle, bearing three bronze figures for 'Law', 'Liberty' and 'Force' to honor the framers of Uruguay's first 1830 constitution. Source: Wikipedia, 'Obelisk of Montevideo'.

markers.name: Sanxingdui Ruins, Guanghan, Sichuan, China
markers.ctx: Sacrificial pits at this Bronze Age site (c. 1700-1150 BC), first probed in 1929 and dramatically re-excavated from 2019, yielded hundreds of bronze masks, heads and trees - including a mask 1.31 m wide - from a lost Shu civilization with no written records, whose art style is unmatched anywhere else in ancient China. Source: World Archaeology, 'The lost world of Sanxingdui' / China Daily.

markers.name: Caral-Supe, Barranca Province, Peru
markers.ctx: Built around 2600 BC and home to over 3,000 people, Caral is the oldest known urban center in the Americas - roughly contemporary with the Egyptian pyramids - with six stepped platform mounds and sunken circular plazas of the Norte Chico civilization; UNESCO listed it in 2009. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caral' / Popular Archaeology.

markers.name: Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Masvingo
markers.ctx: The mortarless dry-stone Great Enclosure - a wall up to 9.6 m high and 250 m long - is the largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa, capital of a trading empire (11th-15th c.) whose African authorship colonial authorities long tried to deny; it gives the modern nation its name. Source: Britannica, 'Great Zimbabwe' / Wikipedia.

markers.name: Persepolis (Takht-e Jamshid), Fars Province, Iran
markers.ctx: Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, begun c. 518 BC by Darius I, with its Apadana audience hall and reliefs of tribute-bearing nations; it was looted and burned by Alexander the Great's army in 330 BC. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Persepolis' / Britannica.

markers.name: Great Ziggurat of Ur, Dhi Qar, Iraq
markers.ctx: A massive Sumerian stepped temple-platform to the moon god Nanna, built c. 2100 BC by King Ur-Nammu near modern Nasiriyah; its restored lower facade sits beside a former Iraqi airbase, and it anchors the ancient city of Ur, traditionally linked to the biblical Abraham. Source: Britannica, 'Ziggurat of Ur' / Wikipedia.

markers.name: Mohenjo-daro, Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan
markers.ctx: One of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (built c. 2500 BC), notable for grid-planned streets, a covered drainage system and the 'Great Bath'; its still-undeciphered script leaves a sophisticated urban society largely unreadable. UNESCO listed it in 1980 and warns of severe erosion. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro'.

markers.name: Nazca Lines, Nazca, Ica, Peru
markers.ctx: Hundreds of giant geoglyphs - animals, plants and straight lines up to kilometers long - etched into the desert plateau by the Nazca culture between roughly 500 BC and AD 500, only fully legible from the air; ongoing drone surveys keep adding newly discovered figures. UNESCO World Heritage since 1994. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa'.

markers.name: Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Boston
markers.ctx: On March 18, 1990, two thieves disguised as police officers spent 81 minutes stealing 13 works - including a Vermeer and Rembrandts - valued at hundreds of millions of dollars: the highest-value museum robbery in history. Unsolved; the museum's $10 million reward stands. Source: FBI; Smithsonian Magazine.

markers.name: Museum of the Bible, Washington D.C.
markers.ctx: Funded by Hobby Lobby's Green family. In 2017 Hobby Lobby paid a $3M fine and agreed to forfeit more than 5,500 smuggled Iraqi artifacts; the museum later agreed to return over 11,000 objects to Egypt and Iraq, and the looted Gilgamesh Dream Tablet was repatriated to Iraq in 2021. Source: U.S. DOJ; Smithsonian Magazine.

markers.name: Humboldt Forum, Berlin
markers.ctx: The Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation agreed in 2021-22 to restitute about 530 Benin Bronzes — looted by British forces in 1897 — held in Berlin's Ethnological Museum to Nigeria, a landmark in the global colonial-restitution debate, though roughly a third are to remain on loan in Berlin. Source: Euronews; Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (smb.museum); Artnet.

markers.name: Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, Paris
markers.ctx: The museum holds around 70,000 sub-Saharan African objects — about two-thirds of France's African holdings; the 2018 Sarr-Savoy report, which estimated 90-95% of Africa's heritage sits outside the continent, prompted France to return 26 works plundered from Abomey Palace in 1892 to Benin. Source: Center for Art Law; Cultural Property News; Artnet.

markers.name: Bardo National Museum, Tunis
markers.ctx: On March 18, 2015, gunmen attacked Tunisia's national museum - home to one of the world's great Roman mosaic collections - killing about 22 people, mostly foreign tourists. ISIS claimed it; Tunisian authorities attributed it to the al-Qaeda-linked Uqba ibn Nafi Brigade. It devastated the tourism sector.

markers.name: Victoria and Albert Museum, London
markers.ctx: The V&A holds treasures looted by British forces after the 1868 Battle of Maqdala in Ethiopia — gold crowns, crosses and royal regalia; in 2018 director Tristram Hunt publicly offered to return the Maqdala collection to Ethiopia on long-term loan rather than as outright restitution, spotlighting UK museums' colonial acquisitions. Source: Victoria and Albert Museum (vam.ac.uk); The Guardian.

markers.name: The Mob Museum, Las Vegas
markers.ctx: Officially the National Museum of Organized Crime and Law Enforcement, it opened in 2012 inside the former federal courthouse that hosted a 1950-51 Kefauver Committee hearing on organized crime, documenting the mob's role in building Las Vegas and its casino skim operations. Source: The Mob Museum (themobmuseum.org); Las Vegas Review-Journal.

markers.name: Museo Egizio, Turin
markers.ctx: Founded in 1824, the oldest museum devoted solely to ancient Egypt, with more than 40,000 artifacts - considered the most important Egyptological collection after Cairo - much of it amassed by French consul Bernardino Drovetti during the colonial-era scramble for Egyptian antiquities. Source: Museo Egizio; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

markers.name: The Venetian Macao / Cotai Strip, Macau
markers.ctx: The anchor of Macau's Cotai Strip, the gambling capital of the world, whose revenues long dwarfed Las Vegas; the VIP junket system that fed it collapsed when Suncity chief Alvin Chau — whose firm held ~40% of the junket market and handled bets prosecutors valued at HK$824 billion — was jailed 18 years in 2023 for running an illegal gambling and criminal syndicate. Source: TIME; South China Morning Post; Al Jazeera.

markers.name: Crown Melbourne
markers.ctx: A 2021 Victorian royal commission led by former judge Ray Finkelstein found Crown Melbourne had facilitated money laundering, had ties to organised-crime-linked junkets and serious governance failures, and was unsuitable to hold Victoria's only casino licence. Regulators later fined it A$80M (2022, illicit China UnionPay transactions) and A$120M (responsible-gambling breaches). Source: Wikipedia; The Guardian Australia.

markers.name: The Star Sydney
markers.ctx: Two NSW inquiries (2022 and the 2024 Bell review) found The Star unsuitable to hold a Sydney casino licence, exposing anti-money-laundering failures — including 'Salon 95,' a secret VIP room with a hidden cash cage — and cash disguised as hotel expenses; the operator was fined AU$100 million and placed under a government manager. Source: NSW Independent Casino Commission (nicc.nsw.gov.au); iGaming Business; Yogonet.

markers.name: Wynn Las Vegas - $130M Money-Laundering Forfeiture
markers.ctx: In September 2024 Wynn Las Vegas forfeited $130.1 million under a non-prosecution agreement, admitting it conspired with unlicensed money-transmitting businesses ('Flying Money' and 'Human Head' gambling) to move funds for foreign patrons outside U.S. reporting rules - believed to be the largest forfeiture by a casino based on admissions of criminal wrongdoing. Source: DOJ / HSI (6 Sept 2024).

markers.name: ASML Headquarters - Veldhoven, Netherlands
markers.ctx: ASML is the only firm on Earth able to build extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines — bus-sized systems priced around €150 million each — and holds effectively 100% of the EUV market; the Netherlands has barred EUV exports to China since 2019 under US pressure, making Veldhoven a linchpin of the global chip war. Source: Silicon Canals / Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASML).

markers.name: NSO Group Headquarters - Herzliya, Israel
markers.ctx: The Israeli cyber-intelligence firm NSO Group, founded 2010, develops Pegasus — a zero-click smartphone spyware classified as a military export and licensed sale-by-sale by the Israeli government. Investigations documented its use against journalists, activists and Palestinian NGO staff, and the US blacklisted the company in 2021. Source: Wikipedia / Amnesty International / OCCRP Pegasus Project (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSO_Group).

markers.name: VECTOR State Research Center of Virology - Koltsovo, Russia
markers.ctx: Founded 1974 within the Soviet Biopreparat network, VECTOR is one of only two WHO-authorized repositories on Earth for the live variola (smallpox) virus, with BSL-1 to BSL-4 capability and ~1,614 staff. A 2019 explosion at the facility drew global attention to its pathogen stocks. Source: Wikipedia / Slate (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Research_Center_of_Virology_and_Biotechnology_VECTOR).

markers.name: DARPA Headquarters - Arlington, Virginia, USA
markers.ctx: The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, created February 7, 1958 in response to Sputnik, funds the Pentagon's emerging-technology research (its ARPANET work seeded the internet). Its 13-story, 353,000 sq ft Ballston headquarters at 675 North Randolph Street meets DoD anti-terrorism standards with an 82-foot secured perimeter. Source: Wikipedia / CoStar (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA).

markers.name: Hikvision Headquarters - Hangzhou, China
markers.ctx: Hangzhou Hikvision Digital Technology, the world's largest maker of video-surveillance gear, is partly state-owned and was placed on the U.S. Commerce Department Entity List in 2019 over its role supplying cameras used in the mass surveillance of Uyghurs in Xinjiang. Its HQ is at No.555 Qianmo Road, Binjiang District. Source: Wikipedia (Hikvision); AFSC Investigate; U.S. Commerce Dept. Entity List.

markers.name: Dahua Technology Headquarters - Hangzhou, China
markers.ctx: Zhejiang Dahua Technology, the world's second-largest video-surveillance manufacturer, was added to the U.S. Entity List in 2019 and its equipment banned from U.S. federal networks over links to Xinjiang surveillance. HQ is at No.1199 Bin'an Road, Binjiang District. Source: Wikipedia (Dahua Technology); U.S. FCC/Commerce Dept..

markers.name: Telangana Integrated Command and Control Centre - Hyderabad, India
markers.ctx: Inaugurated 4 August 2022 in Banjara Hills at a cost of over Rs 600 crore, this complex houses the Hyderabad City Police Commissionerate and integrates over 100,000 CCTV cameras state-wide with AI and analytics modules for real-time monitoring and predictive policing.

markers.name: Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex - Tidbinbilla, Australia
markers.ctx: The southern-hemisphere node of NASA's Deep Space Network, ~20 km southwest of Canberra, is managed by CSIRO; its DSS-43 70-metre dish is the only antenna on Earth able to send commands to Voyager 2. Source: Wikipedia (Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex); CSIRO/NASA.

markers.name: RAF Fylingdales - North Yorkshire, UK
markers.ctx: Operational since 1963 on the North York Moors, Fylingdales is one of three Ballistic Missile Early Warning System sites (with Clear, Alaska and Thule/Pituffik, Greenland); its phased-array radar provides US and UK missile warning and tracks satellites and debris to about 3,000 nautical miles (5,600 km).

markers.name: Maui Space Surveillance Complex (AMOS) - Haleakalā, Hawaii
markers.ctx: Atop Haleakala, this Space Force site (15th Space Surveillance Squadron with AFRL) hosts AEOS, the largest US optical telescope designed for tracking satellites, and one of the three US GEODSS deep-space surveillance sites.

markers.name: Luigi Broglio Space Centre (Malindi Station) - Kenya
markers.ctx: Italian-operated equatorial spaceport off the Kenyan coast near Malindi: 27 launches between 1964 and 1988 (3 from Santa Rita, 24 from the San Marco platform), including orbital Scout launches; it still operates a satellite ground station managed by the Italian Space Agency (ASI).

markers.name: SWIFT Headquarters, La Hulpe, Belgium
markers.ctx: SWIFT, the cooperative that runs the dominant global interbank financial-messaging network, links more than 11,000 institutions across over 200 countries and carries tens of millions of messages daily. Control over SWIFT access has become a key instrument of financial sanctions, as when Russian banks were cut off in 2022. Source: Wikipedia, SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication).

markers.name: DTCC, Jersey City
markers.ctx: The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation clears and settles the vast majority of US securities transactions; in 2025 its subsidiaries processed transactions valued at roughly US$4.7 quadrillion. As the central securities depository, DTCC holds custody of most US stocks and bonds through its nominee, Cede & Co. Source: Wikipedia, Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation.

markers.name: Ugland House, George Town, Cayman Islands
markers.ctx: This five-story building, home to the law firm Maples and Calder, is the registered office for roughly 40,000 companies — a density that prompted President Obama to call it 'either the biggest building or the biggest tax scam on record.' It is an icon of offshore corporate structuring. Source: Wikipedia, Ugland House; Foreign Policy, 'House of 19,000 Corporations'.

markers.name: Corporation Trust Center, 1209 North Orange St, Delaware
markers.ctx: This single Wilmington address is the registered-agent home to hundreds of thousands of entities — reported at over 285,000 in 2012 — including subsidiaries of Apple, Google, Coca-Cola and Walmart, exploiting Delaware's corporate-secrecy and tax regime. Run by CT Corporation (Wolters Kluwer). Source: Wikipedia, Corporation Trust Center; Washington Free Beacon.

markers.name: People's Bank of China, Beijing
markers.ctx: The PBOC is the central bank of China, managing the world's largest foreign-exchange reserves (over US$3 trillion) and issuing the renminbi. It pioneered a state-controlled central bank digital currency (the digital yuan / e-CNY) and is a central instrument of China's financial statecraft. Source: Wikipedia, People's Bank of China.

markers.name: Rothschild & Co, New Court, London
markers.ctx: New Court on St Swithin's Lane has been the London seat of the Rothschild banking house since Nathan Mayer Rothschild established N M Rothschild & Sons there (1809-1811). It hosted the twice-daily London gold fixing from soon after its first sitting (12 Sept 1919) until 2004, when Rothschild withdrew and the fix moved to a telephone call. The firm remains a leading independent M&A adviser.

markers.name: Norges Bank Investment Management (GPFG), Oslo
markers.ctx: NBIM manages Norway's Government Pension Fund Global - the world's largest sovereign wealth fund, about US$2.27 trillion (July 2026), owning almost 1.5% of all listed shares worldwide through small stakes in about 7,200 companies. Source: Norges Bank Investment Management (nbim.no); Wikipedia.

markers.name: Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Abu Dhabi
markers.ctx: Founded in 1976 to invest Abu Dhabi's oil surpluses, ADIA manages an estimated US$1.1 trillion across public equities, fixed income, private equity, real estate and infrastructure in over 50 countries from its landmark Corniche tower. It is among the largest and most secretive sovereign wealth funds. Source: Wikipedia, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; ADIA (adia.ae).

markers.name: Public Investment Fund (PIF), Riyadh
markers.ctx: Saudi Arabia's PIF, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, manages an estimated US$900 billion (May 2026) and is the main vehicle of Vision 2030, funding NEOM, LIV Golf and stakes in firms worldwide. Source: Wikipedia; PIF (pif.gov.sa).

markers.name: Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), Tokyo
markers.ctx: Japan's GPIF is the world's largest public pension fund, managing about 293.6 trillion yen (roughly US$1.9 trillion) as of March 2026 for the national pension system. Its portfolio is split roughly evenly among domestic and foreign bonds and equities. Source: Private Equity International / PERE institution profile; GPIF (gpif.go.jp).

markers.name: China Investment Corporation (CIC), Beijing
markers.ctx: Established in 2007 with US$200 billion to diversify China's foreign-exchange reserves, CIC managed roughly US$1.57 trillion by 2026 from New Poly Plaza. It invests globally in equities, private equity and infrastructure and is a key vehicle of Chinese overseas capital. Source: Wikipedia, China Investment Corporation; china-inv.cn.

markers.name: Bridgewater Associates, Westport, Connecticut
markers.ctx: Founded by Ray Dalio in 1975, Bridgewater is often ranked the world's largest hedge fund, managing about US$92 billion (2025) from its Westport campus. Its 'Pure Alpha' macro strategy and 'radical transparency' culture made it one of the most studied investment firms. Source: Wikipedia; Reuters.

markers.name: Temasek Holdings, Singapore
markers.ctx: Temasek is a Singapore state-owned investment company with a net portfolio of S$518 billion (31 March 2026), holding controlling or major stakes in Singapore Airlines, DBS Bank, Singtel and global firms. Unlike a reserve fund, it operates as an active commercial investor. Source: Temasek annual review; Wikipedia.

markers.name: GIC Private Limited, Capital Tower, Singapore
markers.ctx: GIC manages Singapore's foreign reserves across more than 40 countries and is one of the most active sovereign investors in real estate and private markets. Established 1981; it does not disclose its size - outside estimates range from about US$744 billion (Forbes) to US$1.16 trillion (SWFI, 2026). Source: Wikipedia; GIC (gic.com.sg).

markers.name: Saudi Aramco HQ, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia
markers.ctx: State-controlled Saudi Aramco, with 2024 net income of $106 billion, holds more than 270 billion barrels of proven crude reserves and produced 12.7 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2024. Headquartered in Dhahran.

markers.name: TSMC HQ, Hsinchu Science Park, Taiwan
markers.ctx: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is the world's largest dedicated chip foundry, controlling roughly 60-70% of the global foundry market and producing nearly all of the planet's most advanced (5nm/3nm) processors. Its Hsinchu concentration makes the site a central chokepoint in US-China technology geopolitics. Source: TSMC corporate; CNBC / Wikipedia: TSMC.

markers.name: NSO Group HQ, Herzliya, Israel
markers.ctx: The Israeli cyber-intelligence firm NSO Group makes Pegasus, a zero-click smartphone spyware classified by Israel as a military export; the 2021 Pegasus Project revealed its use against journalists, activists and officials worldwide, prompting a US Commerce Department blacklisting. The company is based in Herzliya, north of Tel Aviv. Source: Amnesty International / OCCRP Pegasus Project (2021); Wikipedia: NSO Group.

markers.name: Vitol HQ, Geneva, Switzerland
markers.ctx: Vitol is the world's largest independent oil trader, moving over 7 million barrels a day and posting revenues around $343 billion in 2025; the secretive Geneva-run firm controls some 250 tankers and has faced US and Brazilian bribery settlements over crude-trading corruption in Latin America. Source: SWI swissinfo.ch; Wikipedia: Vitol; U.S. DOJ (2020 Vitol FCPA settlement).

markers.name: Tencent Binhai Towers, Shenzhen, China
markers.ctx: Tencent's global headquarters, the twin Binhai Towers in Shenzhen's Nanshan tech district, opened in 2017 after a 1.8-billion-yuan build. Tencent operates WeChat, the super-app woven into Chinese payments, messaging and state-linked data governance for over a billion users. Source: Tencent corporate; Wikipedia: Tencent Binhai Mansion.

markers.name: Mt. Gox Office, Cerulean Tower, Shibuya, Tokyo
markers.ctx: The Shibuya-based Mt. Gox exchange handled over 70% of all global Bitcoin transactions before it collapsed in February 2014, having lost roughly 850,000 BTC (worth hundreds of millions then, tens of billions later) to theft and mismanagement. Protesters gathered outside its Tokyo office as it filed for bankruptcy. Source: Wikipedia: Mt. Gox; Japan Times (Mt. Gox coverage).

markers.name: Bitmain HQ, Beijing, China
markers.ctx: Beijing-based Bitmain has been the dominant maker of Bitcoin-mining ASICs, at its peak credited with a large majority of the market (share estimates vary) for mining rigs through its Antminer brand, and it operates Antpool, one of the largest mining pools. Its dominance means even 'Made in USA' Bitcoin largely runs on Chinese-designed hardware. Source: Bloomberg (2024); Wikipedia: Bitmain.

markers.name: Riot Platforms Rockdale Facility (Whinstone), Texas
markers.ctx: Built on an abandoned aluminum smelter, Riot Platforms' Rockdale site is the largest single Bitcoin-mining facility by developed capacity in North America at about 700 MW, and Greenpeace calls it the most energy- and carbon-intensive Bitcoin mine in the US. Riot acquired builder Whinstone for $651 million in 2021. Source: Greenpeace USA; Global Energy Monitor (Whinstone Bitcoin mining facility).

markers.name: Strategy (MicroStrategy) HQ, Tysons Corner, Virginia
markers.ctx: Founded by Michael Saylor, the software firm rebranded from MicroStrategy to 'Strategy' in 2025 and is the world's largest corporate Bitcoin holder, having amassed roughly 597,000 BTC (worth over $70 billion in mid-2025) funded largely through equity and debt issuance. It pioneered the Bitcoin corporate-treasury model. Source: Virginia Business; Bitcoin Treasuries; Wikipedia: MicroStrategy.

markers.name: Bletchley Park, Milton Keynes, UK
markers.ctx: Bletchley Park was Britain's WWII codebreaking center, where Alan Turing and colleagues broke the German Enigma and Lorenz ciphers and built Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic digital computer. It is a foundational site of modern cryptography and computing, kept secret for decades after the war. Source: UK National Museum of Computing / Bletchley Park Trust.

markers.name: HMNB Clyde (Faslane) - Trident Submarine Base, Scotland
markers.ctx: HMNB Clyde at Faslane on the Gare Loch is the home port of the Royal Navy's four Vanguard-class SSBNs carrying Trident II D5 missiles, providing the UK's sole continuous-at-sea nuclear deterrent; the associated RNAD Coulport, 8 miles away, stores and processes the warheads. It is among the most heavily protected sites in Britain. Source: Nuclear Information Service, 'Faslane and Coulport Nuclear Submarine Bases: A Briefing' (nuclearinfo.org); GlobalSecurity.org.

markers.name: Pokhran Test Range - Operation Shakti, Rajasthan, India
markers.ctx: At the Pokhran Test Range in the Thar Desert, India conducted the Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti) series of five underground nuclear detonations on 11–13 May 1998, including a claimed 45-kiloton thermonuclear device, moving India to declared nuclear-weapons status and triggering international sanctions. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pokhran-II'; Nuclear Weapon Archive, 'Operation Shakti: 1998'.

markers.name: Ream Naval Base - China-Backed Expansion, Cambodia
markers.ctx: China financed a major upgrade of Cambodia's Ream Naval Base from 2022, adding a 300-metre deepwater pier, a 5,000-ton dry dock and a slipway; two Chinese Type-056A corvettes have been stationed there near-continuously since December 2023, prompting US concern it could become a PLA Navy foothold on the Gulf of Thailand. Source: CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative; Nikkei Asia; NPR (2025).

markers.name: Sohae Satellite Launching Station - Tongchang-ri, North Korea
markers.ctx: Sohae (Tongchang-ri) on North Korea's northwest coast is the DPRK's primary long-range rocket facility and the site of all seven of its satellite launch attempts since 2012, doubling as a testbed for ICBM development. Following Kim Jong Un's March 2022 visit, satellite imagery has shown near-constant expansion of pads, an assembly building and a new sea port. Source: CSIS Beyond Parallel; 38 North; NTI Facilities Profile.

markers.name: Natanz Nuclear Enrichment Complex - Iran
markers.ctx: Iran's main uranium-enrichment site near Natanz, with underground halls built for tens of thousands of centrifuges. Around 2009-2010 the Stuxnet worm sabotaged its controllers; ISIS estimated about 1,000 centrifuges were decommissioned and replaced - widely attributed to a US-Israeli operation, never acknowledged. Bombed by Israel in June 2025 (above-ground plant partially destroyed, per the IAEA) and by the United States on 22 June 2025; further damage in the 2026 war, with the core underground hall reported not destroyed as of March 2026.

markers.name: HMAS Stirling (Fleet Base West) - AUKUS SRF-West, Australia
markers.ctx: HMAS Stirling on Garden Island off Rockingham is the Royal Australian Navy's submarine home port and the designated site for AUKUS 'Submarine Rotational Force – West': from 2027 up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarines will rotate through, backed by an Australian investment of up to A$8 billion. Source: Australian Submarine Agency (asa.gov.au); Australian Dept of Defence.

markers.name: Khan Research Laboratories - Kahuta, Pakistan
markers.ctx: The Khan Research Laboratories at Kahuta, established 31 July 1976 (as Engineering Research Laboratories) under A.Q. Khan, who brought URENCO centrifuge designs from the Netherlands, are Pakistan's main gas-centrifuge enrichment and weapons-research complex. KRL produced highly enriched uranium by 1985 and is outside IAEA safeguards.

markers.name: Saydnaya Military Prison, Syria
markers.ctx: Saydnaya military prison, about 30 km north of Damascus, where Amnesty International estimated 5,000-13,000 detainees were extrajudicially hanged between September 2011 and December 2015, calling it a 'human slaughterhouse'; groups of up to 50 at a time were taken from their cells for hanging. Opened by opposition forces on 8 December 2024. Source: Amnesty International (2017), via Wikipedia, Saydnaya Prison.

markers.name: Villa Grimaldi (Cuartel Terranova), Santiago, Chile
markers.ctx: A former estate in Peñalolén that Pinochet's secret police (DINA) ran as its most important Santiago torture center from 1974 to 1978; about 4,500 detainees passed through and at least 240 were killed or 'disappeared.' It is now the Parque por la Paz memorial. Source: Wikipedia / Villa Grimaldi Peace Park; Plan Cóndor archive, plancondor.org.

markers.name: Willowbrook State School, Staten Island, USA
markers.ctx: State institution for children with intellectual disabilities (1947-1987). From 1956 to 1971 NYU's Saul Krugman, with Yale's Robert McCollum, deliberately infected resident children with hepatitis to study the disease and gamma globulin; parents' admission of children was reportedly tied to consent. Geraldo Rivera's 1972 exposé brought national infamy; the institution closed in 1987. Source: Wikipedia, Willowbrook State School; C. Elliott, New York Review of Books (Nov. 21, 2024).

markers.name: Kaechon Internment Camp (Camp 14), North Korea
markers.ctx: A roughly 155-square-kilometre 'total control zone' political prison on the north bank of the Taedong River, near Kaechon, South Pyongan, holding an estimated 15,000 prisoners for life; a UN Commission of Inquiry found extermination, enslavement and torture in North Korea's political prison camps. Tracked via satellite imagery by HRNK. Source: HRNK, 'North Korea Imagery Analysis of Camp 14'; Wikipedia, Kaechon internment camp.

markers.name: Tazmamart Secret Prison, Morocco
markers.ctx: Secret desert prison in southeastern Morocco, built in 1972 after the 1971 and 1972 coup attempts against King Hassan II. 58 army officers were held in windowless cells for 18 years; 35 died before the prison was closed in 1991 under international pressure. Source: Wikipedia, Tazmamart; ICRC Missing Persons Platform.

markers.name: Long Tieng (Lima Site 20A), Laos
markers.ctx: A CIA-run airbase and 'secret city' that was the unofficial headquarters of the Secret War in Laos; at its peak the single airstrip handled around 900 daily takeoffs and landings, making it one of the busiest airfields in the world, while the surrounding town of 40,000 never appeared on maps. Source: CNN Travel, 'Long Tieng, Laos: Once the most secret place on Earth'; Wikipedia / Long Tieng.

markers.name: Pinal Airpark (Marana), Arizona, USA
markers.ctx: During the Vietnam era, Marana was the headquarters of all CIA air operations and the main U.S. maintenance base for Intermountain Airlines, a CIA front supporting Air America; later acquired by Evergreen, it is today the world's largest commercial-aircraft storage and heavy-maintenance boneyard. Source: Center for Land Use Interpretation, clui.org; Wikipedia / Pinal Airpark.

markers.name: Udorn Royal Thai Air Force Base, Udon Thani, Thailand
markers.ctx: The Asian headquarters of Air America, the CIA's covertly owned airline, and one of five Thai bases used covertly by the U.S. from 1961; it also hosted 'Headquarters 333,' the Thai command directing forces in Laos. Air America ran operations into Laos from Udorn until June 1974. Source: Wikipedia / Udorn Royal Thai Air Force Base; Grey Dynamics, 'Project 404'.

markers.name: Transit Center at Manas, Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan
markers.ctx: A key U.S. logistics hub for the Afghanistan war until 2014, at the center of a fuel-contracting scandal: a 2010 congressional probe found offshore suppliers Mina Corp and Red Star Enterprises had won over $1 billion in Pentagon contracts and imported jet fuel via opaque structures allegedly deceiving Russia. Source: Eurasianet, 'Deconstructing Manas Fuel Suppliers' Corporate Structures'; U.S. House Oversight subcommittee report (Dec. 2010).

markers.name: Eloy Alfaro Air Base (FOL Manta), Ecuador
markers.ctx: From 1999 to 2009 the U.S. ran this coastal base as a Forward Operating Location, flying E-3 Sentry and P-3 Orion surveillance missions across a 6,400 km swath feeding intelligence to Joint Interagency Task Force South; Manta flights accounted for about 60% of eastern-Pacific drug interdictions before Ecuador declined to renew the lease. Source: GlobalSecurity.org, 'Eloy Alfaro Air Base / FOL Manta'; Air & Space Forces Magazine.

markers.name: Sohae Satellite Launching Station (Tongchang-ri), North Korea
markers.ctx: North Korea's principal rocket-launch and engine-test facility near the Chinese border, used for satellite launches widely assessed as covers for long-range ballistic-missile development; commercial-satellite analysts (38 North, CSIS) closely track its gantry and engine-stand expansions. Source: 38 North (Stimson Center), 38north.org; CSIS Beyond Parallel, beyondparallel.csis.org.

markers.name: Sonnenberg Tunnel Civil Defense Shelter, Lucerne, Switzerland
markers.ctx: Built 1971-1976, this twin-bore motorway tunnel doubled as the world's largest civilian nuclear fallout shelter, engineered to hold 20,000 people behind 350-tonne blast doors, with a seven-storey central cavern housing a command post, hospital, radio studio and prison cells. Switzerland cut its rated capacity to 2,000 in 2002 after concluding the dual-use design was unworkable. Source: Swiss Review (swisscommunity.org); Wikipedia, 'Sonnenberg Tunnel'.

markers.name: Olavsvern Naval Base, Ramfjord, Tromsø
markers.ctx: Cold War Royal Norwegian Navy submarine base blasted into a mountain near Tromsø: 25,000 m² inside under ~274 m of rock. Decommissioned and sold in 2013 for NOK 38 million; then rented by companies linked to Russia's Gazprom, which alarmed Norwegian officers. Bought by a Wilhelmsen subsidiary in 2019.

markers.name: Onkalo Spent Nuclear Fuel Repository, Olkiluoto
markers.ctx: World's first deep geological repository for spent nuclear fuel, built by Posiva ~430 m down in ancient bedrock at Olkiluoto; capacity 6,500 tonnes of uranium, isolation for 100,000 years. Scheduled to begin operation by 2026.

markers.name: China Jinping Underground Laboratory (CJPL), Sichuan
markers.ctx: Now the world's deepest and largest underground laboratory, sited beside a hydropower traffic tunnel under 2,400 m of rock beneath Jinping Mountain; its CJPL-II expansion, operational December 2023, spans about 330,000 cubic metres and overtook Italy's Gran Sasso in both depth and volume. It houses the PandaX and CDEX dark-matter searches. Source: Scientific American; Wikipedia, 'China Jinping Underground Laboratory'.

markers.name: Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP), Carlsbad
markers.ctx: The only U.S. deep geologic repository for defense transuranic (mostly plutonium-contaminated) waste, with disposal rooms mined 2,150 feet down into a 2,000-foot-thick, 250-million-year-old salt bed that slowly creeps shut to encapsulate the waste. Operating since 1999, it suffered a 2014 radiological release from a chemically reactive waste drum that shut the facility for years. Source: U.S. Department of Energy (energy.gov); EPA (epa.gov).

markers.name: Kelvedon Hatch Secret Nuclear Bunker, Essex
markers.ctx: A three-storey Cold War bunker sunk about 125 feet under an ordinary-looking Essex bungalow, walls of 10 feet of reinforced concrete inside a Faraday cage, designed as a Regional Government Headquarters for up to 600 personnel (potentially including the Prime Minister) to administer survivors after a nuclear strike. Decommissioned in 1992 and now a museum. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kelvedon Hatch Secret Nuclear Bunker'; Nuclear Essex (nuclearessex.com).

markers.name: Bunker-42 (Tagansky Protected Command Point), Moscow
markers.ctx: A 7,000-square-metre command complex, 'Facility-02,' built from 1950 on Stalin's orders 65 metres beneath Moscow near Taganskaya metro, intended as a bomb-proof refuge and command post for Soviet strategic nuclear-armed bombers. Staff were reportedly bused in windowless vehicles and kept unaware of its location; it now operates as a Cold War museum. Source: Rusmania (rusmania.com); Wikipedia, 'Tagansky Protected Command Point'.

markers.name: Mount Pony Federal Reserve Bunker (Culpeper Switch), Virginia
markers.ctx: A radiation-hardened 140,000-square-foot bunker excavated into Mount Pony in 1969 as the Federal Reserve's continuity-of-government center; it stored roughly USD 4 billion in shrink-wrapped currency to restart the economy after nuclear war and ran the 'Culpeper Switch' handling the Fed's national wire transfers from 1970-1988. Now the Library of Congress Packard Campus audio-visual archive. Source: Gizmodo/Paleofuture; FAS Nuclear Forces (nuke.fas.org); Wikipedia, 'National Audio-Visual Conservation Center'.

markers.name: Projekt Riese Underground Complex, Owl Mountains
markers.ctx: An unfinished Nazi network code-named 'Riese' (Giant) begun 1943-45 across seven sites in the Owl Mountains and Książ Castle, with about 90,000 cubic metres of tunnels excavated (only ~11% concrete-lined) and its true purpose - Führer headquarters or weapons plant - still undocumented. Built by forced laborers who died in large numbers from disease, starvation and cave-ins. Source: Wikipedia, 'Project Riese'; Atlas Obscura.

markers.name: Yamaguchi-gumi Headquarters - Kobe, Japan
markers.ctx: Fortress-like headquarters of the Yamaguchi-gumi, Japan's largest yakuza syndicate, founded in Kobe in 1915; its address is publicly listed on the National Police Agency's designated-crime-group registry. At the end of 2017 it counted roughly 4,700 full members and about 10,300 total, then roughly 30% of all yakuza in Japan, and it and top leaders were placed under U.S. Treasury OFAC sanctions in 2012. Source: U.S. Treasury OFAC; Japan National Police Agency; Asia Times (asiatimes.com), 'Japan's leading yakuza gangs in US Treasury's cross-hairs,' 2018.

markers.name: Tocorón Prison (Tren de Aragua Cradle) - Aragua, Venezuela
markers.ctx: Tren de Aragua, Venezuela's most powerful transnational gang, was founded inside Tocorón prison around 2014 by Héctor 'Niño' Guerrero (died June 2026), who ran the compound as a fiefdom complete with a zoo, swimming pool, nightclub and restaurant. Venezuelan security forces retook the prison in September 2023, by which point the gang had projected criminal cells into at least three other South American countries; the U.S. later designated it a foreign terrorist organization. Source: InSight Crime (insightcrime.org), 'Tren de Aragua Explained'; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tren de Aragua'.

markers.name: Corleone - Cradle of Cosa Nostra, Sicily
markers.ctx: Corleone is the historic stronghold of the Corleonesi, the most violent faction of the Sicilian Mafia, and birthplace of bosses Luciano Liggio, Salvatore 'Totò' Riina (Cosa Nostra chief 1974–1993) and Bernardo Provenzano, who was arrested in a farmhouse just outside the town in 2006 after 43 years as a fugitive. The Corleonesi seized control of Cosa Nostra through the 1981–1983 Second Mafia War, which left hundreds dead. Source: Wikipedia, 'Corleonesi Mafia clan'; Fox News (foxnews.com), 'Sicilian town had long bloody past before Godfather fame'.

markers.name: Solntsevo - Solntsevskaya Bratva Base, Moscow
markers.ctx: The Solntsevskaya Bratva, one of the world's richest crime syndicates, took its name from the Solntsevo district of southwest Moscow where it coalesced in the late 1980s under Sergei Mikhailov and Viktor Averin. Its position near the MKAD ring road, the M3 highway and Vnukovo Airport let it dominate the post-Soviet car-import racket; a 2014 Fortune/Guinness estimate put its annual revenue at roughly 8.5 billion dollars. Source: Wikipedia, 'Solntsevskaya Bratva'; Guinness World Records, 'Largest criminal organization (profits)'.

markers.name: UWSA Headquarters, Pangkham - Golden Triangle, Myanmar
markers.ctx: Pangkham is the capital of the autonomous Wa State and headquarters of the roughly 30,000-strong United Wa State Army, described as the largest drug-producing organisation in Southeast Asia (attributed). From this Golden Triangle base the UWSA is tied to industrial-scale methamphetamine and heroin production, with casino revenue from Chinese visitors bolstering the group; leaders including Wei Hsueh-kang carry U.S. narcotics indictments and sanctions. Source: VOA News (voanews.com), 'Myanmar's largest rebel group quietly gains strength'; GIJN, 'Guide to Investigating Organized Crime in the Golden Triangle'.

markers.name: Regency Hotel - Kinahan-Hutch Feud Attack, Dublin
markers.ctx: The February 2016 gun attack at the Regency Hotel (now the Bonnington), which killed Kinahan associate David Byrne during a boxing weigh-in, ignited the Kinahan-Hutch feud that left more than a dozen dead. The U.S. Treasury sanctioned the Kinahan Organised Crime Group in 2022 with a 5-million-dollar reward for its leaders; alleged boss Daniel Kinahan was extradited from the UAE to Dublin in August 2026. Source: BBC News (bbc.co.uk), 'Kinahan crime gang: UAE freezes assets after US sanctions'; Al Jazeera (aljazeera.com), 'UAE extradites alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan,' 2026.

markers.name: Mozambique LNG (Afungi site) - Palma, Cabo Delgado
markers.ctx: On 24 March 2021 Islamic State-linked insurgents (locally 'al-Shabab') overran Palma, beside TotalEnergies' Afungi LNG site; one tally put civilian deaths at more than 1,190, with about 40,000 displaced. TotalEnergies withdrew staff and declared force majeure on the project in April 2021. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Palma; Combating Terrorism Center at West Point.

markers.name: Nord Stream Pipeline Sabotage Site - off Bornholm, Baltic Sea
markers.ctx: On 26 September 2022 underwater explosions ruptured three of the four Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines in the Baltic, north-east and south-east of the Danish island of Bornholm, at depths of about 80-110 m; seabed surveys found blast craters and Swedish prosecutors called it gross sabotage. Sweden and Denmark closed their investigations in February 2024 without naming anyone; German prosecutors are pursuing Ukrainian nationals. No state's responsibility is established. Pin at the Nord Stream 1 leak site. Source: Wikipedia, Nord Stream pipelines sabotage; RFE/RL; BBC.

markers.name: Lachin Corridor - Nagorno-Karabakh
markers.ctx: Azerbaijan blockaded the sole road linking Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenia from December 2022, starving Stepanakert of food, fuel and medicine for nine months. After a September 2023 military offensive the ethnic-Armenian enclave capitulated and over 100,000 Armenians fled within a week, effectively emptying the region. Source: Amnesty International; BBC — amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/02/azerbaijan-blockade-of-lachin-corridor-putting-thousands-of-lives-in-peril-must-be-immediately-lifted/.

markers.name: Siachen Glacier - Karakoram, Ladakh
markers.ctx: At roughly 18,000-22,000 ft, the Siachen Glacier is the world's highest battlefield, contested by India and Pakistan since India's 1984 Operation Meghdoot. With temperatures reaching -50°C, more soldiers on both sides have died from avalanches and cold than from combat. Source: GlobalSecurity.org; WorldAtlas — globalsecurity.org/military/world/war/siachen.htm.

markers.name: Crimean (Kerch Strait) Bridge - Kerch, Crimea
markers.ctx: The road-and-rail bridge (about 18 km) Russia built across the Kerch Strait after its 2014 annexation of Crimea is the main military supply artery to the peninsula. A truck-bomb blast on 8 October 2022 collapsed two road spans and killed five people; the bridge has been struck again since. Source: Wikipedia, Crimean Bridge; 2022 Crimean Bridge explosion; CNN.

markers.name: Guerguerat Crossing / Moroccan Berm - Western Sahara
markers.ctx: Guerguerat sits on the roughly 2,700 km Moroccan sand berm, the world's longest operational military barrier and longest continuous minefield, dividing Morocco-controlled Western Sahara from the Polisario-held Free Zone. A November 2020 flare-up at the crossing ended a near-30-year UN ceasefire, reigniting armed conflict. Source: Wikipedia 'Moroccan Western Sahara Wall'; Georgetown Security Studies Review — en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Western_Sahara_Wall.

markers.name: Fort Brecqhou (Barclay family), Channel Islands
markers.ctx: 74-acre islet off Sark. David and Frederick Barclay bought it in September 1993 for GBP 2.3 million, built a mock-Gothic castle and fought years of disputes over Sark's feudal constitution. Sir David Barclay died on 10 January 2021. The family's ownership of the Telegraph ended in 2025; the island remains theirs.

markers.name: Runit Dome, Enewetak Atoll, Marshall Islands
markers.ctx: Concrete cap built by the US in 1977-80 over a nuclear blast crater on Runit Island, entombing about 100,000 cubic yards of radioactive soil and debris from Enewetak tests. A 2013 DOE report found minor cracking, and that the soil around the dome is more contaminated than its contents; the concern is tidal groundwater moving beneath its unlined base. Marshallese officials and the UN have warned of leakage.

markers.name: Capella, Sentosa Island, Singapore (2018 Trump-Kim Summit)
markers.ctx: The secluded Capella hotel on Sentosa, a resort island a quarter-mile off Singapore's coast, hosted the first Trump-Kim summit on June 12, 2018 under a heavy security lockdown. The Foster + Partners-designed resort was chosen partly because the island setting could be sealed off from the public. Source: CNN Politics; TIME.

markers.name: Tagomago Private Island, Ibiza, Spain
markers.ctx: Tagomago is a roughly 600,000-square-metre privately owned islet about 900 m off Ibiza's east coast, marketed as one of the Mediterranean's most exclusive private-island rentals with a single luxury villa and a staff of around twelve reserved for one group at a time. It lies within the EU Natura 2000 protected network yet is held as a fully private retreat. Source: Rental Escapes; Tripadvisor (Tagomago Private Island Retreat).

markers.name: Muruntau Gold Mine, Uzbekistan
markers.ctx: One of the world's largest open-pit gold mines - about 3.5 km long, 2.7 km wide and 600 m deep - second by output after Grasberg (61 t in 2014). Run by Uzbekistan's state Navoi Mining & Metallurgical Combinat; industrial mining since 21 July 1969; reserves estimated at 71.4 million ounces.

markers.name: Simandou Iron Ore Project, Guinea
markers.ctx: The largest untapped high-grade iron ore deposit in the world, holding at least 3 billion tonnes averaging 65.3% iron. At roughly $23 billion it is Africa's biggest-ever mining project, co-developed by Rio Tinto/Chalco (Simfer) and China's Winning Consortium Simandou, with 600+ km of new rail built to export up to 120 million tonnes per year. Source: African Business / Rio Tinto (african.business/2024/02, riotinto.com/operations/africa/simandou).

markers.name: El Teniente Copper Mine, Chile
markers.ctx: The world's largest underground copper mine, with more than 3,000 km of tunnels, run by state-owned Codelco in the Andes east of Rancagua. Industrial mining began in 1906 under the US Braden Copper Company (later Kennecott) before Chile nationalised it in 1971. A collapse after a tremor on 31 July 2025 killed six miners.

markers.name: Weda Bay Nickel Mine, Indonesia
markers.ctx: The world's largest nickel mine (opened October 2019) on Halmahera, feeding the EV battery chain through the Weda Bay Industrial Park. Majority-owned by China's Tsingshan (57% since 2017) with France's Eramet running mining. Reporting links its expansion to deforestation and threats to one of Indonesia's last uncontacted peoples (attributed: Mongabay, VOA).

markers.name: Thacker Pass Lithium Mine, Nevada
markers.ctx: Largest known lithium deposit in the US and one of the largest in the world (Humboldt County). Lithium Americas 62%, General Motors 38%; the Department of Energy took a 5% stake in October 2025. Opposed by Indigenous groups over sacred-land impacts.

markers.name: Kalgoorlie Super Pit (Fimiston Open Pit), Australia
markers.ctx: One of Australia's largest open-pit gold mines, about 3.5 km long, 1.6 km wide and over 675 m deep on the historic Golden Mile, producing about 430,000-460,000 oz of gold a year. Owned by Northern Star Resources since 2020; it consolidated many 1890s underground leases into one pit.

markers.name: World Economic Forum HQ - Cologny, Geneva
markers.ctx: The WEF, founded by Klaus Schwab in 1971, runs from its lakeside headquarters at 91-93 Route de la Capite in Cologny, Geneva. It maintains a top 'Strategic Partner' tier of roughly 100 of the world's largest corporations that pay premium membership fees and shape its agenda. Source: World Economic Forum / Geneva Environment Network (genevaenvironmentnetwork.org).

markers.name: Davos Congress Centre - WEF Annual Meeting, Davos
markers.ctx: The 12,000-square-metre Congress Centre has hosted the World Economic Forum's flagship annual meeting since 1971, drawing around 3,000 heads of state, CEOs and financiers each January under heavy security. The venue can accommodate up to 5,000 participants across a plenum and 34 rooms. Source: Davos Congress Centre — Wikipedia / davos.ch.

markers.name: Chatham House (Royal Institute of International Affairs) - London
markers.ctx: Founded in 1920, Chatham House occupies a Grade I-listed former residence of three British prime ministers at 10 St James's Square, donated to the institute in 1923. It originated the globally used 'Chatham House Rule' of source non-attribution and is consistently ranked among the world's most influential think tanks. Source: Chatham House (chathamhouse.org) / Wikipedia.

markers.name: Munich Security Conference - Hotel Bayerischer Hof, Munich
markers.ctx: Held annually since 1963 at the Hotel Bayerischer Hof, the Munich Security Conference is the world's leading forum on international security policy, gathering heads of state, defense ministers and NATO leadership. Landmark speeches there, including Vladimir Putin's 2007 address, have marked shifts in global geopolitics. Source: Munich Security Conference (securityconference.org) / Wikipedia.

markers.name: Ditchley Foundation - Enstone, Oxfordshire
markers.ctx: The Ditchley Foundation, an Anglo-American educational trust established in 1958 at a 1722 James Gibbs mansion, hosts around twelve private conferences a year of roughly 40 senior figures from politics, business, the military, media and academia. All discussions are held under the Chatham House Rule. Source: Ditchley Foundation (ditchley.com) / Wikipedia.

markers.name: Obelisk of Senusret I (Al-Masalla), Heliopolis, Cairo
markers.ctx: The 20.7 m, roughly 120-ton red-granite obelisk raised by Pharaoh Senusret I around 1940 BC is the oldest standing obelisk in Egypt and the sole surviving element of the great Temple of Ra-Atum at ancient Heliopolis, now swallowed by Cairo's Matariya district. It marks the ancient priestly-solar power center that gave the West its obelisk form. Source: Wikipedia, 'Al-Masalla' / EgyptToday, 'Meet the Obelisk of Senusret I'.

markers.name: Pantheon Obelisk (Macuteo Obelisk), Piazza della Rotonda, Rome
markers.ctx: A 6.34 m Egyptian obelisk bearing Ramesses II's cartouches, from Heliopolis, later in Domitian's sanctuary of Isis; excavated in the 14th or 16th century and set on the fountain before the Pantheon by Pope Clement XI in 1711. One of the 13 ancient obelisks in Rome.

markers.name: Tower of the Juche Idea (Juche Tower), Pyongyang
markers.ctx: Completed 1982 for Kim Il Sung's 70th birthday, this 170 m granite spire is the tallest granite structure in the world, built from 25,550 blocks (one per day of the leader's first 70 years) and capped by a 20 m illuminated metal torch - a state monument to the ruling Juche ideology. Source: Wikipedia, 'Juche Tower'.

markers.name: Monument to the People's Heroes, Tiananmen Square, Beijing
markers.ctx: A 37.94 m granite obelisk built 1952-58 at the exact center of Tiananmen Square to honor revolutionary martyrs; designed by architect Liang Sicheng, it later became a focal gathering point during the 1989 pro-democracy protests. Source: Wikipedia, 'Monument to the People's Heroes' / TravelChinaGuide.

markers.name: Karahan Tepe, Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey
markers.ctx: Excavated since 2019, this Pre-Pottery Neolithic ritual complex (c. 9400-8200 BCE) is the 'sister site' of Göbekli Tepe, 35 km east, and part of the Taş Tepeler network of at least a dozen sites; its T-shaped stelae and carved figures push the origins of monumental religion back some 11,000 years, before agriculture. Source: Heritage Daily / Ancient Origins, 'Karahan Tepe'.

markers.name: Machu Picchu, Cusco Region, Peru
markers.ctx: A 15th-century Inca royal estate perched at ~2,430 m on a ridge above the Urubamba valley, unknown to the outside world until Hiram Bingham publicized it in 1911; its precision ashlar masonry and astronomical alignments (e.g. the Intihuatana stone) survive intact. UNESCO World Heritage since 1983. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu'.

markers.name: Çatalhöyük, Çumra, Konya Province, Turkey
markers.ctx: A 9,000-year-old Neolithic proto-city of densely packed mudbrick houses entered through the roof, housing up to ~8,000 people with no streets, elaborate wall paintings and burials beneath the floors - a key site for understanding the origins of settled urban life. UNESCO World Heritage since 2012. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Neolithic Site of Çatalhöyük'.

markers.name: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor / Terracotta Army, Xi'an, China
markers.ctx: The tomb complex of Qin Shi Huang (d. 210 BC), guarded by an estimated 8,000 life-size terracotta soldiers discovered by well-diggers in 1974; the central burial mound, described by historian Sima Qian as containing rivers of mercury, remains unexcavated. UNESCO World Heritage since 1987. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor'.

markers.name: M+ Museum, West Kowloon, Hong Kong
markers.ctx: Asia's largest museum of visual culture opened in November 2021 under the shadow of Hong Kong's National Security Law; pro-Beijing figures pressured it over its collection and it withheld from display Ai Weiwei's 'Study of Perspective: Tiananmen Square,' which the artist cited as evidence the museum is 'clearly under censorship.' Source: ARTnews; South China Morning Post; Al Jazeera.

markers.name: National Museum of Afghanistan, Kabul
markers.ctx: During the 1990s civil war and Taliban rule, an estimated 70% of the museum's roughly 100,000-object collection was looted or destroyed, including some 2,500 statues smashed as idolatrous in 2001; the fabled Bactrian Gold survived, hidden in Central Bank vaults and rediscovered in 2003. Source: Britannica; Artnet News; Science (AAAS).

markers.name: Neue Galerie New York
markers.ctx: The museum's centerpiece is Gustav Klimt's 'Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I' (the 'Woman in Gold'), Nazi-looted from a Jewish Viennese family and restituted to heir Maria Altmann in 2006 after a U.S. Supreme Court case, then bought by museum co-founder Ronald Lauder for a reported $135 million — a landmark in Holocaust art-restitution. Source: The New York Times; Republic of Austria v. Altmann (2004).

markers.name: bet365 Headquarters, Stoke-on-Trent
markers.ctx: Founded in 2000 by Denise Coates from a portable building in a Stoke-on-Trent car park, bet365 grew into one of the world's largest online gambling firms, serving over 90 million customers; Coates has drawn scrutiny for pay packages exceeding £250 million in a single year. Source: CNN; BBC; Wikipedia, 'bet365'.

markers.name: Flutter Entertainment (registered seat), Dublin
markers.ctx: Flutter is the world's largest online betting company, owner of FanDuel, PokerStars, Paddy Power, Betfair and Sky Bet; formed by the 2020 merger of Paddy Power Betfair and The Stars Group, it dominates the U.S. sports-betting market via FanDuel while keeping its registered base in Dublin. Source: Flutter Entertainment (flutter.com); Wikipedia; CNN Business.

markers.name: Hong Kong Jockey Club - Happy Valley Racecourse
markers.ctx: The Jockey Club holds a legal monopoly on Hong Kong betting and is the city's single largest taxpayer, contributing a record HK$35.9 billion to the community in 2022/23; its 2025/26 racing turnover reached HK$143.3 billion, and its charities trust ranks among the world's largest donors. Source: South China Morning Post; Hong Kong Jockey Club (corporate.hkjc.com).

markers.name: Malta Gaming Authority, Kalkara
markers.ctx: Malta licenses much of Europe's online betting. The Daphne Project (OCCRP/IRPI, 2018) documented Italian mafia use of Maltese-licensed sites: a Palermo prosecutor called online gambling an 'ATM with a continuous cash flow' for the clans, and one Cosa Nostra-linked operator, with 'Ndrangheta brokers, grew profits to EUR 16 million a month on Maltese licences. In 2015 the MGA suspended Betuniq and Betsolution4U after an Italian probe; six Italians including 'Ndrangheta point-man Mario Gennaro were arrested. Source: OCCRP (Daphne Project); The Shift News.

markers.name: Illegal Sports-Betting Ring - U.S. Courthouse, Santa Ana
markers.ctx: At this federal courthouse in 2025, Orange County bookmaker Mathew Bowyer was sentenced to a year and a day for running an illegal sports-gambling business used by Shohei Ohtani's interpreter Ippei Mizuhara, who placed at least 19,000 bets and stole nearly $17 million from the MLB star to cover his losses. Source: U.S. Department of Justice (justice.gov); ESPN; Sportico.

markers.name: Entain plc - London office (HQ: Douglas, Isle of Man)
markers.ctx: Entain - owner of Ladbrokes, Coral, bwin and partypoker and co-owner of BetMGM; headquartered in Douglas, Isle of Man. In Dec 2023 it entered the UK's first Crown Prosecution Service deferred prosecution agreement, paying £615 million in total over GVC's failure to prevent bribery (Bribery Act 2010, s.7) in its former Turkish-facing business, 2011-2017. Source: CPS; Wikipedia.

markers.name: Woody Island (Yongxing) - PLA Outpost, Paracel Islands
markers.ctx: Woody Island (Yongxing), the largest of the disputed Paracels and seat of China's Sansha city, hosts an ~8,900-foot military-civil runway able to handle nuclear-capable H-6 bombers, plus reinforced hangars, radar sites and HQ-9 surface-to-air missile batteries, functioning as the administrative and military center of China's South China Sea presence. Source: CSIS (Gregory Poling); Newsweek; Radio Free Asia; CNBC.

markers.name: Željava Underground Air Base (Objekt Klek 505), near Bihać
markers.ctx: Yugoslavia's largest air base and underground hangar, under Plješevica mountain on the Croatia-Bosnia border near Bihać; designed to survive a direct 20-kiloton nuclear hit; four runways, the longest 2,500 m. The withdrawing Yugoslav army blew it up in 1992.

markers.name: Second Thomas Shoal (BRP Sierra Madre) - Spratly Islands
markers.ctx: In 1999 the Philippines deliberately grounded the WWII-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre on the shoal, in response to China's occupation of Mischief Reef; rotating marines still garrison the hull. Chinese coast guard vessels first blocked resupply in March 2014 and have since repeatedly blocked, rammed and water-cannoned Philippine boats (notably 2023-24). Source: Wikipedia, Second Thomas Shoal; CSIS AMTI.

markers.name: IBM Corporate HQ, Armonk, New York
markers.ctx: Headquarters of the company whose founding product was population registration. Herman Hollerith's tabulating machines were built for the 1890 US census; the firm became CTR and then IBM in 1924. The through-line this map follows is not a company's character but a capability - turning a population into a machine-readable index, sold to whoever is doing the registering. See report Section X for the full tiering, including what IBM disputes.

markers.name: IBM Endicott, New York - the origin plant
markers.ctx: Endicott is where IBM's manufacturing began and where the punch card was industrialised - the company town, the 'Homestead', the origin of the culture. The card itself is the artefact worth noticing: a physical object encoding a person as a pattern of holes, sortable at machine speed. Every later capability in this section - the smart-city camera, the licence-plate reader, the biometric index - is the same operation performed faster and without the paper.

markers.name: Dehomag works, Berlin-Lichterfelde (approx.)
markers.ctx: Deutsche Hollerith-Maschinen GmbH - Dehomag - IBM's German subsidiary, whose Berlin plant supplied the tabulating machinery used in Reich census and registration work. Location approximate to the Lichterfelde district. DOCUMENTED: CTR/IBM acquired 90% of Dehomag in 1923, leaving founder Willy Heidinger 10%; Dehomag equipment was used in Nazi census and administrative operations; Thomas J. Watson Sr. accepted Hitler's Merit Cross of the German Eagle with Star in Berlin in 1937 - the first American to receive it - and returned it in June 1940 under sustained pressure. CONTESTED: Edwin Black's 'IBM and the Holocaust' (2001) argues continuous New York knowledge and control through the war; IBM's position is that the subsidiary was seized by the Nazi state and the parent had no control over use. A Feb 2001 Alien Tort suit was voluntarily withdrawn the following month, so the question has never been adjudicated on the merits. Sources: Black (2001); IBM statements; JTA (Mar 2001).

markers.name: Apartheid population register administration, Pretoria
markers.ctx: The administrative centre of South Africa's racial population register - the system that assigned every person a classification and an identity document, and made the pass laws enforceable at scale. From 2002 the Khulumani/Ntsebeza Alien Tort Statute litigation alleged that IBM and Ford purposefully facilitated violations of international law by enabling denationalisation and the suppression that followed. The case ran fourteen years and ended in 2016 when the US Supreme Court declined to hear it - again without any ruling on the merits. TIER: the register and its function are documented history; the corporate-facilitation allegation was pleaded and never adjudicated, and is recorded here as an allegation. Sources: In re South African Apartheid Litigation; GroundUp / Daily Maverick (Jun 2016); Harvard IHRC statement.

markers.name: Kodak Hawkeye Works, 1447 St Paul St, Rochester NY
markers.ctx: Kodak's classified plant, and the reason Rochester belongs in this section. From 1954 Kodak's role was to develop and process the special film flown in the U-2 - built in Burbank - and then in the CORONA reconnaissance satellites. CORONA was operational 1960-72: over 100 spacecraft, more than 800,000 high-resolution images, declassified in February 1995. The returned negative was cut into manageable lengths, titled frame by frame, duplicated onto black-and-white print stock and boxed; a single mission's output shipped out of Rochester by the ton, including the special enlargements prepared to brief the president. THE END OF THE LINE: the NRO flew KH-11, the first American electro-optical satellite, in Dec 1976; the last KH-9 HEXAGON film-return vehicle was lost on launch in 1986. Kodak sold its government business to ITT in 2004, and the photographic operations centres at Hawkeye and Lincoln were gone by 2009. Sources: CIA/NRO CORONA declassification (Feb 1995); Rochester Business Journal (2012); NRO KH-11 record.

markers.name: Eastman Business Park (Kodak Park), Rochester NY
markers.ctx: Kodak's primary photographic manufacturing site since 1890 - the industrial base under both the consumer film business and the classified one. SCALE: Kodak's Rochester employment peaked above 60,000 in 1982; after the January 2012 bankruptcy it is a fraction of that. WHAT OUTLASTED THE INDUSTRY: hazardous-waste releases at the park and into the Genesee River, a $49 million cleanup trust under the bankruptcy settlement, and documented contamination of river sediments, wetland and floodplain soils and biota. Sources: US Attorney SDNY / EPA settlement announcement; NYSDEC Eastman Business Park record; EPA hazardous waste cleanup file.

markers.name: Laboratory for Laser Energetics (OMEGA), University of Rochester
markers.ctx: Established 1970 and funded principally through the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration. The OMEGA laser delivers about 30 kJ from 60 beams onto a millimetre-scale target in under a nanosecond - among the most powerful laser systems in the world - as part of the US inertial-confinement-fusion programme. It anchors a regional optics, photonics and imaging cluster of 150+ companies and roughly 19,000 employees, described in trade coverage as central to US defence readiness. TIER: the laboratory, the laser and the funding line are documented. ICF is dual-use by design - the same physics serves stewardship of the nuclear stockpile and civil fusion research - and this marker asserts nothing beyond that. The point for this map is structural: when Kodak's consumer half collapsed, the optics competence did not leave Rochester, it stayed in the defence-facing institutions. Sources: University of Rochester LLE; NNSA programme documentation; Rochester Business Journal (2025).

markers.name: L3Harris Communications & Spectrum Dominance - 1680 University Ave, Rochester NY
markers.ctx: Segment headquarters of L3Harris Communications & Spectrum Dominance, the Rochester region's largest manufacturer (~3,800 employees, RBJ Aug 2026). Origin: RF Communications, a Rochester radio maker acquired by Harris in 1969; Harris merged with L3 in 2019. Product: the Falcon tactical radio line; in July 2026 Rochester took an $84M US Army order for next-generation Falcon manpacks. The segment's name states what it sells: the electromagnetic spectrum treated as terrain. On 17 Aug 2026 Christopher Aebli (with the company since 1991) became segment president, filling the seat vacated when Sam Mehta, who had led the SMS and CSD segments, became CEO - after the board's investigation found that CEO Christopher Kubasik's conduct was inconsistent with the company's Code of Conduct and he and the company agreed to end his employment (SEC 8-K).

markers.name: L3Harris Technologies HQ - Melbourne, Florida
markers.ctx: Corporate headquarters of L3Harris Technologies, formed by the 2019 merger of Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies; about 47,000 employees (2025). Three reporting segments as of 2026: Space & Mission Systems, Communications & Spectrum Dominance, and Missile Solutions - the last built on Aerojet Rocketdyne (acquired July 2023), the solid-rocket-motor maker, consolidating much of US missile propulsion in one prime; in Jan 2026 it agreed to sell a majority of Aerojet's space propulsion business. On 17 Aug 2026, after a board-led investigation found that chairman and CEO Christopher Kubasik's conduct was inconsistent with the Code of Conduct, he and the company agreed to end his employment, without severance; the 8-K says the conduct did not involve financial reporting, controls, customer relationships or operational performance. Sam Mehta became CEO and Lewis Hay III independent chairman.

markers.name: Arlington Hall Station, Arlington, Virginia
markers.ctx: FOIA-SOURCED (NSA reading room, read 18 Aug 2026). Arlington Hall - a former girls' school seized under wartime powers in 1942 - was the headquarters of NSA's predecessors, the Army Security Agency and the Armed Forces Security Agency, until the move to Fort Meade in the 1950s. It is where the VENONA decryption effort against Soviet cable traffic was run. NSA has declassified over 800 photographs of the site covering the mid-1940s to mid-1950s, with a downloadable photo index, and solicits public help identifying people in them. The campus now houses the State Department's Foreign Service Institute and an Army National Guard facility. Source: NSA Historical Releases - Arlington Hall collection.

markers.name: USS Liberty (AGTR-5) attack position, off Sinai
markers.ctx: 8 June 1967 (position approximate). FOIA-SOURCED (NSA reading room, read 18 Aug 2026). The USS Liberty, a US Navy signals-intelligence ship, was attacked by Israeli aircraft and torpedo boats in international waters during the Six-Day War; 34 Americans were killed and about 171 wounded. NSA's declassified collection runs to 17 pages of material - attack reports, situation summaries, operational orders and authorisation memos, an 'Aftermath of Israeli Attack on USS Liberty, 22 June 1967' report, and contemporaneous press coverage from 11 and 17 June. TIER: the attack, the casualties and the documents are documented; whether the attack was deliberate or a misidentification remains disputed between the US and Israeli official accounts and this map does not settle it. Source: NSA Historical Releases - USS Liberty collection.

markers.name: USS Pueblo (AGER-2) seizure position, off Wonsan
markers.ctx: 23 January 1968 (position approximate). FOIA-SOURCED (NSA reading room, read 18 Aug 2026). North Korean forces seized the US signals-intelligence ship USS Pueblo off the east coast of Korea; one crewman was killed and 82 were held for eleven months. NSA released 19 pages of material in July 2021, including 'Lessons Learned' reports comparing the Pueblo and EC-121 incidents, NSA response and action reports, cryptologic-impact assessments, SIGINT reflections covering 23-26 January 1968, and documentation of attempts to recover the material lost with the ship. The Pueblo is still held by North Korea and is moored in Pyongyang as a museum - the only commissioned US Navy vessel in foreign captivity. Source: NSA Historical Releases - USS Pueblo collection.

markers.name: C-130 60528 shootdown site, Sasnashen, Soviet Armenia
markers.ctx: 2 September 1958. FOIA-SOURCED (NSA reading room, read 18 Aug 2026). Soviet MiG-17 pilots shot down a US Air Force reconnaissance-configured C-130 over Soviet Armenia; all 17 crew were lost. NSA released roughly 13 documents in July 2021 - incident reports, Russian-language intercept transcripts with translations of the fighter pilots' own radio traffic during the engagement, audio files, crew and casualty records, and a survey of reconnaissance incidents 1949-1960. The intercepted cockpit traffic is the reason this case is unusual: the shootdown is documented from inside the attacking formation's own communications. Source: NSA Historical Releases - C130 Shootdown collection.

markers.name: Bigelow Aerospace / BAASS, North Las Vegas, Nevada
markers.ctx: FOIA-SOURCED (DIA reading room; contract-status PDF text extracted directly, 18 Aug 2026). Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) held DIA aerospace contract HHM402-08-C-0072 under the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP/AATIP). DIA's own status brief records: performance 'has been excellent and they are in full compliance'; 12 project management plans and 26 detailed research reports delivered by 30 June 2009 - 'twice minimum requirement'; '$12 million for the continuation of this contract by DIA/DI has been submitted in the FY10 defense budget'; the contracting officer extended the contract to 30 September at no additional cost, and BAASS indicated willingness to operate 'at risk' in option year 1 until FY10 funds arrived. Deliverable titles include Warp Drives, Wormholes in Space Time, Antigravity Studies, Metamaterials and Invisibility, Brain-Machine Interfaces, and Field Effects on Biological Tissues; one author organisation survives redaction as Sandia. Redactions are marked (b)(3):10 USC 424, the statute shielding DIA organisational detail. TIER: the contract, the money and the report titles are documented in DIA's own release; the existence of recovered craft is NOT documented by any of it. Source: DIA FOIA reading room, AAWSAP/AATIP collection, Aerospace_Contract_Status_Bigelow_Aerospace_Advanced_Space_Studies.pdf.

markers.name: Defense Intelligence Agency HQ, Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling, DC
markers.ctx: FOIA-SOURCED (DIA reading room, read 18 Aug 2026). DIA headquarters, and the agency whose electronic reading room holds the AAWSAP/AATIP collection: 53 released items covering the Bigelow contract chain and 37 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on subjects from inertial electrostatic confinement fusion to traversable wormholes. The collection also holds the paper trail of Senator Harry Reid's interest - memos on his visit to DIA, and his letter to the Deputy Secretary of Defense seeking Special Access Program status for the effort, which was reviewed and, per the same file series, not granted in the form requested. Other DIA reading-room collections indexed the same day: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, POWs/MIA/Detainees, Weapons Development and Proliferation, China Mission Group, and annual FOIA request logs 2001-2023. Source: DIA FOIA Electronic Reading Room.

markers.name: Welding shop shooting - Miami, Florida
markers.ctx: 8/20/1982. Venue type: other. Killed: 8. Injured: 3. Total victims: 11. Junior high school teacher Carl Robert Brown, 51, opened fire inside a welding shop and was later shot dead by a witness as he fled the scene. Source: Mother Jones mass-shootings dataset (1982-2026); row sources: http://www.nytimes.com/1982/08/21/us/gunman-in-miami-kills-8-in-rampage.html; http://www.nytimes.com/1982/08/24/us/no-ch....

markers.name: Dallas nightclub shooting - Dallas, Texas
markers.ctx: 6/29/1984. Venue type: other. Killed: 6. Injured: 1. Total victims: 7. Abdelkrim Belachheb, 39, opened fire at an upscale nightclub after a woman rejected his advances. He was later arrested. Source: Mother Jones mass-shootings dataset (1982-2026); row sources: http://books.google.com/books?id=Hr3OBwP-lbUC&pg=PA38&lpg=PA38&dq=Abdelkrim+Belachheb+mental&source=bl&ots=D56pgdNnnl&si....

markers.name: San Ysidro McDonald's massacre - San Ysidro, California
markers.ctx: 7/18/1984. Venue type: other. Killed: 22 (MJ count, includes the perpetrator; 21 victims killed). Injured: 19. Total victims: 41. James Oliver Huberty, 41, opened fire in a McDonald's restaurant before he was shot dead by a police officer. Source: Mother Jones mass-shootings dataset (1982-2026); row sources: http://www.utsandiego.com/san-ysidro-massacre/; http://www.vpc.org/studies/wgun840718.htm.

markers.name: United States Postal Service shooting - Edmond, Oklahoma
markers.ctx: 8/20/1986. Venue type: workplace. Killed: 15 (MJ count, includes the perpetrator; 14 victims killed). Injured: 6. Total victims: 21. Postal worker Patrick Sherrill, 44, opened fire at a post office before committing suicide. Source: Mother Jones mass-shootings dataset (1982-2026); row sources: http://news.google.com/newspapers?id=dm8aAAAAIBAJ&sjid=pyoEAAAAIBAJ&pg=2297,4870051&dq=patrick+sherrill&hl=en.

markers.name: Shopping centers spree killings - Palm Bay, Florida
